I will admit that I have a weird sort of soft spot for Call of Duty. It's an absurdly simple franchise that never changes, but it never tries to appeal outside its target demographic. And hey, Black Ops 2 was surprisingly decent. So Ghosts could've been good, right?
The key word here is "could".
Ghosts is a ♥♥♥♥ing trainwreck. The campaign is awful, 4 hours long, and poorly written to the point where we've finally reached the stage where the villains literally are faceless brown people. The multiplayer is broken to hell and back with its spawn points and god-awful netcode. The lag compensation that hampers a player's experience is amped up to a degree in which it's never been in the Call of Duty franchise.
Oh, and the porting job. This is one of the absolute worst PC ports of all time. It doesn't look good, it runs like garbage on any setup, and it's filled to the brim with micro-stuttering and frame skipping. If you want to jump through the billion hoops this game requires to achieve a smooth gameplay experience, all you will get yourself is a drab and boring rehash. Everything Treyarch attempted to freshen up the series, Nu-Infinity Ward retracted. Stay far away from this.

Same Call of Duty mechanic. For all of you run and gun lovers, this game is more action packed than ever. So if you liked Call of Duty before, don't hesitate to buy this one. If however you didn't or you think that they should have improved, then the 'improvements' are rather small.
Singleplayer packs a nice, short, concentrated storyline. No spoilers. It has a brave attempt at a briliant attachment between characters, but the short missions and many characters leave it, sadly, lacking (compared to the previous great story, Modern Warfare).
Multiplayer is much more focused on the soldier and him on the ground. The killstreaks stay in the same mechanic as in Modern Warfare 3, where you have the Assault, Support and Specialist Strike Packages. Some new addition to it is the fact that you don't have only classes, but you have a soldier that wears those classes. In total you can unlock (through in-game money purchase - which I find unnecessary; I hate the pricing on Call of Duty titles) ten soldiers, visually customizable and levelable. You theoretically prestige your individual soldiers.
A new addition is Squads. A 'co-op like' part of the game, in which you (and your friends, if you have any) team up and level up your (like in you, not them) squad, in different game modes, that include:
Facing of a team of bots (variable difficulty) on Multiplayer game-modes;
Fighting with your AI Squad against another player and their AI Squad (not party allowed).
Survivor mode: facing endless waves of enemy AI and scavaging the environment.
This new 'addition' is quite nice to spend the time on - but it relies on friends to be enjoyable.
Brand new Extinction mode, isn't much innovative, it's sort of like zombies, but it takes a different approach to the way the enemies behave. You fight aliens which are much more agile.
The difficulty on this mode cannot be set and is, in my oppinion, abominably hard. Playing it alone would be suicide (as in, you would stroke out due to anger). I'm saying this, having played all previous Call of Duty games on Veteran as my favorite difficulty.
This game is a lot of fun, especially with some friends.
It does not elude the Call of Duty genre, so make sure you did like the previous (non-futuristic) installments. If so, you might enjoy this, on a Steam Sale, perhaps.
Hope you enjoyed the review, and I hope I stayed as objective as possible.

At first I wasn't interested in this game, because of its conveluted introduction. The start is well written from a story perspective, but it just threw too much at me in one go. It went from realistic to arcadey pretty quickly. Having never played a Far Cry game before, I thought it had a severe learning curve. There are a lot of game mechanics to get used to very suddenly. However, once I got over that initial shock, I began to really enjoy the varied gameplay.
Anyone who has played a Ubisoft game before will recognise a number of game mechanics that they often use in other games. I saw aspects that I have seen in Splinter Cell, Assasin's Creed and Watch_Dogs. There's stealth, action, platforming, exploration, side missions that are fun arcade style games. It has a whole lot of everything thrown into one game.
The story is extremely well written. I went from hating the main character and his friends to caring about them, and even respecting Jason by the end. Even though there's only one meaningful choice  in the game, it still felt like I was the one pushing the story on -instead of just being dragged through a story.

With a huge open world to explore and many intelligent and ruthless enemies (including the local wildlife) to make that exploration difficult, Far Cry 3 has many many hours of entertainment and satisfying gunplay to get absorbed in. The day/night cycle, the beautiful islands and the effects from the array of weaponry are all a fantastic sight. The satisfaction to be had from 'liberating' an outpost by stealthily doing some recon and tagging all the soldiers before picking them off one by one is equally as much fun as doing it the less subtle way. Enemy AI is intelligent enough to not make it that easy for you to just run off in to the woods and hope they leave you alone, making for some very intense moments waiting for them to step on the tiger instead of you.
The slight disappointment with this game was the main story. At times dark and sombre, at others just downright strange, and with the odd moment of humour it was as though the game didn't quite know what it wanted to be. It was fun, and the hunt for the psychopathic Vaas has some fantastic character portrayal to keep you entertained but the whole thing culminates in a somewhat unsatisfying ending, leaving you to wonder what the hell just happened. You're left to scrambling around the islands to mop up the side missions and do the grind of finding relics and other inconsequential items. Overall though there is plenty to like about Far Cry 3, and I will probably give it a play through again at some stage, on a higher difficulty as the challenge of taken down outposts is worth it alone.

Far Cry 3 is like your favourite action movie. It has snipers, exploding vehicles, and a maniacal villain named Vaas. Already this may sound like a clichéd shooter, but Far Cry 3 does so many things well, that it’s hard not to dive back into its world again.

Along your perilous journey, you will climb up a radio tower, cover yourself in magical tattoos, and drive a quad-bike into a river. All of these elements, while definitely daredevilish, don’t feel out of place in Far Cry 3. The map is vast, and allows you to explore to your heart’s content. Hunt wild animals to collect their skin, or liberate enemy outposts to gain respect amongst the civilians. In Far Cry 3, it’s completely up to your how you approach situations.
Beneath the crazy guise that Ubisoft paints with Far Cry 3, lies a character that actually cares. Jason Brody, along with his other twentysomething friends, travel to the remote Rook Islands, for a holiday. But all is not what it seems. Vaas, a psychopathic leader of Rook Island, captures Jason and his friends. Jason escapes, but his other friends are not with him. Jason must meet with local islanders to find his friends and go home. Playing Far Cry 3, I thought Jason was an excellent character with a determined, hard-working spirit, who wants nothing but to keep his friends safe.

Vaas is a wonderful villain, with humour, but also a sort of finess on how he handles situations. The strange calmness he portrays is intimidating, but at the same time, left me uneasy. He is definitely a unique character, and one that I welcomed into the game. The only this is, Vaas seemed to swear a lot, often too much. This took away from his character slightly, and was one of the only disappointments I had with this game.

Far Cry 3’s gameplay is diverse, entertaining and never gets old. One moment, you will be fighting for your life setting pirates on fire, and the next you will be jumping out of a plane in a wingsuit. All of these never felt nuanced or out of place, and whether you are using a keyboard and mouse or a controller, the controls are easy to pick up, and similar to other games of its genre.
The game’s campaign mode is quite long, and lasted me around twelve to fourteen hours. While it is definitely the main aspect of Far Cry 3, after you finish your missions on Rook Island, there are still so many other places to explore and new things to discover. Loot is found everywhere throughout the vast map, hidden in crates. Bodies can also contain money and trinkets, which can be sold for money at stores. Plants are also found on the minimap, each a different colour. I found the Green Leaves especially useful for crafting important medical syringe kits, which have saved me from death countless times.
The customization of weapons in Far Cry 3 is amazing. If you really want to, you can add a Red Dot Sight to a .44 Magnum handgun, or an extended magazine to an ACE assault rifle. All of these can also be customized with decals and camos, letting you find the weapons that are more suited to your play style. You can equip an M249 SAW, an LMG, and a LPO-50 Flamethrower and torch the lot, or go in silently with a silenced Z93 and a Recurve Bow with a Reflex Sight. In Far Cry 3, it’s completely your choice.
Vehicles in Far Cry 3 could have been much improved. There were only three “classes” of vehicles, like the army-like 4WDs or the sedans and quad bikes. These all handle basically the same, and I personally am not a fan of first-person driving and was disappointed you couldn’t change this. Also, vehicles are scarce around Rook Island, and I was often without a ride and sprinting for ages to get to a destination in time.
Overall, Far Cry 3 is an amazingly diverse, creative and humongous first-person adventure, and one that will keep you glued to your monitor in excitement and anticipation as it shows you a fantastically good time.

I'm a first person shooter junkie and I can't resist getting my hands on every decent FPS I see. Since I fell in love with the original Call of Duty years ago (the original that was actuallly a TRUE PC TITLE) I've been faithful to the series (on PC only of course.) Throughout the years it turned into a yearly re-hash using the same engine feeling like glorified map packs and very short campaigns. Since I enjoy the single player portion of games primarily I was very disappointed for the last several years in the CoD franchise although I stuck with it because I support PC gaming and since the roots of CoD essentially went to consoles the fact that us PC gamers at least got semi-decent ports kept me coming back for more. The last 3-4 installments in the franchise were very mediocre kind of like watching a glitzy Michael Bay movie that you just can't get into the plot. This new one is no exception however they did seem to get the single player portion feeling right this time and to me it was the best CoD single player since CoD1 which is a huge compliment in my book. As I said earlier I could care less about multiplayer but this time I reallly enjoyed the SP and finally feel the purchase was validated. Even though I finished the game in less than 7 hours and I really really took my time playing through itI feel satisfied and recommend it to other players who love a fun solo campaign. I'll most likely play it in a harder difficulty sometime in the future but for now I'm done with it. Hopefully they will continue making better solo campaigns as Ghosts was and I might actually become a fan again. Just for note: I purchased the game at $40,00 because of coupons I had and at that price I'm satisfied... at $60.00 I'd be much less willing to recommend it at that price range.

Single-player: Like basically every Call Of Duty, the single-player portion is solid. The story is pretty long this time, around 8-9 hours and there's plenty of variation. But there's no story branching like in Black Ops 2, so in a way it's actually a step back. Since the story is about two brothers you can actually relate to them, more so than the previous games anyway. The game also ends with a nice cliffhanger.
The graphics have been upgraded, but it's nothing game changing. Yes, the textures are sharper and there's more color, but it's still no Battlefield 4.
In the end it looks like Infinity Ward played safe by not changing the formula too much. Treyarch has actually become the better developer between the two. At least they try to improve their games.
Multi-player: Terrible. The past COD games were way, way better. The connections suck, there's lag, giving other plays quite the advantage. The maps are dull, there's a lot of spawnkilling (spawnpoints were actually handled extremely well in the previous CODs) and the maps are too big. I hate it. Battlefield 4 has become my new multiplayer game for now, hell, even I was surprised it had to come to this.
I don't expect Infinity Ward to patch things, considering the patches they made for their other games (practically non-existent). Again, take a look at Treyarch, Infinity. Their games *work*.
In other words: Call Of Duty Ghosts is quite the disappointment.

This is not a good game and I'm going to help you understand why.
You don't know until the combat starts but your charcter has X-Ray vision eye-balls. Yes. Really.
Once you shoot an enemy all his movment and location are highlighted to you, meaning if the enemy runs away to hide behind a wall you can still clearly see him highlighted.
The game has no immersion what so ever. Allow me a moment to explain.
It's a 'Sandbox Game' that isn't a Sandbox at all. This is not Skyrim with guns.
The game presents a huge island to explore. Unless you have a mission to do.
Then your charcter teleports back to the start of the mission you were on. Leaving you feeling like the game slaps you on the hand and says "Bad player. Get back on track!!"
The game is too easy and to run in shooting has almost no downsides what so ever as landing a head shot rewards just as much XP as a sleath kill.
This game treats the player as an idiot in many different ways. As far as I can tell it's impossible to fail a mission.
Yep.. did a bad job sneeking up on that enemy? who cares!!! Not skilled enough to stealth? Who cares!! You can't fail the missionsl!! This game treats you like an idiot.
All the bad guys use the AK47 which means after you pick one up you're never worrying about ammo agian. Non of the guns seem to have recoil.
The game looks very impressive but a quarter of the screen is taken up by a Mini map you can never toggle off and if you're on a mission you better believe the mission description takes up the left hand side of your HUD too.
Farcry 3 cleverly tricks the player by using what I can only describe as a 'fake distance'. Meaning although you can clearly see mountains and such in the background the actual local area visable is only ever quite limited but disguised in quite a clever way, even on Ultra graphics settings.
As a console port the FOV is a decent 110, along with Direct X11 and Ultra graphic settings do make the game look very nice. However in the middle of a thick jungle at night time without lamps and such it isn't actually dark.
The game allows Alt tabbing, but don't expect to be able to play it once you've tabbed back in. It becomes unplayable.
Aside from some good visuals and good charcters (the main bad guy is actually really decent and intresting) the game is weak in so many areas. I'm glad i picked it up for £3.75 last Christmas. I would have been devastated to pay full price for this effort.
Avoid it and play a better shooter unless you're after a pretty looking no brainer FPS to hold your hand as you play.

The german tanker comes stock with the mp34 and the pz1.Then we have the fighter piolts who fly around in planes bombing anything of the ground. I do not have any personal expenriance with the fighter piolt, but i believe that there are 2 diffrent types of planes you can choose from, and a veriaty of planes in each type. There is also a recon class which is basicly a sniper. Then there are the generals, which is the rts part of the game, which i dont care about. last but not least we have the paratroper which i believe is the exact same as the infantry exept they spawn jumping out of planes.
I would recommend this highly. Also to note there are no OVERPOWERD items that can be bought. Only one problem. Macrotransactions (Not a typo).

Many free to play games suffer a huge problem: Pay to win. You won't find that here. The game provides you with ample Credits to work with if you stick with the game because you recieve and increasingly large quanity of cash for match completion has you rise in rank, regardless of your proformance (For you filthy casuals), and even the "Paid for" currency can be obtained at a rate of 5 gold per day, so long as you play a match once a day, Now that might be slow, but it still offers the abillity to buy "Paid" content without paying. And even if you are saying "I don't want to grind 5 gold a day to unlock features" there is still the fact that almost everything in the game can be bought with the credit currency, If you want an itme early, before you qualify to use it or such things, you can buy it, but after playing the game for a while, I can say that no peice of equipment is any much better than any other piece of gear unless you upgrade it, and unlocking an upgrade tier cannot be done through gold (Even though the upgrades themselves can be bought) so even if you blew, lets say....200 USD's on the game, and bugh absolutely EVERYTHING you wanted, you might not be any better off then that player down the road with the sniper he went through the time to buy with his battle credits, learn how to properly use it through gameplay, and unlock the various upgrade tiers for it. But the Free to play system is only one small bit of the game, the class system is pretty unique, and rewards players for choosing a specialization (Can be a bit risky since they have only certain items they can use and can be defeated as units more easily). For example, at the cost of loosing the abillity to use most weapons, the tank crewman can buy devastating tanks that can rip apart infantry, making the invaluable for crowd control and defence, but usless in the offensive game for doing things such as capping points, since getting out of the tank to run inside and cap a point is suicide for a tank crewman, who likely has no weapon (You can take in an SMG, but the SMG you can take that uses less then 6 inventory slots costs quite a penny) The vehicle system is prety nice, I like the idea that you need to repair and refill your vehicles, and I think the prices they set up for doing so are fair, if not a bit of a steal in favor of the player, considering how much use you are getting out of them, and the Weapon system makes be very happy, since unlike every other FPS F2P, Once you buy a weapon it's yous, and there is not crappy maintenance function for your weapons, not even a hybrid version of the balanced maintence seen in their own vehicle system, however I will mention that you DO need to repair MODS you put of your weapons, which, just like with vehicle repairs, are dirt cheap. You will also need to replenish your ammo reserves, or you might find yourself charging into battle with no bullets, but yet again, The ammunition for everything is dirt cheap (Grenades being the possible exclusion, since the higher tier grenades can cost quite a bit), which makes me feel like the ammo and repair system isn't really so much a job, or nagging task you need to do, but a tool for immersion. And speaking of immersion, BIKES DIRTBAG, BIKES. Yes, bikes. Go look up some footage of the bike functions. It is literally one of the best features in the game, not because the game is bad, but because if the bikes didn't exist, Infantry would never show up on time to capture points, and the game would take itself far to seriously. The bikes are literally the way the game reminds us it's a game, it brings unspoken comedy into the battlefield. The Jeeps can do somethins similar, when you consider they can carry, like, I don't now, 12 FREAKING PEOPLE. Did I mention those same jeeps only have four seats and a gunner's table? Next bit; Unlocking. Not going to lie, unlocking guns and such is a chore. a huge chore, They cost exhorbant ammounts of credits, and some require ribbons to be unlocked, but the game, once again, rewards loyalty. As I mentioned before, with the more XP and rank you gain, the more credits you will earn, so as long as you just sit back and play, you will find that unlocking what you want will become progressively easier. Finally finished the campaign and write a review.   FYI I am a COD fan and as such perhaps too forgiving of what some people hate about the series.
So, if you hate COD Ghosts is not going to win you over. However, having said that I still think its a very solid entry into the series. It has its up and downs, but I would give a very solid 8.5/10.
It has an innovative story of a potential future.  It is interesting to play the SP. The characters are still generic or atleast over-used cliche. And the plot device of the single ueber-villian who won't die is really starting to get on my nerves. They come up with a super Tom Clancy-esqe story and then they have to ram in mr-sobstory, evil guy who seems to out-whit you at every turn. I hated that in previous games, here too.
MP is ok this time around. I like how at launch the assault rifles seem to trump smgs. So its pretty much curtains for the run-and-gun players. You have to move slowly and watch your angles. CQ maps are still ruled by the smg though. Overall, I prefered Black Ops 2's MP to ghosts. It just felt meatier.
Now, the best part IMO. The extinction mode. This time around, no zombies, just aliens. Its a ton of fun to play, almost like its own game. Plenty of people playing, not like zombies which was too hard and lost 90% of players.
Final verdict. All pc players should play it. In the end, if you Ignore a juggernaut like COD just out of spite, you are the only one loosing out. IMHO. there is no monthly fee (yet) like on an mmorpg so its super value for your buck.

Alright, I'm sorry for my first review. I made myself look like an idiot by NOT listing anything I found wrong with it. I am sincerely sorry for the stupid review. I will revise it now.
Pros:
- Weapons are pretty cool-looking and are of decent variety.
- The second mission of the campaign is decent.
- Decent-looking camos.
- The new Create-A-Soldier is a VERY good system. First, it allows players to make 10 totally unique soldiers (the first one is free, the second through fifth are 3 Squad Points each, in my case anyway) with their own weapon loadouts and each being prestige-able. Second, it allows players to play with any soldier they want to, whether it's one they've already prestiged (in that case, it would usually be for the sole purpose of getting more Squad Points to progress their low level soldiers easier) or a lowbie they're working on to get another prestige.
- Nice variety of challenges to complete. Always gives you something to work towards.
Cons:
- Runs awfully on a computer that should run it on high-ultra with no problems. I can NOT stress this enough that this should be an immediate turn-off from the game. Don't believe me? Look up "TotalBiscuit WTF Is Call of Duty: Ghosts" on YouTube and see what TB has to say about it.
- Field of View is locked at 65 with no way to adjust the FoV without downloading and using a 3rd party hack to change it. I recommend FoVely and 80 FoV if you hate 65 FoV.
- Game has a tendency to crash for no particular reason.
- Cheaters (FoV-Changer users not included) make up a good 50-75% of the game's current population. This is INSANE with the amount of money and resources Activision and IW have at their disposal.
- The developers (IW) were too lazy to actually make the copy-and-paste CoD we know Ghosts to be, so they hired multiple 3rd party developers (including Treyarch, Raven Studios [I think that's their name], and Sledgehammer Games) to do it for them. You can tell, too.
- Requires a 28 GB install (was supposed to be 50 GB, but apparently that was a lie). What is the 28 GB for? Dog A.I.?
- Developers have the guts to LIE directly to the PC community's face. I can easily think of 2 things they lied to us about. 1. Call of Duty: Ghosts is a next-gen experience, improving on everything CoD. FALSE. Ghosts actually plays worse than BO2 and WaW did (admittingly, WaW didn't play that badly, but enough that it was my 3rd least-favorite CoD in terms of gameplay), and BO2 was also quite bad. 2. Ghosts has the next-gen Anti-Cheat matched by nothing else. FALSE. There has been and will never be an anti-cheat of Ghosts. Even after at least 1-2 months, the game STILL has no anti-cheat. There were rumors of PunkBuster being integrated into Ghosts, but this was never confirmed and was never actually implemented. 3. CoD would have next-gen graphics. FALSE. The graphics look like they were from 2000. 4. Server browsers and servers. FALSE. They instead released it and only revealed that they lied and used a hybrid system, much like BO2's. If you played BO2, you know how bad it is, like I do.
- Frequent stuttering.
Overall, NEVER buy this game. This game isn't even worth the 99-cent bin at stores like WalMart and Target. Oh, by the way, I forgot to add something that will help sway you. The MetaCritic review was a 78, more than BO2. The MetaCritic USER reviews were a 0.2 or 0.6, something like that. Hmm, the paid-off MetaCritics gave a game that was absolute CRAP a 78 and the USER reviews (the only reviews you should look at) were a 0.6. Anything suspicious?
By the way, I have around 110 hours on the Multiplayer and about 15 minutes on the Single Player. Sorry if this caused any confusion.

So, you start as this frat kid with an older army frat brother and, really, things stay fratty the entire game. In the course of several days you go from this kid who probably doesn't know how to properly fire a gun, to a kid who can throw a knife into someones skull from the distance of 20 feet. Then again, escaping logic, traditionally, is something incredibly common in videogames and doesn't necessarily make a game bad. It was probably developed this way to try to find common ground with its primary target audience - but the other far cry installments were not like this. Really, parts of it were very anticlimactic for me but the gameplay all in all is great and offers a lot of leeway on how you as the player chooses to go about it.

There I was, side by side with my fellow grenadiers, as we tried to push across a bridge while under heavy American fire. Tank shells bombarded both sides, and my comrades fell, one by one. We held out though, our reinforcements were too much for the Yankees. As I broke from cover to move up, the man next to me took a bullet to the head, and he fell forward, flat onto his face. He fell forward. This shot had come from behind. I ducked behind a cobblestone wall, and worked up the courage to take a peek to our rear. I waited, and I watched. After what had felt like hours, but in reality was no more than a few minutes, I saw the flash of the muzzle and heard another German skull crack. He was in a small woodland storage shack, set up in a second level window. I gathered myself, and then bolted towards the woods and dove behind a rock. After hearing the ricochet of the round off of the stone I darted again, this time making it to the broad side of the building, where he had no line of sight. I crept slowly towards the door of the structure, my heart pounding fifty times every second. I braced against the cold, stone wall, just next to the wooden door frame. My breathing was heavy, and I prepared myself for the end. After what felt like an eternity, I quickly peeked my head in for a glimpse, and felt my heart fall down into my stomach. I pushed myself off the wall and hit the deck. I heard the handle and pin patter on the stone floor of the building, and I feared that my luck had finally run out. The blast peppered me with shrapnel, I felt the searing burn of hot metal scattered about the right side of my body. I wasn't sure how badly I was hurt, but I forced myself back onto my feet, and slipped as quietly as possible around the corner. I kept my rifle, a standard issue Gewehr 43, trained on his window, hoping that for some improbable reason he would peak his head directly into my sights. After several moments I rationalized that I was dealing with a sniper, trained in the art of patience. I would have to make the move. I snuck around to the opposite end of the building, and mustered enough bravery to peek into the door. I instantly ducked back, but I had seen enough. To my relief, there was a wall in the middle of the building, dividing the structure in half. I saw that there were flimsy planks covering the rafters, acting as a crude second story floor, in the same fashion as the other half had, where the sniper was positioned. More notably, I also saw that there was a ladder and a sizeable gap in the wall, on the second level. I planned to sneak up there and try to get him through the opening. I stepped around into the doorway, and to my horror, his eyes were peering down on me through the hole. Shockingly, he looked just as surprised as I was. I regained myself and raised my rifle, quickly, lined up my sigh- BANG. The shot shook my whole body. I felt my eyes clinch shut, my shoulder rattle. After a moment, I forced myself to open my eyes. The shot had landed right between his eyes. I claimed his rifle as my own, then sat out and enjoyed the cool, countryside breeze.

I do like the graphics and general gameplay of Ghosts, especially the single player. If you liked the other CoD games then you'll like this. The levels are fun to play and keep the general action theme to them.
You get to run around in tanks and helicopters and even control the loki satelite at the end to blow lots of stuff up. If you like action it won't let you down, although the story takes an odd dive here and there but its just trying to set it up for the next one. I don't know if I'll be as hyped about Ghosts II.
Though as always its let down by its lag in the PvP multiplayer. With no proper dedicated servers you end up with hosts disconnecting, lag and dying a lot from enemies you don't even see until the killcam shows you they stabbed you in the face.
The idea behind the Co-Op multiplayer is very nice with the alien infestation and the survival mode. It gets very tricky and a good team is needed to see the levels through to the end. If you don't know people to play with and make your own team it can be very frustrating with people disconnecting or not doing what they are supposed to, to complete challenges to complete achievements or just to make it through to the end.
I'll be very blunt... it isn't worth the money I paid for it for the enjoyment. I'd recommend waiting till it goes on sale but knowing CoD games they never get discounted much.

If you've ever wanted to be a medieval warlord, then this is the game for you. Deck your character out in armor, load yourself up with weaponry, and engage in up-close, hand-to-hand combat using a twitch-based swordplay system that simulates realistic medieval fencing. You can operate solo or with a small band of guards, or build yourself the biggest personal army possible by engaging in battle and increasing your Renown. Your main character (along with a number of recruitable heroes) benefits from a RPG-style leveling system, allowing you to gain strength and new abilities as you hack your way through bandits, raiders, deserters, and even opposing military forces.
The realistic fantasy world of Calradia is an open sandbox that provides many different viable options for you to increase your fame and fortune amongst the nobility of the lands; there are seven different factions in control of different pieces of the country, and each of them has need of traders, vigilantes, vassals, and mercs as they wage war against each other in an endless cycle of conquest and carnage. You can ally yourself with one faction, sell your services to the highest bidder, or even conquer territory and create your own kingdom to rival the others.

. Das Kampfsystem. Für mich ist das das entscheidende und kein anderes Spiel hat etwas vergleichbares zu bieten. Wer M&B kennt muss sich diesbezüglich an Warband ersteinmal gwöhnen aber nach kurzer Zeit ist klar das hier eindeutig verbessert und verfeinert wurde. Egal ob Single oder Multiplayer, das rockt!
2. Multiplayer. Ich bin persönlich ein Fan von Multiplayer Games, Warband ist da keine große Ausnahme. Es ist extrem schwierig und fordernd gegen gute andere Spieler zu kämpfen, besonders im Nahkampf. Wenn man aber erst einmal den Bogen raus hat, gibt es kein halten mehr (heisst nicht, dass man unbedingt extrem viel Zeit damit verbringt. Die Spiele gehen schnell rum und es ist gut möglich, Abends mal eben für eine Stunde zu zocken). Insgesamt sind Waffen, Truppen und die meisten Karten (vor allem Siege) sehr gut ausbalanciert.
Dabei gibt es die ähnlich einem Shooter üblichen Gamemodes: Battle, Siege, Deathmatch, Teamdeathmatch, Capture The Flag..., die sich sehr unterschiedlich spielen.

If you've ever wanted to be a medieval warlord, then this is the game for you. Deck your character out in armor, load yourself up with weaponry, and engage in up-close, hand-to-hand combat using a twitch-based swordplay system that simulates realistic medieval fencing. You can operate solo or with a small band of guards, or build yourself the biggest personal army possible by engaging in battle and increasing your Renown. Your main character (along with a number of recruitable heroes) benefits from a RPG-style leveling system, allowing you to gain strength and new abilities as you hack your way through bandits, raiders, deserters, and even opposing military forces.
The realistic fantasy world of Calradia is an open sandbox that provides many different viable options for you to increase your fame and fortune amongst the nobility of the lands; there are seven different factions in control of different pieces of the country, and each of them has need of traders, vigilantes, vassals, and mercs as they wage war against each other in an endless cycle of conquest and carnage. You can ally yourself with one faction, sell your services to the highest bidder, or even conquer territory and create your own kingdom to rival the others.

As a F2P FPS, I'm pleased with the amount of detail and work invested into the game. But as such, it is a given that many features are priviledged to the paying player, therefore having early access to tanks, planes and whatnot. The fact that everything can simply be bought through micro-transactions greatly undermines any effort put in by the non-paying player, which ironically reminiscences real war-time when the person who had the gold dictated the flow of the battle.
The biggest flaw of the game, is undoubtedly the weapons available to the player. I believe that the arsenal of weapons available to soldiers far outnumber a mere 10 weapons, a few of which barely differ from another, (this is the best one) and one that simply has a scope added on it, that costs twice its counterpart. The power of the machine gun is suprisingly underwhelming, given that it was known as a terror on the battlefield, decimating enemy forces.
Additionally, in trying to create the atmostphere of a large-scale battlefield, there is hardly enough infantrymen on the fields, each lobby only making up a total of 40 players at most, which does not simulate nearly as large-scale a battle as it would seem. A way to circumvent this, is by adding AI-soldiers, and allowing squad leaders more power over the control of their troops, instead of only choosing 'attack' and 'defend' points.
Regardless, the game is enjoyable and the many facets of war available to the player makes for a very diversified gameplay.

I beat it today, and I am sure glad I waited for it to be on sale.
Once the initial shock value of the introduction wears off, the story begins to get very predictable in Ubisoft fashion as they follow a traditional three act structure. You start being able to say things that will happen before they happen, they heavily forshadow everything that occurs. I liked the reluctant hero angle, but once the open world begins Jason is basically more talented than any previous far cry protagonist. The ending is a typical good/bad decision they sort of foreshadow constantly once the third act begins. I hate how every boss fight is just context button whack a mole, it removes a lot of the closure provided by finishing them off; not to forget the trippy "beast inside" theme that makes Jason hallucinate during these fights.
Onto the actual game itself. There are fun and annoying mechanics, FC3 was apperently made in the item collection boom when Ubisoft decided every game requires hundreds of tiny insignificant items to collect for no real reason. Once you get in the hundreds of a single type of item I must collect, I quickly lose interest. The radio tower activity is boring, the final towers are frustrating, and in general is padding derived from Assassins Creed. It made me jump right past the numerous side missions as you get pretty much everything for free if you quickly hunt everything you need in the mid game after grinding from tower to tower.
The guns are a mixed bag, you quickly pick your favorites and figure out your strategy. As in previous Far Cry titles, the game rewards you for trying new things. Fire spreads, troops move around in various ways, stealth is a valid tactic when it decides to work right. The game tricks you at the beginning making you think you are not a lone wolf and that the Rakyat will actually be doing anything. After the first act you hardly ever see many of the important characters, and Rakyat only seem to hang around bases you capture and in the areas surrounding them; they won't help you take bases or follow you.
Graphically, it's gorgeous if you don't mind the rampant use of the same few assets throughout the game. My issue is that the story is at it's peak in the first act and suffers from the guise as this "open world game" that in reality is just a linear story on a gigantic map with way too much busywork included.
My verdict? Get it cheap when you can like any Ubisoft title. The combat is fun, the story starts fun, and you kill what must be the entire population of the island. I never understand why these "be the hero" stories seem to drop the ball in a "open world" setting.

Mount and blade warband is a unique game. You will find non other like it. It has potential to be great, and it does just that, but there are a few things you should note before deciding to pick it up yourself. I will tell you everything I know, as I've played countless hours of the game and basically achieved everything you can learn within the game. So, lets get started.
First off, the game will be confusing if you have just started. You think there is a campaign, quests, or something to guide you? There is not. You have the power to go wherever you want, join whatever you want, and be whoever you want. The game does not decide anything for you, you decide it yourself.
Starting off can be hard, like really hard. So hard, you probably will rage quit if you do not know what to do. The early game has bandits, Looters, Outlaws that will chase you down and take your prisoner. To counter this, you can raise an army by going to a nearby town and recruiting villagers. Note, these villagers are not good. You will have to upgrade them to win, and the start of the game will depend on you, and rarely the troops you have.
There is a total of 5 different factions, and you get to choose which ones you will join, ally with, or seige war with. All the factions have different troops, weapons, and soldiers to make the game more unique. Some have better infantry, others archers, or calvery.
Then you have companions which tag along side with you. They will never die, but can be wounded, upgraded, and you have the choice of what their stats will be, and what they are equipped with. Overall, companions are really good once you get them to the point where they help with fighting, and give you an additional point in skills. If they have +3 in Surgery, that will combine with your +2 to make a total of +5. They are helpful, and are recommded.
Being a vassal to a kingdom is where the game starts to get intense. You get assigned a random fief(Town, castle, or a city) in which will pay you a weekly tax. Note, castles do not pay anything, only a place to store troops at and keep your council members. Being a vassal to a king, you will get to join military seiges. The marshal to the faction will send you a message to gather some troops and join him in a march to fight the enemy. If you decide to join, your relation with the faction and marshal will go up.
That brings us to relationships. This can be a pain. You normally start of with your relationship with everyone set at 0. To make it go up, you will have to ask for tasks you can fulfill. Every task you take, the relationship goes up by +1, and rarely +2. Every time you get your relationship up 20 points, the lord will change relationships with you. Friend, Trustworthy, Devoted, etc. The more he likes you, the better the odds of persuasion, Marrying their daughter, owning more fiefs, and more.
To own a fief, the king grants you it. They usually seek vassals without any fiefs, or their friends. That is why relationships with a lot of lords will help.
Marrying a daughter to a lord will improve your status a lot. It also gives more diplomatic options in your council, which is located at your castle or small town. Note, not many women like to marry a man without a castle or city. Don't mix a City with a town. A town is a small, poor village. A city has a market, etc. To continue, to make a women like you, you will have to speek to them and click the option, "I am your admiror" or something like that. That will either benefit you, or quite the opposite. Then she will send you a letter every 7 days to come visit her. Visit her until you get a relationship of 25+, then you ask to marry her.
Renown is the amount of lords that talk about you. Getting this up will help you get more known, which causes people you've never even met like you. You can get this up by fighting bandits, defeating enemies, marrying, etc.
Honor affects your interactions with other lords and causes certain events. A high honor can increase the likelihood of a mercanary accepting an offer, or of you being elected as marshall. Lords will like you for having positive honor, and every 3 points in honor will increase relationships by +1. Lower honor can result in a bounty on your head, or a war being declared on your faction.
Right to Rule is, well. Self explanitory. If you have a low right to rule, do not start your own faction. This will result in every kingdom to think you are an outlaw, "Not worthy enough to own a kingdom" and will declare war on you. Start your kingdom when it reached about 80.
Starting your own faction is, well. Kind of easy actually. Its for a late game, when you've married, and have become lasting allies with another faction. Once you want to start your own faction, you have to go rogue. Break up your alliance with your current kingdom, and attack an enemy. Take the castle, and you will have the option to choose a flag/banner. You basically are your own king, and can hire vassals, or make your companion a vassal. To make a companion a vassal, talk to them and give them a fief. They will isntantly leave your army, make their own, and assist you in war. You can also persuade other lords into joining your own. You need to have the persuasion skill, and they need to have problems with their current king before you can have them switch over.
From then on, you basically conquer all of the map. Thats very late, late end game. The overall singleplayer can last hundreds of hours, which is why this game is unique.
Overall, the game is amazing, and is well worth it in my opinion, and I recommend it to everyone who loves roleplaying.

If you've ever wanted to be a medieval warlord, then this is the game for you. Deck your character out in armor, load yourself up with weaponry, and engage in up-close, hand-to-hand combat using a twitch-based swordplay system that simulates realistic medieval fencing. You can operate solo or with a small band of guards, or build yourself the biggest personal army possible by engaging in battle and increasing your Renown. Your main character (along with a number of recruitable heroes) benefits from a RPG-style leveling system, allowing you to gain strength and new abilities as you hack your way through bandits, raiders, deserters, and even opposing military forces.
The realistic fantasy world of Calradia is an open sandbox that provides many different viable options for you to increase your fame and fortune amongst the nobility of the lands; there are seven different factions in control of different pieces of the country, and each of them has need of traders, vigilantes, vassals, and mercs as they wage war against each other in an endless cycle of conquest and carnage. You can ally yourself with one faction, sell your services to the highest bidder, or even conquer territory and create your own kingdom to rival the others.

Actual quote from the campaign: "DAD. YOU. WERE. A. GHOST. QUESTION MARK. I NEVER WOULD HAVE KNOWN. SURPRISED FACE"
One of the most disappointing Call of Duty games to date. Frequent crashes, poor framerate issues in a graphically unimpressive game, and weird mouse smoothing issues are just a few problems I've encountered within a few minutes of gameplay. Aside from the (extremely) poor optimization for PC, the storyline is dull and the voice acting will often make you cringe at how cheesy it is. Overall the campaign feels rushed, and absolutely nothing about it feels original or new. If you've played Battlefield 3 or 4's singleplayer, you might catch yourself noticing that most of the missions feel like dumbed down versions of that games' campaign missions.
Multiplayer isn't necessarily bad as it is literally nothing new from previous entries. Once again they reorganized the class and leveling system, but the gameplay hasn't changed at all. The maps aren't very good, and most games will consist of you getting shot in the back from someone who just spawned behind you. That's for Team Deathmatch. I would comment on other gametypes, but there never seems to very many people on any other playlist. Multiplayer basically feels like MW3 with better graphics and "different" weapons.
Don't get me wrong, I'm not a stereotypical anti-CoD pc gamer. I was actually really looking forward to ghosts as I was hoping that IW would've learned from their mistakes with MW3 and improve upon their system. Sadly, since West and Zampella got fired it seems Infinity Ward is just a shell of what it used to be, and the IW-made CoD games, which used to be the best ones, are now turning out to be worse than Treyarch's entries.
Unless you are a die-hard CoD fan who isn't interested at all in the story mode or any noticeable changes in gameplay, you'd be better off spending your money on Battlefield 4, a game that actually improved and innovated on its previous entry. TL, DR: To many issues for me to really enjoy. Maybe buy it on sale, but never at full price.
At first I really liked this game, but now I am not so sure. There are just too many things that all add up to make my experience very miserable at times.
First off, delayed actions. When you get low on health, or set on fire, a pop up will appear saying "press q to [heal/put out fire]. But you have to wait for a few moments before pressing q, because if you press q as soon as the pop up displays game ignores you, and you die. A similar delay happens with quests. As soon as a main quest is finished, a new one become available, and the game will tell you this. But if you, as soon as a quest is over, open your map to see where the new quest is, you can't find it, because it isn't there, you have to close the map, wait for a bit, and then reopen the map. This isn't a huge issue, but it's just plain annoying and it gets worse the longer I play.
Second, fall damage. I get that fall damage is real and that you can die from falling to far, but this game just seems way to harsh. I slide down a hill and almost kill myself. I jump off a small ledge and its like I got shot.
Third, unskipable cutscenes everywhere, and checkpoints before the cutscene. These things appear multiple times per main mission. I could handle a couple here and there, but it seems like there are 4-7 every mission. Kill some bad guys, cutscene! Walk near this person, cutscene! Open a door, cutscene!
Fourth, not enough weapons. While there are about 30 weapons, a lot of them are very similar. All but one of the assault rifles are full auto, all of the snipers are bolt action, and there are only about 5 different attachments for them, most of which are scopes.
When I add all this up, it just makes for an okay game. It has some really fun features that will probably keep me playing, like the camera and crafting/hunting, but it's a close battle between the negatives and positives in my mind. I don't want to seem like a hater, but those are my honest complaints.
All in all, it's a good game some of the time, and if it's on sale, considering buying it, but I do NOT recommend buying this game are full price.
Overall rating: 6.5/10

Call of Duty: Ghosts, however, with its slapdash campaign and unambitious multiplayer, contains enough factory-standard cynicism to earn itself plenty of scorn. It exists to exist, a stopgap bit of filler spat out as the industry transitions from one generation of consoles to another.
Contrary to the old saying, you can teach an old dog new tricks. Black Ops II demonstrated that with style. Ghosts, however, is a dog that simply doesn't want to change. It knows what it is, and sticks with it. It would be a respectable endeavor, if it didn't lead to such an underwhelming and predictable little product. What a sleepy, sleepy dog.

I would highly reccomend this game if you're a fan of ww2 games, battlefield, or planetside 2. This game combines large map gameplay with typically 24-32 players per map.
The shooting mechanics are a bit above average but to the point where you can get some real satisfaction taking out enemies from either up close when you're capturing points or sniping from distances of hundreds of meters away. The vehicles are another strong point of this game given the fact that theres a huge variety of tanks and several other transport vehicles such as jeeps and bikes. Scale is another strength of Heroes and Generals as the maps are a perfect size that allow you to fully atain what you and your teammates are capable of doing, be it spawning a jeep and getting comrades together to flank a base and capture a objective or spawn at an outpost preparing to guard it from invaders. Another positive note is that this game is not pay to win. This is a shooter giving you a very capable pair of guns from the start and the means to get much better equipped after the first couple hours of gameplay. Heroes and General's role system is very refreshing. Instead of games like battlefield where Cory, the local 14 year old who seems to be banging your Mom every friday night, gets to go into a tank or into a transport and ruin everyones day, Heroes and Generals makes it so that you have to earn your right to pilot tanks, pilot tanks, or be a paratrooper or recon sniper. This system allows new players to get a feel for their equipment and games mechanics instead of jumping into a game deciding role such as a tank that has to support a squad of infantry capturing a key objective.
With any game, there are flaws. The most obvious flaw is the poor menu interface and the integration of the campaign system. Don't get me wrong, I love this game but as I'm typing this I still don't understand what I'm supposed to do at the campaign screen. Many areas of the menu and the games mechanics are unexplained or difficult to figure out without researching online. The graphics are another fault let down as textures can often repeat themself such as grass giving the look of a game made in 2007. I personally don't care that much if graphics aren't up to par if the gamplay makes up for it, which it does. Thirdly, there is a lack of weapons and maps. For example, for the Germans there are only two smgs and two types of bolt action rifles, althought the deep modification system does alleviate this to a degree. The maps are well designed but there aren't enough of them. Balance is the final issue. Many times I've seen squads of infantry go agaisnt an enemy force consisting of tank after tank. Yes, tanks are supposed to be strong but this is a video game first and foremost and balance is crucial. The main anti-tank gun for infantry, the Panzershreck, costs almost 90,000 credits which is insanely expensive for being the most important after your rifle.
While I am being fairly critical, this is becaise this game is in Early Access. Many of the cons listed above will most likely be fixed or improved in the coming months and i'm sure quite a few of the positive factors will only get better.
The future is quite optimistic for Heroes and Generals

Overall it's a fine game. It comes at a prize though. As fun as the open world baddie camp shoot-ups are, as boring are other parts of the gameplay. Hunting animals grows old really fast but has to be repeated way beyond that point. The story is rather uninspired, bad guy kidnaps friends, protagonist goes and kills bad guy. Through several iterations of increasing bad guyness the actual killing is a simple quick time event with age long cut scenes around it. Other highlights include: pressing W to walk through a cut scene, pressing nothing and wait for the usual yadda yadda to be over and shooting a monster over and over with a bow.
I did not care one second about the friends of the protagonist. The opener shows some rich asshats partying and skydiving and being US american tourist jerks and then they get kidnapped. Hoorray I'd say, but the player has to save the friends without building up any relationship to them. When they (almost) die it's just another NPC in danger. The evil punk is just a cartoonish bad guy whose plot develops just as expected and who would have thought that there is an even badder baddie behind evil punk?
I'm saying all this because many people were boasting about how great the story telling was and how colourful the characters. I found them all dull and foreseeable.
On the plus side: Gameplay is great, though simple. Up until the end there was no real challenge except for missing a quick time event. Running, sliding, shooting, paragliding, all is fun and works well. But as versatile as the protagonist is, as stupid are the enemies. When sniping a few of them in a base the rest hides, but comes back out after less then a minute. When discovered they run in a more or less straight line towards the player, maybe seeking the nearest cover. "Liberating" 34 outposts was never a challenge, although it was definetely fun. I enjoyed sneaking up bases more than the story line, that often puts the player on rails and pushes him through the level. Raiding outposts, especially with self chosen difficulties, like using only the bow, only doing melee kills or sniping everyone without being noticed, is rewarding and fun. Too bad the number of outposts is limited and after raiding them all there is not much left to do.
The open world works quite well, it gives a sense of discovery while not being too open like Just Cause 2, where the numbers say "bazillion square miles" but in all this land mass there is nothing to do except for endless forests. FC3 hides treasures and other collectibles around the island, so the player is diverted from time to time from his/her actual goal.
Summing up: Great gunplay, good open world, uninspired generic story line. Buy it for the shooting, not for the story.
Bonus: Lovely pair of breasts held in the player's face on several occasions.

US and Germany was a horrid imbalance ot begin with. US noob with an M1 VS. a German officer with a huge bloody hand-held MG. Who's going to win?
Back then, the US would whine about how OP the Germans are and the Germans would whine about how 'supposedly' OP the US was, despite all Germans having a 3/1 kdr, at least.
Then, they have the GREAT idea to add Russia! And not only as an allied country, no. As an enemy. A 1v1v1. A total bloody mess of a map. It's not fun either. It's not fun to know you have two factions trying to rip your jugular out.
To add to that, pilots get rocket launchers, Paratroopers get jeep-mounted MG's, officers get the Gustav Karl and the Germans get Wolfenstein tech.
Afterwards, the squad update jacks everything up, there are even further terrible balance issues and it's even less fun than it was before.
Tank can spawn camp you, still- the game isn't out of beta, they ask for a hell of a lot of cash and the level of grind is a sin worthy of the 7th ring of Hell.

I'm hoping we can look back on this game as the tipping point, when the oversaturation of growly military FPS games finally hit its peak and started to roll back.
The single player campaign is passably entertaining at best, and at worst it's just boring. The only interesting thing about it is how much it oscillates between the two.
The beginning sucks to an almost impressive degree. There's zero actual characterization, you're on rails the entire time, and the plot is ridiculous to the point of it basically being impossible to care about even if you genuinely want to.
The plot never really improves. The game, however, does.
The middle of the game is far and away the best part, where you do a series of "Invade this base, blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, escape" missions. At this point the maps widen out and there's less of a feeling of you being herded from place to place so you can rotely stare at the next explosion. These missions actually get legitimately fun, although it has less to do with good level design and more to do with the fact that those kinds of missions are just inherently fun in and of themselves, and well suited to arcadey shooter games. One of Half-Life 2's standout levels is the assault on Nova Prospekt; Moden-day Wolfenstien's best level by far was an assault on an underground Nazi base; hell, even Quake 1 was full of these kinds of levels. They're just fun to play, and thankfully those missions in Ghosts stand up as being quite fun, if not exactly super-memorable.
Things ramp up in bombast near the end of the game (which is saying something considering this game has an impressive explosions-per-minute rate even on its slowest levels) and it dumps a lot of variety as the narrative starts to urgently jerk around to different people in the same stage, so at the very least the final stages aren't as dull as Act 1, but they do bring back the funnel with a vengence. The final stage, while technically very impressive to look at, is almost literally a straight line from point A to point B; admittedly this is because you're on the back of a moving train, but it still means there's only one direction to go and only one way to do it.
The Multiplayer...Well, it's Call of Duty. What do you want me to say. Did you play pretty much any of the other ones? It's more of that. Whether this is a bad thing or not really depends on whether you like that kind of thing. Honestly, modern-day CoD is basically what Counter-Strike/Day of Defeat was back in '99-2002, and Quake/Goldeneye/Whatever before that -- I played the hell out of Counter-Strike back in the day, so it's hard for me to hate on the CoD MP. It's either a scene you're into (in which case you already own this game) or it isn't (and you may spend a lot of time mystified as to why it's popular). Either way, you don't need me telling you anything about it.
Final Verdict: If you don't have it already (read: You don't care about the MP), wait for a deep discount. Otherwise pass. It's not the worst thing ever, but if you really want to play a Call of Duty game for whatever reason, just go for Black Ops 2. It's a much better in virtually every way.

Mount and Blade: Warband is personally one of my favorite games.
Yes, despite it's obvious low-budget production, it's still one of the best games I've played, especially for those into the Action genre, but want important RTS and RPG elements.
You also gotta pay respect to the developers, Taleworlds. They didn't have much money when they started out, ( actually they almost had none ) and they started in a garage for the first game, but it slowly upgraded into this glorious masterpiece. Mount and Blade: Warband is a great game because it has a level of depth and complexity that is further developed by it's design.
The combat is one of the best things about Mount and Blade: Warband, because it promotes skill, it promotes variation, and it promotes seperate playstyles. Do you like spears, swords, or what? You can literally pick from lots of different weapons, and these weapons are just copy/paste reskins. They all have another depth to that as well. Weapons do various types of damage and effects. Blunt weapons, for example, will knock enemies out in singleplayer, allow you to sell the enemy after battle to a slave trader. So you can make some money. Piercing damage weapons allows you to penetrate armor, and cutting weapons allow you to chop light armored enemies in half. You can see on the weapon's stat page what kind of stats it has. It may be a faster, but shorter weapon, or a longer and slower weapon.
You may ask 'Why do I want a blunt weapon in multiplayer?' Well, for 1 reason, you can knock down people with it. As in, take them to the ground, where you can beat them silly.
There are also weapons that 'aren't balanced'. This means, you can stun the enemy if they decided to block you, and if your weapon is heavier.
Personally, I like the default spear. It's weak, shorter than other polearms, and not as fast as some. However, I very much enjoy the weapon because it fits my playstyle. It's a flexible weapon, one that can perform in all situations, and perform exceptionally well in open fields and against cavalry.
The multiplayer for Mount and Blade: Warband is also very good. It has the standard TDM, FFA, and all sorts of things, but it also has Duel and Siege. You can duel other players in a match of skill of the blade, or you could play in large battle sieges. Some servers allow for 64v64 player sieges, which is VERY fun to play. The sieges are exactly how you would see castle defence/offense. Archers firing down to the besiegers, crossbowmen firing up to soften the defence, infantry fighting it out on the walls in a tense close quarters melee battle, and warriors emerging from the siege towers.
The Singleplayer for Mount and Blade: Warband, is less about skill, and far more about being much, much smarter. You start off has a foreigner, with different stats and starting equipment, depending on the choices you make. You can also be a male or female, which DOES change which options you have available to you. You can start as a male noble, and have an easier start, as you will have most things you need, such as extra gold, renown ( for getting lords to recognize you ) and a banner ( for looking cool ). It's not like there isn't a challenge. You can start as a commoner female for a harder path if you want. The challenges are sexist, by the way, so don't get upset over nothing. If you still do, get out. Now. Anyways, if you are a female, you may have an alternate way of rising to power.
As a male, you do the generic stuff. You gain renown, become a vassal ( or become another... )
You court a lady you like, and battle for women and fight for their honor in tournaments.
As a female, it is much different. You can talk to lords, some may even already like you, others may insult you for being a woman. You can use this to your advantage. A woman in Calradia can manipulate the balance of power by marrying into a stronger/wealthier family and in turn, using him as a means to rise into power.
As for the other things in the singleplayer, there's many viable playstyles. You don't HAVE to participate in combat 24/7. Maybe you can if you want to. You can be a trader, who buys and sells and owns businesses throughout the land. You can be the plain old adventurer, doing quests for rewards, or you could be a slaver, knocking the enemy out, and selling them to the highest bitter. Of course, there are multiple playstyles available, as I said. My personal favorite is the 'Arena Hero/Tournament Champion' type style. I gain money from fighting in the arena to fund my troops, and I use my troops to help fight bandits, and fight deserters.
As you get further into the singleplayer, you will eventually become a vassal. You can manage fiefs, basically plot of lands, and tax them accordingly, managing the economic state of your area by helping the place out. Towns and Villages will have different types of things to do.
In towns, you will find that there is much to do. You can go to the inn, look for recruits, ask fellow travellers about things, find slavers, book merchants, and companions.
( Companions are like the player, you can customize them and level them up. )
There are also many merchants in town, where you can buy armor, weapons, mounts, and supplies.
In villages, you can recruit peasants of the faction you are at. So if you go into faction A's village, you will recruit faction A's peasants. If another faction takes over those will still be Faction A's peasants.
Also, you will need to manage morale. Being constantly defeated, being forced to surrender, leaving troops to die while you escape... Those will hurt morale. ( Low morale = Deserters )
And yes, you can be beaten. There are no checkpoints. If you fail, you must suffer the consequences of your actions. But, in Calradia you don't die. That doesn't make you special though. No one else really dies, other than the generic soldier. You and every other lord are against each other, friendly or not. Like a particular lady? Better make sure Count Gutlans doesn't sweep her off her feet first. Maybe you'll have to duel him so Gutlans won't see her again.
But let's say you get captured before you can get to Gutlans. You were defeated by bandits and captured. You didn't get to escape for a long, long time. The lady you like is now going to marry him. You've failed in your goal to marry her, and do you know why? It was your fault. Every action in Mount and Blade has a consequence, so making choices are important.
Mount and Blade: Warband's singleplayer is an open-world sandbox. If you want, you can be an adventurer all the way until there is only one kingdom left. Yup, that's perfectly fine. There is no forced objective. You, as the player, are able to decide what you want to do, and when you want to do it. And of course, how you want to do it.
Do you know if you're a top-notch fighter? Think you can take on everyone alone with your boys? If you can do it, go ahead. It's entirely possible to have a team of ultimate fighters against hordes of men.
Mount and Blade: Warband's greatest strength is the use of it's module system. This allows for VERY easy mod use, you just put your mods into 'Modules' and just open the launcher, BAM. It's there. That's all you had to do.
Warband's modding community has developed some incredible mods, mods which improve the game tenfold, mods which completely change the genre of the game, and mods which completely change the way the game is played in and out of itself. They aren't tiny mods that change 1 or 2 things, but legitmately, they are mods that are on par with other triple A titles themselves.

If you'd like a realistic game, where leadership wins, stay away. The AI is like a Zerg. They'll rush you, or take your orders a bit too literally.
However, it is a good arcade slasher in single player mode. Difficulty settings can be tampered with rather extensively, allowing you to create whatever challenge you'd like. Too hard, or too easy? Change it whenever.
Multiplayer is also a rather interesting endeavor, though it may be a bit discouraging to the newer players. To put it lightly, it is a bit tricky to get used to the much more different pace than in singleplayer.
And the mods. Dear god, there are many interesting ones out there. Starting from the general improvements that the Diplomacy mod brings (a must-have for all players playing singleplayer) to the online campaign of the cRPG mod, there is a lot of extra content just waiting to be experienced.
It is a fun game. I'd say it definitely was worth getting it. Whether you want to be a simple mercenary, or rise to the challenge of becoming king. Or maybe you want to partake in grand multiplayer battles? The choice is yours to make.

Upon starting this game for the first time I was greeted with a familiar site. What at first appeared to be a quick attempt to throw together dated graphics, and a pay-to-win profit model cloaked in a well used FPS genre, turned out to offer more than my initial reaction gave credit for. While that reaction is harsh, the game does contain dated graphics(eg. 2010), and a profit model that allows paying players to progress more quickly. What Heroes & Generals also offers is solid gameplay, progressive customization, and well balanced maps, all painted in a coat of FPS nostalgia.
With most free-to-play titles the first thing people criticize is the monetezation features, and this was one of the first areas I investigated. I'm glad to see that Heroes & Generals does a great job of avoiding the pay-to-win pitfall. By making all equipment available for both in game credits, and Gold purchased with real funds, H&G developers made it possible for people, paying or not, to access the same gear, albeit at different times. Monetization features allow players to purchase pre-trained soldiers, increase Credits/Warfunds earned in battles, unlock/purchase equipment/skins, purchase Assault Squads, and unlock 1 extra badge/equipment slots.
Overall Heroes & Generals is a balanced experience, and a game I will continue to play. While at points the game may seem unfair due to people having better equipment than you, it is actually a nice dose of realism, as in war you are not always evenly matched technologically. This game is still in Early Access, so expect minor bugs and glitches, but at this point I've encountered very few. This game is at the perfect point to start playing and becoming active in the community. For the price I highly suggest taking some time to play this game, and develop your own opinions, and if you have suggestions don't hesitate to voice them on the forums, because that's the whole point of the Early Access system.
