I was excited to play FarCry3 at this time, with FarCry4 coming out soon. I jumped at the sale price. I liked what I saw of the reviews and playthroughs. 'It's a must have', right?
But I have played only a few hours and am about to give up, because I already played TOMB RAIDER and loved it.
Yeah, this game is like TR quite a bit. You visited an island that you shouldn't have. You were captured. You now have to survive and escape. Become the warrior. Bow and arrow, hunt for supplies, upgrade weapons, jumping puzzles and platforming (yes FarCry3 has platforming!) Even running out of burning buildings, searching for relics at shrines, stealth kills, limited ammo, zip lines, radio towers, alarms you have to disable, the ability to purchase map pieces to reveal locations of rare items, wildernessd skill progression, combat skill progression, unlockable takedown skills....
I mean it's a TR knockoff in every way. It's even set in the south china sea, on an island which has it's own flavor of asia-pacific culture and mysticism. There are WWII coastal defense cannons scatered about the map, but they don't look nearly as cool or as genuine as the beautifully rendered, imposing, crusty old cannons in creepy bunkers famed in TR. THOSE are coastal defense cannons. So with all of these cheap imitations, I feel FC3 is not it's own game.
These are story-driven games. FPS + RPG is a great genre, which started with Mass Effect (as far as I know) but they have to have a story leading the player through the game to the end. FC3, in my opinion, has a basic premise, not a story. The premise is that your friends were captured and you have to save them. That's it. No disaster to avoid, no cataclysm to stop, no reason to be afraid to continue for the weight of the story bearing down on your fragile character. Just go and kill people, because you're invincible. No death, no impending doom, no story. There is fun. But there's no fear; if I could compare ME and TR to FC3, that would be what's missing. Being scared. Not knowing what was going to happen next. No insurmountable odds to overcome at the end of the story, thus making you and your character true heroes in the process. Just: become the warrior and strealthkill everyone on the map with ease in normal mode. Le sigh.
TR had bullet-time close quarters combat, which is truly awesome, now that I find it missing from FC3. When an animal lunges at you in FC3, he just eats your face, and you have to mash some random button in order to survive (sometimes it's E which is 'use', sometimes it's spacebar which is jump, but it hasn't been F yet, which would make sense since it's the melee key), then you heal up and you're OK. Or, he eats your face and you respawn, and you're OK. Sometimes you die before the key indicator shows on screen... so it feels like it doesn't matter what key you press. In TR, it mattered which key, and when. It was the melee key, as I recall, and it was all done in slow-mo, because once that animal had his teeth in you it was game over. Damn that was cool.
The only real improvement over TR is that the open world is explorable. You can jump in a car and drive anywhere. So if you didn't like TR's one-path map, then you will like FC3's big, open world.
Another thing: FC3 instantly reminded me of 'Watch_Dogs' when I got in a car. Same engine, same mechanics. Ubisoft, I love you. Open world RPG FPS. Really. I just need more story because I'm spoiled by TR and ME. :D
Honestly there's not much replayability in FC3 or TR, unlike ME where you could choose another class with a new skillset, or another choice of dialog options which gave you a different ending ala "Choose Your Own Adventure" books. So why did I play TR through a second time? There's nothing I can do differently, except find all the hidden stuff on the map. I guess it was so good that I wanted to do it again.
Sad news: from preliminary reviews and previews of FC4, it sounds to be just like FC3 with a couple new skills and mechanics. Same thing, different place, different characters and story. God, I hope it has a story.
So, If you've played TR and liked it, like I did, then you might want to skip FarCry3 and FarCry4, unless you really want more of the same in an open world, instead of a narrow path.

I was excited to play FarCry3 at this time, with FarCry4 coming out soon. I jumped at the sale price. I liked what I saw of the reviews and playthroughs. 'It's a must have', right?
But I have played only a few hours and am about to give up, because I already played TOMB RAIDER and loved it.
Yeah, this game is like TR quite a bit. You visited an island that you shouldn't have. You were captured. You now have to survive and escape. Become the warrior. Bow and arrow, hunt for supplies, upgrade weapons, jumping puzzles and platforming (yes FarCry3 has platforming!) Even running out of burning buildings, searching for relics at shrines, stealth kills, limited ammo, zip lines, radio towers, alarms you have to disable, the ability to purchase map pieces to reveal locations of rare items, wildernessd skill progression, combat skill progression, unlockable takedown skills....
I mean it's a TR knockoff in every way. It's even set in the south china sea, on an island which has it's own flavor of asia-pacific culture and mysticism. There are WWII coastal defense cannons scatered about the map, but they don't look nearly as cool or as genuine as the beautifully rendered, imposing, crusty old cannons in creepy bunkers famed in TR. THOSE are coastal defense cannons. So with all of these cheap imitations, I feel FC3 is not it's own game.
These are story-driven games. FPS + RPG is a great genre, which started with Mass Effect (as far as I know) but they have to have a story leading the player through the game to the end. FC3, in my opinion, has a basic premise, not a story. The premise is that your friends were captured and you have to save them. That's it. No disaster to avoid, no cataclysm to stop, no reason to be afraid to continue for the weight of the story bearing down on your fragile character. Just go and kill people, because you're invincible. No death, no impending doom, no story. There is fun. But there's no fear; if I could compare ME and TR to FC3, that would be what's missing. Being scared. Not knowing what was going to happen next. No insurmountable odds to overcome at the end of the story, thus making you and your character true heroes in the process. Just: become the warrior and strealthkill everyone on the map with ease in normal mode. Le sigh.
TR had bullet-time close quarters combat, which is truly awesome, now that I find it missing from FC3. When an animal lunges at you in FC3, he just eats your face, and you have to mash some random button in order to survive (sometimes it's E which is 'use', sometimes it's spacebar which is jump, but it hasn't been F yet, which would make sense since it's the melee key), then you heal up and you're OK. Or, he eats your face and you respawn, and you're OK. Sometimes you die before the key indicator shows on screen... so it feels like it doesn't matter what key you press. In TR, it mattered which key, and when. It was the melee key, as I recall, and it was all done in slow-mo, because once that animal had his teeth in you it was game over. Damn that was cool.
The only real improvement over TR is that the open world is explorable. You can jump in a car and drive anywhere. So if you didn't like TR's one-path map, then you will like FC3's big, open world.
Another thing: FC3 instantly reminded me of 'Watch_Dogs' when I got in a car. Same engine, same mechanics. Ubisoft, I love you. Open world RPG FPS. Really. I just need more story because I'm spoiled by TR and ME. :D
Honestly there's not much replayability in FC3 or TR, unlike ME where you could choose another class with a new skillset, or another choice of dialog options which gave you a different ending ala "Choose Your Own Adventure" books. So why did I play TR through a second time? There's nothing I can do differently, except find all the hidden stuff on the map. I guess it was so good that I wanted to do it again.
Sad news: from preliminary reviews and previews of FC4, it sounds to be just like FC3 with a couple new skills and mechanics. Same thing, different place, different characters and story. God, I hope it has a story.
So, If you've played TR and liked it, like I did, then you might want to skip FarCry3 and FarCry4, unless you really want more of the same in an open world, instead of a narrow path.

This game is amazing with a great story, amazing visuals and really good shooting mechanics.
Gameplay-
The shooting mechanics in this game are brilliant. The guns feel very nice to use and there are a lot of different types to use. Enemies can shoot through thin walls which is both realistic and amazing, and cover is done really well too. If you hide behind something you can aim down the sights and you will lean out or fire over the top.
Scattered across the map are radio towers and enemy strongholds. Radio towers are useld like veiwpoints in Assassins Creed, where you have to go to the top and trigger an animation to be able to veiw that area on the map. Another bonus to these is that you get some really nice veiws from the top. Unlocking radio towers unlocks free weapons in stores, so you never have to pay a large amount for a gun. Enemy Strongholds can be taken out by lots of different ways, stealthily stabbing everyone, sniping all the pirates or just running in all guns blazing (which is likely to get you killed).
There are several different vehicles in the game to get you from A to B. They are really fun and feel nice to drive with a keyboard and the handling is very arcade-y. There are also 3 types of boat and handgliders scattered across the map for fun transport. Enemies and friendlies will patrol in these as well and some really fun situations can emerge where you find an enemy roadblock and try to run from it, only to be pursued by two cars filled with pirates.
The first part of the game is very survivaly as you are unequipped and have low health. Hunting and crafting are used to improve your equipment and skills are used to improve yourself, such as adding more health, not running out of stamina and being able to hold your breath under water for a lot longer.
I would reccomend playing on hard or very hard difficulty otherwise the game just becomes too easy within about an hour.
The Map-
The first half of the story takes place on an absolutely stunning jungle island. It is absolutely huge and is covered with stuff to find. Temples, outposts and caves dill the map with stuff to do. The second half of the game is located on an island about a kilometre south that is made up of mountains and to me, wasn't as impressive. It was still very good but there just wasn't as much stuff on it to do but the outposts and enemies there are a lot more challenging, so that's fun.
Story/Missions-
The story missions ranged form burning fields of weed with a flamethrower to shooting pirates to exploring ancient tombs in search of a treasure. The characters are really well written and the voice acting is brilliant. After completing the game there are still many side missions to do aswell as hunting activities and bounty quests. However, one of the biggest problems with the game becomes apparent during the missions, the checkpointing. Sometimes it is fine but other times you will die and be reset to 5 minutes earlier, that becomes annoying.
AI-
The AI is very good, especially on the higher difficulties. They react to sounds and their dead bodies and don't just look for you for ten seconds and then stop, they will keep on searching. Also, they don't just follow paths, their movement seems very dynamic and don't patrol a small area on a repeated loop.
Graphics and Sound-
On a GTX 760, intel i5 4690 3.5GHz and 8GB RAM, I get about 60FPS in 1080p and everything at ultra, apart from a few things which are at high. The game is beautiful and colourful and the FOV goes all the way up to 110, which is better than most games (ahem Skyrim).
The sound is brilliant aswell and the way enemies react to sounds feels real. If htey hear a gunshot they will search in the direction it came from to find it. All weapons have a unique sound that is very luad, like a gun should be, unlike other games where an assualt rifle sounds like a cough.
Overall-
The game is amazing and really fun. The checkpointing is the only real issue I have with it but otherwise it is brilliant.

No. Just no.
The game is a big step-up from its predecessor and it is really good when you're free roaming the island taking out pirate camps, exploring the monotonous but beautiful landscape. And it looks pretty nice. But that's about it.
There are a lot of problems with the pacing. Half an hour in the game and I was carrying a modern french assault rifle and a silenced sniper rifle with free access to unlimited ammo if visiting the right places.
The crafting mechanics are completely contrived (why do I need tiger-skin to make bigger pouches?) and there is a lot of dissonance between gameplay and story. The protagonist lies in doubt about his actions, about killing other people while ingame recklessly slitting throats of pirates like there is no tomorrow.
The story itself is very unengaging and the characters in it are just as boring.
The supporting cast ranges from "meh" (the friends) to "completely braindead and annoying" (everyone else).
The big shaman girl is just a ♥♥♥♥♥, calling the main character "no warrior" after he single-handedly defeated a dozen pirate camps while her so-called warriors did nothing at all.
The half-enemy strange guy that kidnapped your best friend attacks you with a knife. And for some contrived reason your player character pulls out his knife instead of just shooting him with the MACHINEGUN IN HIS HAND. Argh.
Vaas, the big-bad from the beginning of the game waits around corners to punch you like... fifty times. It gets old VERY fast.
Lots of setpieces don't make the slightest sense.
I have a clear shot at the big-bad-evil-guy and am carrying around a Remington sniper rifle. Can I take the shot? Nope. Because cutscene.
I escape the pirates and decide to steal a helicopter instead of just slipping into the jungle... why exactly? Oh right, because Vaas needs to recapture the player.
I finally get the opportunity to attack Vaas' hideout and decide to kick in his front door and go in guns blazing. Alone. Not to mention the combat in this game works best if you rely on stealth and hit&run attacks. Riiiight.
This level design belongs in a Micheal-Bay-Style FPS like Call of Duty and not in something with this kind of survival-vibe.
Also the kills on the antagonists aren't even satisfying because they're just boring QTEs.
In conclusion:
If you want a free-world action game get GTA or Just Cause 2. If you want a spectacle shooter get CoD. If you want a shooter with an engaging anti-war story get Spec Ops: The Line. If you want a first-person survival game.. uhm.. Metro? Stalker?  But not this.

(Scroll down for Pros and Cons) 82 hours and one of my most played games on Steam (I have over 220), it is amazing. Far Cry 4 will be similar, and I know everything about it so far. If you like FPS, adventure, open-world, fun, b00bs, guns, parties, Co-Op (unfortunately not open-world, but WILL be in 4), and games worth your money, you found the right one!
Pros:
-The enviroment. A huge map and probably my favorite open-world game, ever! The second part of the map opens after half way through the game. While the enviroment isn't as detailed as Far Cry 4's will be, it's still an amazing treat.
-The graphics. They look the best for 2012. 'Nuf said.
-The characters. Interesting and awesome (especially Vaas, in my top 3 favorite villians of all time) and a story that will keep you interested even after the game is over!
-The weapons and cars. While there is no flyable helicopters (Which there will be one in Far Cry 4 called the Gyrocopter), the cars are varied with random encounters with Pirates (Grunts) down the street. The boats are awesome and that comes to our next pro.
-Hunting and Scavenging. In Far Cry 3 you can hunt animals (don't worry, they're virtual and not real) and pick flowers. With animals, you can make upgrades, like more holsters for guns, ammo pouches, and sick stuff. With picking flowers, you can make "medicene" (drugs) which boost things in combat, hunting, and health.
-Co-op and Multiplayer. They didn't stop with the Singleplayer, and it still would have been an amazing game, just look at my hours! (86+ hours) Unfortunately, the Co-op is linear but a nice touch, and the Multiplayer isn't just stapled on. They have a cool decoding system and Battle Cries, which are very helpful. It gives a lot more teamwork than Call of Duty ever would.
-B00bs. You probably say Nudity on the Rating, but how could I not put this in? Seriously?
-$30.00. You've got to pick up this game for that price, no matter what kind of gamer you are!
-Mini-games. From Throwing Knives to hunting Legendary Animals, there is some Minigame for you!
Cons:
-No Open-World Co-op. There will be Open-World Co-op in Far Cry 4, which I can't wait for. My biggest con.
-The enviroments are a little empty in some places, which it will be fixed in Far Cry 4.
-No Elephants or the Gyrocopter, until Far Cry 4.
-No worth-while DLC. (Besides Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon, and for $15.00 you should pick up if you like this game!)
-When it ends. Great choices at the end you can pick from and I loved the game.

Date of review: 10.24.2014
Platform: PC
Released in 2012, Far Cry 3 became a huge success, considered by many the game of the year (or at least the FPS of the year), something which I also believe it fully deserves. An open world FPS experience has never felt so polished before.
Story:
In the third installment of the Far Cry series you take over the role of Jason Brody, a 25 year old american daredevil who is currently on a holiday with his friends and brothers in Thailand. Everything is party and fun until the group goes skydiving over the supposedly uninhabited Rook Islands, only to land on a world occupied by pirates who deal with kidnapping and human trafficking…
While the plot is not as mature and meaningful as the one of Far Cry 2, it’s more than first meets the eye, being a carefully built satire.
Characters are very deep, and Vaas Montenegro is one of the coolest antagonists ever to show up in a game.
Though not directly related to the main plot/story line, the detailed history of Rook Islands (going back all the way to ancient China), the Rakyat (the native people of the islands) the Japanese occupation during the second world war, etc. adds a lot to the game and to the immersion.
9/10
Visuals:
Far Cry 3 looks absolutely stunning. Colorful yet wild, the tropical world has never looked so good and alive before, with breath taking landscapes and dozens of animals roaming/flying around. This is definitely one of those games you just enjoy by looking at. The variety is also impressive, from the lush jungles to the sandy beaches, from ancient temples to small villages, it’s simply a pleasure to roam around, and explore, and the small details really make it feel rewarding.
Combat also looks and thus feels great, with brutal animations and beautiful explosions, making firefights incredibly fun.
The day-night cycle (although somewhat short) is present as well and adds a lot to the visuals, creating sights which will easily take your breath away.
Of course, such visuals will require a decent system in order to run smoothly on High and/or Ultra detail settings. On the test rig (for reference see test system specifications at the bottom of the review), I could run Far Cry 3 at 1080p Ultra details and 2xMSAA with very good frame rates. I did get some rare fps drops in very intense fight scenes, but even then the game was more than smooth enough to be played. Turning MSSA over 2x however, pretty much killed my frames, but this is absolutely acceptable considering the visual quality. All in all, you will need something like an Intel Core i5 3570K or an AMD FX-8350 CPU paired with a GeForce GTX 770 (GTX 680) or an AMD Radeon R9 280X (HD 7970 Ghz Edition) GPU to be able to play on Ultra settings with 2-4xMSAA at 1080p resolution. However, I also know people who play Far Cry 3 on low end PC's or laptops and they were still able to get decent fps rates on low to medium detail settings, so the game seems to be quite well optimized... thumbs up for Ubisoft (for a more in depth analysis on system requirements I advise you to check the "Far Cry 3 Performance Test: Graphics & CPU" on Techspot).
10/10
Gameplay:
If you thought visuals were the game’s greatest strength, you were wrong… the gameplay is simply fantastic. Far Cry 3 takes over where Far Cry 2 left off, but delivers so much more in a significantly more polished way.
The main plot is long, with varied and fun to play missions. The secondary missions/quests may not be as meaningful as in Far Cry 2 for example, but the game more than makes up for them with the unbelievably fun exploration, hunting, gathering, collectibles, etc. Really, collecting stuff and exploring has never felt as rewarding and as fun, whether you are searching for relics or letters from the Japanese soldiers (who occupied the islands during the Second World War), or whether you are hunting a rare white tiger or gathering herbs, you will have fun.
You could probably rush through the main plot in 15-20 or so hours, but if you allow yourself sucked into the world of Rook Islands you can spend 75+ hours and you will still have plenty of stuff to do. Simply awesome.
Of course this is an FPS, so one of the main questions here is, how are the guns? Short answer: great! There are well over 20 weapons to choose from, pistols, sub machine guns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, light machine guns and even exotics like the flame thrower or the re-curving bow. Also, almost all weapons are customizable, you can attach sound suppressors, scopes, extended magazines, etc. providing a truly varied arsenal which you can configure to perfectly fit your play style.
Long range and close quarter combat is usually viable in every FPS, but Far Cry 3 will also be completely playable using stealth tactics, even more, you will be rewarded for stealthy kills and takedowns (which are awesome by the way), or carefully and tactically liberating outposts without getting detected. Oh and do you remember the outpost re-spawn problem from Far Cry 2? It's gone! In Far Cry 3 a libreated outpost is taken over by the Rakyat, and will serve as a safe house.
As in the previous Far Cry installments, vehicles are also available. And I have to say (at least for me personally), the cars handle better and are more fun to drive than in many racing games… which is not something we are used to from an FPS.
But Far Cry 3 is so much more than a simple open world FPS… the introduction of RPG elements might sound scary for some hardcore FPS fans, but Far Cry 3 nailed it. During your adventures you gain experience and eventually level up, which is rewarded with skill points which you can use to unlock some incredibly cool and brutal takedown moves and other bonuses. The skills feel balanced, you’ll never become a Terminator, but they are also rewarding enough to make you want to unlock them.
And we are still not done, Far Cry 3 also has crafting! Now don't imagine a complex gathering/crafting system. You can gather skins and furrs from animals to create ammo bags and pouches, and different plants for different syringes which can heal you or provide different short term bonuses. Date of review: 10.24.2014
Platform: PC
Released in 2012, Far Cry 3 became a huge success, considered by many the game of the year (or at least the FPS of the year), something which I also believe it fully deserves. An open world FPS experience has never felt so polished before.
Story:
In the third installment of the Far Cry series you take over the role of Jason Brody, a 25 year old american daredevil who is currently on a holiday with his friends and brothers in Thailand. Everything is party and fun until the group goes skydiving over the supposedly uninhabited Rook Islands, only to land on a world occupied by pirates who deal with kidnapping and human trafficking…
While the plot is not as mature and meaningful as the one of Far Cry 2, it’s more than first meets the eye, being a carefully built satire.
Characters are very deep, and Vaas Montenegro is one of the coolest antagonists ever to show up in a game.
Though not directly related to the main plot/story line, the detailed history of Rook Islands (going back all the way to ancient China), the Rakyat (the native people of the islands) the Japanese occupation during the second world war, etc. adds a lot to the game and to the immersion.
9/10
Visuals:
Far Cry 3 looks absolutely stunning. Colorful yet wild, the tropical world has never looked so good and alive before, with breath taking landscapes and dozens of animals roaming/flying around. This is definitely one of those games you just enjoy by looking at. The variety is also impressive, from the lush jungles to the sandy beaches, from ancient temples to small villages, it’s simply a pleasure to roam around, and explore, and the small details really make it feel rewarding.
Combat also looks and thus feels great, with brutal animations and beautiful explosions, making firefights incredibly fun.
The day-night cycle (although somewhat short) is present as well and adds a lot to the visuals, creating sights which will easily take your breath away.
Of course, such visuals will require a decent system in order to run smoothly on High and/or Ultra detail settings. On the test rig (for reference see test system specifications at the bottom of the review), I could run Far Cry 3 at 1080p Ultra details and 2xMSAA with very good frame rates. I did get some rare fps drops in very intense fight scenes, but even then the game was more than smooth enough to be played. Turning MSSA over 2x however, pretty much killed my frames, but this is absolutely acceptable considering the visual quality. All in all, you will need something like an Intel Core i5 3570K or an AMD FX-8350 CPU paired with a GeForce GTX 770 (GTX 680) or an AMD Radeon R9 280X (HD 7970 Ghz Edition) GPU to be able to play on Ultra settings with 2-4xMSAA at 1080p resolution. However, I also know people who play Far Cry 3 on low end PC's or laptops and they were still able to get decent fps rates on low to medium detail settings, so the game seems to be quite well optimized... thumbs up for Ubisoft (for a more in depth analysis on system requirements I advise you to check the "Far Cry 3 Performance Test: Graphics & CPU" on Techspot).
10/10
Gameplay:
If you thought visuals were the game’s greatest strength, you were wrong… the gameplay is simply fantastic. Far Cry 3 takes over where Far Cry 2 left off, but delivers so much more in a significantly more polished way.
The main plot is long, with varied and fun to play missions. The secondary missions/quests may not be as meaningful as in Far Cry 2 for example, but the game more than makes up for them with the unbelievably fun exploration, hunting, gathering, collectibles, etc. Really, collecting stuff and exploring has never felt as rewarding and as fun, whether you are searching for relics or letters from the Japanese soldiers (who occupied the islands during the Second World War), or whether you are hunting a rare white tiger or gathering herbs, you will have fun.
You could probably rush through the main plot in 15-20 or so hours, but if you allow yourself sucked into the world of Rook Islands you can spend 75+ hours and you will still have plenty of stuff to do. Simply awesome.
Of course this is an FPS, so one of the main questions here is, how are the guns? Short answer: great! There are well over 20 weapons to choose from, pistols, sub machine guns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, light machine guns and even exotics like the flame thrower or the re-curving bow. Also, almost all weapons are customizable, you can attach sound suppressors, scopes, extended magazines, etc. providing a truly varied arsenal which you can configure to perfectly fit your play style.
Long range and close quarter combat is usually viable in every FPS, but Far Cry 3 will also be completely playable using stealth tactics, even more, you will be rewarded for stealthy kills and takedowns (which are awesome by the way), or carefully and tactically liberating outposts without getting detected. Oh and do you remember the outpost re-spawn problem from Far Cry 2? It's gone! In Far Cry 3 a libreated outpost is taken over by the Rakyat, and will serve as a safe house.
As in the previous Far Cry installments, vehicles are also available. And I have to say (at least for me personally), the cars handle better and are more fun to drive than in many racing games… which is not something we are used to from an FPS.
But Far Cry 3 is so much more than a simple open world FPS… the introduction of RPG elements might sound scary for some hardcore FPS fans, but Far Cry 3 nailed it. During your adventures you gain experience and eventually level up, which is rewarded with skill points which you can use to unlock some incredibly cool and brutal takedown moves and other bonuses. The skills feel balanced, you’ll never become a Terminator, but they are also rewarding enough to make you want to unlock them.
And we are still not done, Far Cry 3 also has crafting! Now don't imagine a complex gathering/crafting system. You can gather skins and furrs from animals to create ammo bags and pouches, and different plants for different syringes which can heal you or provide different short term bonuses. Not much but it perfectly fits the game and the setting.
10/10
Sound:
While the previous Far Cry games were ok when it came to sounds, they never really managed to impress me. Far Cry 3 is different, the soundtrack finally contains some memorable tunes, the ambient sounds are great, the guns, the explosions and combat in general sounds brutal, and the voiceovers are some of the best I heard in a long time, again with Vaas stealing the show.
10/10
Replay value:
Far Cry 3’s plot is linear, and there aren't many choices you can take, you won’t replay the game for the different endings, but for everything else, because Far Cry 3 is pure fun. And... for Vaas!
9/10
Conclusion:
The third Far Cry game really managed to put an incredibly polished and fun gameplay onto the table. It would be nice if developers finally understood that visuals and content are important, but in the end, it’s the gameplay that will really make a game fun to play… because a good game is fun to play.
Great games however, are not only fun to play, but also look great and also have tons of content, and Far Cry 3 is one of these, it simply delivers in everything. Definitely a must have!
9.5/10

I tried to like this game.
I really tried.
That's not to say Far Cry 3 is a bad game. It has some very interesting features and there are a lot of improvements over the previous game (Far Cry 2), for example:
- Better stealth. Enemies can no longer spot you from miles away and snipe you with a pistol.
- No more infinite vehicle chase. If you come across an enemy patrol, you can outrun them instead of having them follow you till the end of Earth.
- More animals. Far Cry 2 had animals (Zebras!), but thtey were extremely rare.
- No more weapon deterioation. F*** the gun jamming mechanics in Far Cry 2. All it did was to force the player to visit a gun warehouse in between mission.
- Weapon customisation - horray for red-dot sights
- Stealth take down - in Far Cry 2 if you sneak up to someone and stab them in the back you will alert everyone nearby, but in Far Cry 3 you can actually perform a stealth kill with a melee weapon and even hide their body.
- Better fast travel - I can't remember how many bus rides I took during Far Cry 2.
- Crocodiles. I will never forget the first time I see an unsuspecting NPC get dragged into the river by a crocodile.
However, this game also has a lot of flaws, some I found critical, other annoying enough to put me off the game:
- You can't save during a mission. Sure you can quick save (which btw isn't mentioned in the game manual) to keep the loot you have found, but you will lose any other progress if you don't complete the mission in one sitting. Far Cry is supposed to be an open world game, so why the heck do I have to go to the menu to abandon quest if I change my mind half way through?
- Too bloody many tigers. More than once I have seen an outpost (that I am supposed to conquer) get slaughtered by some wild tiger/komodo dragon. While it's funny to watch the first time, it rapidly gets less interesting after that.
- NPCs keep repeating the same line. It's as if they only know 20 words in total.
- Immersion break. If the locals have formed a resistance group against the pirates, aside from the occansion patrols, why is is that I seem to be the only one fighting?
- Terrible health system that forces you to choose a stealthy approach. Even with a bullet proof vest, you can only last for a few seconds in a gun fight before you health is completely depleted. You pretty much have to thin the enemy out from a distance using a silenced weapon in order to survive.
- Odd graphics. This game has some very weird shading that reminds me of cell-shaded games. It is as if the developers can't make up their mind on whether to make the game look realistic or cartoonish.
I know that a lot of people will disagree with my opinion and there are a lot of positive reviews out there regarding this game. However, I feel that I have given this game a fair chance and I just cannot get around to enjoying myself playing it.

Heroes and Generals is a game with both positives and negatives.
The positives: There aren't many ww2 games out there, much less free to play.  The semi-auto rifles are extremely pleasing to fire, and feel very meaty.  It's quite enjoyable to shoot people in this game as a result.
The negatives: Much of your time is going to be spent walking or riding bikes to your objectives.  The game has a low time to kill, anywhere from 1 to 4 shots with the starting rifle, that you will be taken out often, and have to make the long trek back to the capture points. I have had the game freeze mid-match for me several times, which is strangely cleared up by ending the game window and relauncing from the mission window.  The battles can be very one-sided if your generals do not deploy armor or air to counter the enemy, as the basic infantryman has little to no tools to combat armor, without spending a lot of your ingame money to buy new weapons such as the bazooka.
All in all, it's a fun game. The bugs can be frustrating, and battles can be hopeless.  I'd recommend downloading, but don't put too much hope in the game.

It all began when I read Swiss Family Robinson as a kid and watched Gilligan's Island reruns on television. It probably continued while watching Fantasy Island, (and Herve Villichaize in the belltower shouting "de plane! de plane!") during a harsh Indiana winter. I'm referring to my love for the South Pacific Ocean. My love for that place was finally requited when I spent two and a half years there in the US Navy on a forward deployed Fast Frigate. I left the Navy, and those cherished waters never to return again save for my dreams and memories. And that's the sucky part about aging. Each passing year makes the details a little more fuzzy, a little more distant. Sometimes I feel as if they're the memories of an entirely different person.
And then I played
Guam, Diego Garcia, The Indian Ocean. It was all there for me, revisited on my computer screen. It was like an odd sense of coming home. Not only did the game's protagonist, Jason Brody, share the same adventurous locales as I did at his age, we also went through a deflowering of innocence all men take the path of, albeit mine occurred over years. Poor Brody's innocence was shattered the moment his brother and friends were accosted by the villians, Vaas and Hoyt, drug and slave traders who inhabit the gameworld like monsters.
As I lead Brody through a dark passage of rites in rescuing his friends and a preciptious push into manhood I've gotten to know the island like my own backyard. I've not been affected by a game like this in ages. When I haven't been playing I've been listening to the game soundtrack so efficiently and appropriately helmed by Brian Tyler (e.g. Constantine, Iron Man 3.) Driving down the Indiana countryside looking up at these gray autumn skies and listening to this music, it just makes me yearn so much to go back to the island. It's a desire only fulfilled when I can sit in front of my computer again and lose myself entirely in the gameworld.
The game will soon end for me. I'm on the last long downhill leg of the roller coaster. And it's been an ecstatic ride. Watching the end credits will be bittersweet, I'm sure, because I'm going to be reacquainted with that old feeling of leaving home once again.

Pleasantly surprised is probably my general feeling about this game- it's okay, but not great, except as compared to its thoroughly awful predecessor, Far Cry 2. FC3 is an open-world sandbox game set on a fictional Pacific island, populated by various missions, time trials, a buttload of item collecting quests and a general overarching plot.
The plot is basically that of a 90s action movie. You play a California Bro, out exploring Asia with the rest of his Bros and Broettes, who decide to end their vacation by parachuting onto a picturesque island in an x-treme fashion.  You and your bros are captured, abused, you escape and you embark on an adventure to free your friends, to find yourself, and to get even. Etc.
It suffers like most open-world games in that a lot of attention is placed either in developing the world or fleshing out the gameplay, but not usually both. In this case there is really little of note to do- most of the missions involve killing waves of dozens of identical soldiers before you can proceed to the next. There are a few standouts like the famous weed-farm burn mission, where you light up a marijuana plantation with a flamethrower while Skrillex blasts over the violence, but for the most part, the game is a sequence of boring set pieces that never quite satisfies. If you love pointless item collecting there's a ♥♥♥♥ing ton of it. I don't.
It's a ♥♥♥♥ing pretty game though, especially when you have a computer capable of cranking the graphics options (this is of course a Crytek engine) and it's really easy to feel like you're actually in the jungle wandering around the island. The sound DESIGN is okay, but tends to be populated by the three repetitive voice files your cardboard enemies say.
It's a decent play. Everyone probably owns this already, but if you want to experience the star of 2012, go for it.

Now most of you may be wondering why the heck I have wasted OVER 1000 HOURS ON THIS GAME! Well, the answer is simple. It is Mount & Blade: Warband. Aka, 1 never ending singleplayer sandbox rpg game, 1 200+ player server 700 servers medieval online game, 1 200+ player realistic skillful Napoleonic Wars dlc, and over 27,882 total mod conversions. Yeah, it is like 27,885 games in one.
The singleplayer game is a sandbox free-roaming medieval RPG that allows you to travel around the world of Calradia, and literally do anything you can dream of. There is no official end to the game so it is limitless. Become a merchant and travel the map selling goods, start up your own chains of businesses in the major cities, fight as a mercenary for your local lord, or become a bandit and harrass peasants. Fight as a soldier in one of the 6 kingdoms fighting for total domination, become a lord in one of these factions and raise your own army, as well as gain your own castle/village/town fiefdoms. Create your own faction and become the sole ruler of Calradia, the choice is yours.
Online is is a basic medieval game with many modes such as siege, team deathmatch, battle (1 life), etc, with up to 200+ player servers. It was the birthplace for War of the Roses. It is far better than War of the Roses online however with the combat system being so easy to learn yet so hard to master.
The Napoleonic Wars dlc derived from a mod called Mount and Musket, it was made a standalone expansion dlc in 2012 and is a sole-online 200-250 player server multiplayer game set in the final years of the Napoleonic Wars. You can fight as one of the main coalition forces at the time (Great Britain, Prussia, Austria, or Russia) or France itself. There are many game modes such as huge sieges with controllable artillery and destructible environments, Battle with over 200 people on a large map playing life size napoleonic battles, and when you are dead, you are dead. Commander battle where each player controls a squad of bots. And many many more modes. The dlc has musicians which play music orchestrated by real bands for the game and which give buffs to nearby teammates. There are huge amounts of teamwork necesarry with such a variety of balanced classes, and the combat system ensures that skill is the master of the battlefield. If you get bored of just playing on public servers then there are hundreds of clans or "regiments" that have formed and who organise and do events that are like the 200 player battles but where everyone is listening to officer orders and fight as lines, creating a warming community.
There are also ofc the mods, all of which I would stuggle to tell you about in this review. The main mod I would recommend however is Persistent World. It is a roleplay type mod where you join a server with a large free roaming custom map, with multiple castles and towns, and you and all of the other players roleplay as medieval citizens. You can work in the mines and earn some coin with the balanced economic system, you can become a Master Smith and forge new weapons or armour, or if you feel like fighting you can join one of the many factions in each server and fight in wars for your lord. Maybe even become the lord of a faction yourself? The choice is yours.
I would highly highly rate Mount & Blade Warband as it is such a complex yet simple game with more content than any other game I have ever played including Skyrim.
Thanks for reading, buy this game!

I discovered FC3 a few days ago and let me tell you I had no idea what I was getting into. I generally hate FPS, One of the main reason is I can't stand the first person POV. But FC3 is much more than a basic FPS. It has a real story with lots of crazy characters (Vaas, Hoyt, Sam, Dennis) and a beautiful setup : Kyrat Islands.
The adventure of Jason Brody will let you experience the depth of insanity with funny banters, some well placed reference to movies, books, etc and a wide range of weapons that you can customize (paints, sound suppressor, night vision and more).
Action driven, the game offers some side quests, some are enjoyable, others will not let you the greatest memories but all in all you have lots of things to do, and that often involve killing pirates, mercenaries, tigers, bears, komodo dragon, riding vehicle such as buggies, quads, jeeps, boats, delta wings...
The two islands are open world and quite huge, and even if there is a fast travel component, you'll often want to wander in the jungle to search for hidden treasure, or outposts to free from pirates and mercenaries.
As an FPS, the gameplay is quite basic but add some close combat components with impressive takedowns with a machete, and the 3 talent trees offers a variety of upgrades to your skills (range, survival and close combat).
Graphics are stunning (although It may require a good gaming rig to enjoy it in ultra) but I wasn't too fond of the musics in the game. Some missions will impose you ONE music over and over until the mission is over and it can prove very hard to listen to those after some time.
I haven't encountered any bugs during my nearly 40hrs of gameplay so I'd say that this was a good experience.
I'll end this review by stating once again the quality of the story : I laughed a lot and I sometimes reacted like the character with lots of f words and other bad language (I'm french and we have quite a lot of very explicite words for that !).
This was quite a trip, and I can't wait for FC4 to come out in november !

Whilst I've only played the game for 5 hours, I'm just going to say that there is a lot of content in this game and if you can get past all the really stupid stuff I'm sure you'll have a lot of fun. Personally though, I found the menus really create a huge amount of friction, so much so that I wanted to stop playing.
The game world itself is fun to explore, and the huge number of animals wandering around in it help it feel alive. Driving around fighting enemies and doing (some of) the missions was also generally enjoyable, but there doesn't seem to be a great deal of variety, and there is so much annoying stuff that I felt that I was merely pushing forward to get to the end of the game, or find something that would make it more fun, rather than playing it because I was enjoying it. As a result, after about 5 hours of playing, I've given up for now.
The menus, which are polished and have obviously had a lot of work put into them just create a huge break in immersion, and are cumbersome to use. To top it off, the game CONSTANTLY (especially at the start) notifies you of new things in the game and tutorials by showing messages in game, further taking you out of the game.
Whilst I like that there are a lot of items you can craft, there is very little discovery involved in the recipes; they simply unlock in the menus when you craft lower tier items and collect ingredients. Far Cry 3, a story driven first person shooter.
I purchased the Deluxe edition of the game when it was on the summer 2014 sale for $9.99 and have played a total of 7 hours as of this writing.
I would fit this game into the FPS genre and add that this is more then just an FPS, its a Story Driven FPS. There is a compelling and interesting story to go through with the solo campaign of the game and the game starts off with an intense beginning.
My first several hours into the game and I have to wounder why I didn't get into the Far Cry series before. Far Cry 3 is the first game in the series I have played and I am pleased with it thus far. I do want to keep playing more and finish the story line to see how it all comes to conclusion.
There is more to the game if you play a multiplayer coop campaign but I have not yet tried that as I want to experience it all at my pace and not run and gun through it all. I will eventually play coop but not for a while.
There is lots to do in the game other then the main missions. I have spent time hunting down animals for there skins, collecting plants and exploring sunken ships, caves and ruins.
The crafting in the game is simple, its not overly complex like other games with crafting. If you want to upgrade your wallet to hold more money then you will need to collect animal skins of a certain animal. You will see what kind of animal skin is needed when you select the upgraded version and then on the map you will see the symbol of the animal. In that area somewhere you will find it, kill it and skin it. This will be how you will go about hunting animals to get there skins so you can upgrade your various gear, like, Loot sack, ammo pouch, weapon holster and so forth.
When gathering plants (Green, Blue, Read, White) you will use them to make syringes for restoring health or to make a boost in abilities. I have only made health restorative ones as of yet.
There is allot more to the game beyond the main missions. There are random supply drop's side missions where you will drive a vehicle from point to point (a marked flare on the ground) till you get the supplies to the needed person. Hunting various wildlife, timed runs, finding lost relic's, letters and video memory cards.
The game map starts off with a small section visible and as you activate radio towers throughout the map more sections become visible. The areas that are not visible also do not show up on the mini-map making it more interesting to explore and find the path the to other radio towers.
Hang-gliders are also around the island to use and sale through the air to other sections. Its kind of nice to to glide in the air over the island areas and see what there is around.
Far Cry 3 is very Xbox 360 controller friendly. Button arrangements are done well and its a joy to play with the controller over keyboard and mouse.
I didn't like that I have to access the game menu to get to the crafting and would have rather seen an option of a work table or something in a safe zone (or in the game world) for doing crafting. Other then that, I have to say that this game is very impressively done and UbiSoft did an excellent job. I am looking forward to the next Far Cry game.
Having waited during the Summer Sale of 2014 for the Deluxe edition of the game to go on sale and getting it for $9.99 I have to say a resounding Yes! I am sure that subsequent sales will have the game on sale as well. Look for it during the Holiday Sale folks.

The Far cry series is kinda weird in that the titles aren't really connected. Far Cry one did some things better than Far Cry 2 while Far Cry 2 introduced some elements that were really cool...
All 3 games so far have the same common denominator: An awesome story.
In many ways, it's just another open-world FPS, and many open-word FPS games do a better job at being "open world FPS games" than Far Cry does, but Ubi Soft has stuck with their Assassin's Creed vibe, and provided tons of extremely amusing ways of getting around in this game. If you ever wanted a game where you could go from para-gliding to diving with sharks in less than 3 seconds, you've found your title.
The amount of extreme sports represented in this game is amazingly high, and while the classic annoying ubi-soft elements are ever present in the game (collect 100 of these meta-items to unlock this slightly better weapon..), these minor nuisances pale in comparison to the story and the amusing game-experience.
I list the game as low-replayability for a reason though. Once the story in this game is complete, there is no point in playing anymore, just like with all other ubi-soft games (except maybe the new Splintercell titles).

Far Cry 3 might be one of the best singleplayer shooters I have ever played. The action is great and you can have fun running and gunning your way through your enemies or take the sneaky approach stabbing them in the back and chaining together multiple enemies to take down at once. It is loads of fun and highly replayable. I'd recommend this to anyone.

Far Cry 3 is one of Ubisofts better releases. The games combat is pretty fun, though I recommend consistently going at it with a stealth approach, as I found the jungle settings and the verticality of the island made that the most enjoyable method of approach for me. The story is fairly strong for the most part, and a few of the characters fit the "love to hate" bill pretty well. It took me a few hours before I really started to "get it," but the experience of playing it off and on for a few months ended with me plowing through the last half of the game in a weekend as I discovered what it really had to offer.
I would wait for a good sale before picking it up.

So you like the concept of games like Civilization or the Crossroad Keep contruction/defense portion of Neverwinter Nights 2 but find yourself either too far removed from tactical command in the former and too little involved beyond a single battle in the latter?  Mount and Blade - Warband is your niche then.  Every battle features you in full frontline command of your forces to deploy and employ how you see fit.  Beyond the battlefield though you have to curry favor with major factions in the world then when you've decided to either carve your own niche into the world or pledge yourself to one of the existing factions you're responsible for garrison management, finances, and building plans with a dose of political manuvering thrown in for good measure.  If you're the sort of control freak that demands full control of your empire from top to bottom and back again then this is just about the most perfect commander and ruler game you can find.

After playing the immensely entertaining Blood Dragon expandalone and hearing so much praise I decided to try the base game as well. What a bombastic disappointment.
The biggest downside of this game I found to be the characters and story. While having a crazy villain can be an interesting thing it soon turned out that almost every one in the game is complete nutjob. The story is dragged out (more on this below) and littered with pointless busywork and unbelievable twists - souring what's in principle a very engaging narrative. The player character is jarringly inconsistent and unrelatable in his reactions and decisions. The hallucination scenes I found to be more annoying than cool due to the silly decision to turn them into on rails walking installations instead of proper cutscenes. And the Alice in the wonderland "cutscenes" only reinforced the impression that the developers thought way more of their "artistic abilities" than was warranted.
The crafting/unlocking/progression system was equally badly designed and cumbersome. Putting highly restrictive limitations on inventory space in the early portions of the game where looting is most important and making you swim in it when you no longer need it. In the same line money is essentially pointless because you quickly gather enough good weapons for free or on the cheap to not really needing anything anymore once you start raking on tons of money. Instead of a fun motivator to explore it's nothing more than a hindrance and cheap grind mechanic to lengthen a game that would already outstay its welcome anyway.
The combat however is for the most part very good and the world feels alive, rich and very beautiful. Being able to take different approaches to clearing bases, seeing enemies interact with the environment and getting bonus points for a stealthy approach is very rewarding. Unfortunately the hunting side missions, racing and shooting challenges are uninspired and repetetive. And since you're quickly swimming in money there's no real motivation to do them either.
Add on top of that some highly annoying quirks and bug like getting a phone call for your current mission every single time you died or enemies that can occasionally see through walls and wreck your attempt at stealth liberations. This turns Far Cry 3 into a game that's far too often frustrating, unrelatable and grindy.

In short:
+ Big, open battles with tons of room to choose your own approach
+ A career system that provides a great overall motivation to win every match
+ The option to eventually choose your own role in the war (tank commander, infantry, paratrooper, sniper etc.)
+ A good balance between realism and back-to-the-action gameplay
+ Free to play, with a paying option that basically only speedens up career progress. No pay to win.
- Single battles are easy to join, but the queues for battles from the war screen are long, and have an unreliable timer
- There does not seem to be a voice chat option, which makes teamwork quite hard in a game that's perfect for it
- Minor bugs like tanks bouncing on their side after bumping against a bicycle and player names popping up too late over teammates, resulting in friendly fire.
Review
If you enjoy games like Day of Defeat and Red Orchestra, then you definitely should give this a shot, because it brought me back to the days when WW2 shooters were king and all my free time went into playing them.
The battlefields are large and provide a great amount of freedom in choosing how to conquer objectives. Don't expect small maps for compact Call of Duty-like battles, but large maps with outstretched forests, rocks, hills and fields.
You will start as a simple soldier, but by playing the game you will progress along a career path. At certain points the option will open up to change your profession. This way, you can choose to start a career as a tank operator, paratrooper or others.
The free to play in this game does not lead to a pay to win model. If you decide to invest money, your will earn more points during play and thus progress faster. At the time of writing a player who plays for free can achieve the same as a paying player, but it will simply take longer. What most of these people are saying is true.
Yes, weapons and vehicles cost a lot! Which means you should focus your attention on what you need the most, not just buy any old thing. Personally, I switched to SMG on my main guy ASAP, and did a lot of assaulting and defending flags. For indoor fights, SMGs beat everything but grenades. The down side to getting an SMG is that you're useless at range.
Yes, switching classes after the first free switch has a cost. But you're free to purchase (with ingame funds) multiple characters, rather than switching. I have a Tanker and a general infantryman.
All in all, the game's lack of constant user interface elements to make you aware of every old thing means that if you're standing in the woods, you're looking for signs of movement. Did someone just move behind that bush, or is it the wind?
Or, while in a tank - is that a boulder in the far distance on that hill, or an enemy tank?
I've never been much into (semi)realistic war games, but this game has me loving it. The sheer satisfaction when you realise that's not a pile of leaves but a guy in camo gear laying prone and sniping your buddies is immense - even if it's short-lived if he happens to be looking your way.
If you're on foot, and an enemy tank is looking at you, you're toast. But if you're in cover, or dancing around it, it has no way of defending against you. If you brought a handy Panzerschreck, take it out from behind - if you didn't, maybe he'll pop his head out to get a better look at things, and you can shoot him and take his tank. Failing that, just hovering near and looking at him will make him 'spotted' - so there's a marker where he's last been spotted. And if you're constantly looking at him, it updates. So friendly tanks, or AT people can take it out.
It's a bit rough around the edges but very enjoyable in it's current beta state. 7/10 Would recommend to friends.

OLD REVIEW
I really don’t like giving thumbs up or down so I just explain my experience, but I have found this gaming experience more negative than positive. I started playing and really enjoyed the open environments. Then, I realised you could shoot someone in the chest with a M1 and they would survive. There would be blood to register the hit but they would keep coming. Then I fully comprehended the significance of the health bar. It means that you do damage as opposed to inflicting injury. A person of 100% health operates to the same relative level of effectiveness as someone with 1% health. This made the game very arcade-y and clearly established the precedent that weapons damage is more important than deployment tactics (flanking, defence, offence etc). What counts in Heroes and Generals? Your weapon not your tactics.
And here’s the kicker. Players with better weapons can kill you faster. This would be fine if you could not buy weapons with real money. This game is totally ‘pay-to-win’ (which is fine) but the free-to-play players (which is not me in this case) are often completely destroyed by those with purchased equipment. This means that there is no challenge! Or, there is not point to playing.
Let me give you an example. I was, at first, a free-to-play player. I spawned and was gunned down by a tank. I had absolutely no way of killing this tank, nor did any other player spawning in the house. We were trapped inside and had absolutely no recourse. The enemy had won because they had a tank. So people were leaving the server in frustration due to the hopelessness of the situation; a situation exacerbated by people leaving and coming constantly.   I spawned six times before the tank went away. In chat, his team were asking him why he left and he replied “this is boring”. When I got out of the spawn zone, I was ambushed by three tanks further down the road. It is hopelessly (literally there was no hope) unbalanced.
I paid $25 and became a member. This is when I realised that weapons are hugely expensive and even with the XP upgrade, the grind was extremely slow. Eventually I got an anti-tank weapon. Mine was the only one on the team. I hit a tank, but because I had not paid enough for the bigger weapons, the tank shrugged it off. I was then killed by two tanks and bombed by an aircraft.
I pressed on however and continued the grind, not spending my gold and determined to win via skill. This is when I realised that there were only five maps – and most of the time you are only playing on two. This made the grind highly repetitive. Not only that, the maps generally favour specific sides during an engagement, meaning it is extremely difficult to win certain maps as specific sides.
I have had some good kills and a little fun. However, the game at the moment does not capture the essence of World War II and instead constitutes nothing more than a pay-to-win (oh yes!) generically arcade-y FPS. Disappointing considering what they could have done. I’ll play for a little while longer (when I can be bothered) but I will only continue if the game DRASTICALLY changes.

This game is only in its beta stage, yet has A LOT of potential.
On the outside, this game is another WWII FPS/TPS. But when you sit down and explore what it has to offer, this game is very different than other WW2 shooters out there. It's multiplayer only and executes it very well, with counters to all of the seemingly 'invincible' vehicles or 'overpowered' weapons (a personal favorite for me) seeing as anyones vehicle can carry anti-tank weaponry and other tanks with some tactical prowess can eliminate any threat to its comrades. The game starts all of us off as the basic "when you say jump i say how high" grunt, armed with a semi-auto weapon and a few nades. after ranking up enough, you'll unlock your basic smg's and other killing tools including my favorite, the trench shovel, used to go commando when your gun starts clicking! After a few levels you'll be 'ranked' enough to become a more specialized soldier, becoming anywhere from a tank commander to a paratrooper to even an ace pilot. You'll be able to use different weaponry and purchase a variety of vehicles suited to your classification. On another note, no gun can honestly become that overpowered beast that you see everyone using. All primary weapons will produce single-hit kills when it's a headshot. This and the good range for the semi-auto rifles you start with make it a very balanced shooter, rarely seeing one player outdo the rest of his team (unless his whole team is made up of trolls and vegtables)
For now, the only playable countries are the Germans and the Americans, but in the future the devs say they'll add the Japanese, the British, and the Russians into the game for playable countries.
For a F2P game, it goes above and beyond.

Far Cry 3 is one strange game, on the surface, it appears to be a first person mash-up of Just Cause 2’s open world enemy outpost attacking and Tomb Raider’s ledge platforming/strange occult happenings on the Island. Yet when you dig a little deeper, you discover that it is exactly those things... with the main difference being that bows are less fun to use, as well as the absence of a grappling hook, lack of interesting characters or an understandable story and all those other things that tend to make games more enjoyable to play.
The story itself is pretty awful, you, your brother, his girlfriend, your girlfriend, your other brother and 2 other friends have all been kidnapped by a creepy mohawk guy who I can’t for the life of me remember the name of! You’ll just have to escape and free the others. So begins about 8 hours of confusing alliances with yet more people with interchangeable names, during which, you rescue, one-by-one, your useless friends, who do nothing really to help you other than to comment on how heavily armed and tattooed  (sorry tataued?) you’ve become. Speaking of tattoos, they are a rather interesting way of showing your progression through the skill trees, as with each new skill, you earn another tat, classy. Through the tense and action packed storyline, you get to meet, among others, an American guy who likes flamethrowers, a really creepy Australian guy and an even creepier woman who likes wacky rituals… These “characters”, apart from all being completely psycho, contribute to help or hinder you as you travel “your path” of revenge against the Mohawk guy from the beginning. I personally didn’t really want revenge on this guy, much preferring just to go home, but that’s alright, because I don’t have to make those sorts of decisions! The only real choices you get in this game are pretty much just relegated to what weapons you get to carry, which in some cases is cut down by having to carry a plot-significant heavy weapon like a flamer that my long range sniper build didn’t need.
In between my character’s illogical decision making, the game actually gets fun. Generally, you’re allowed to leave the plot missions for a while and go explore which typically involves climbing defunct radio towers to reveal parts of the landscape (something I think was done better in this title than Assassin’s Creed!), then finding the nearest pirate outpost and taking it over. Whilst I’ve read a lot of praise for this part of gameplay, (which is undoubtedly fun), I rarely found it necessary to scout out and silently kill all the guards to avoid setting off the alarm, since I tended to forget about that and charge in with a HMG armed technical, mowing down even armoured pirates with ease. Besides, when you’re in a vehicle, dogs, leopards and angry cassowaries can’t hurt you!
The animal life in the game is pretty cool, with all sorts of deadly creatures out to get you, including but not limited to snakes, crocs, tigers, bears and tortoises - although the tortoises are about as deadly as a speed-bump (which I often used them as, sorry cuties...). Aside from the fact that these animals seem to be armoured and unless strictly classified as “prey” will not scatter when shot, instead preferring to go out in a blaze of glory and charge me, they seem pretty realistic, and it always adds a bit of fear to wandering off the roads into the jungle (which I do not recommend if in a vehicle).
The vehicle handling is pretty well done, although like in FC2, the available choices are usually limited to different coloured jeeps and technicals, with the rare cargo truck or buggy scattered around the place. That’s not to say the devs haven’t tried to make each technical look different, I was particularly impressed by the different rust patterns and colours I found, at times wondering whether any of my weathering pigments could approximate that hue… they won’t if you’re wondering.
Overall, the game is pretty good, but I’m left feeling a little sickened after the main storyline, since mutilation isn’t really my thing… Other flaws contribute to making elements of the game just painful. For instance, I was constantly getting stuck when running on stairs and other small rocks in the ground, which if I was playing battlefield wouldn’t be a problem (come on this is basic stuff, even for a 2012 game!). The extremely cluttered hud with massive text reminding you of your objective was also pretty distracting, bring back FC2’s minimalist one! Thankfully, once the main story is complete, you can free-roam to you heart’s content, so I may still play it for that, but the flaws do add up, so I definitely would not recommend paying full price for the game, the fact that it got GOTY awards when others from 2012 like ME3 didn’t really surprised me. I’d say definitely play it, just get it in a sale first :D

Whether you want to explore a massive jungle, hunt animals with a variety of weapons, kill bad guys, blow up cars/buildings or set terrain on fire - this is the game for you.
Far Cry 3 continues on the foundation of Far Cry 2 except it's not as punishing in terms of equipment, by which I mean that you don't need to swap your weapon for a new one or repair them after firing them once.
+ Ammo isn't too hard to come by. You pick it off fallen enemies or use the cash you scavenge to refill your stock at safehouses.
+ To heal you actually need medicine which is acquired by crafting it using green (types of) plants that you collect in the jungle. You don't regenerate all your health (you start out with 2 slots of health) by just standing around, stepping away from the more commonly used auto-heal-regen these days.
+ The soundtrack is lovely.
+ Amazing scenery!
- Day/night cycle mechanic based on your movement, both WASD and mouse. You can stand perfectly still (WASD) but still move time forward by wiggling your mouse.
- Wonky AI at times. If one enemy detects you they all know where you are even if it's never announced (by a shout/gunfire/etc), even if said enemy only detected you AS you performed the silent takedown.
- Platforming (for climbing signal towers among other things) can be tricky. Ledges that can be climbed are marked in a certain way but you can't climb them unless you are given the indicator to climb them. Except that you can if you spam your jump-button, unless it doesn't trigger because you spammed it.
All in all - very much recommended!

I started playing this game back when it was still in the browser.  Ever since CoD: UO I've been a big fan of WWII shooters but nothing really hits the spot quite like H&G.  There are two sides to the game, the fps side and the tactical side.  I've seen wars dominated by generals working together to dominate the campaign map as I've seen battles won by a small group of soldiers who work together like a well-oiled machine.
One of the things that works so well in H&G is that there's a system of progression in place for the soldiers that you create.  You name the soldier, modify his weapon to fit your playstyle and hop into a game to get your "pay" according to your rank's payrate.  Over time you'll unlock various ribbons, badges, weapons and weapon modifications that can be used to turn your rookie into a hardened war vet.
The f2p model is done very well.  And, to be fair, I'm very picky about f2p games.  With real money you can purchase cosmetics for your soldier or his weapon (which is nothing really out of place).  Also, you can optionally choose to purchase a new class or weapon sooner rather than later as well as xp boosts.  The prices are relatively reasonable if you do choose to purchase anything, however they are not at all neccessary in the long run.  Anything a player can buy they can buy with in-game credits as well (barring cosmetics).  Also of note is that progression is already well-paced so the game doesn't make you feel like you HAVE to pay to be competative.
All in all, I've had a lot of very fun moments in this game that I wished I had recorded.  When your units are limited, the last thing you want to do is get killed and have to play as another class so survival and knowing your role is key to victory.  Being able to team up with a friend or two is a plus.  There are plenty of ways to play the game so pick what you enjoy and help lead your team to victory!

A lot of what you do in Far Cry 3 raises perplexing questions: why would a rucksack made from the skin of the Undying Bear hold more than the one I made from four dead dingoes earlier? Can't I just make one out of six dead dingoes? What is it about Undying Bear skin that facilitates a particularly capacious rucksack design? And more to the point: if it's never died, how would anyone know?
But as I scramble away from it, panic-firing my traditional tribal pump action, what I'm actually wondering is this: when did Far Cry 3 become so good?
We'd been told it was an 'open world' game, but everything Ubisoft showed of it made it look like a monologue-heavy, tightly scripted adventure, its freedom limited to small mission areas. That is in there, it turns out: there's an absurdly long series of missions about rescuing your friends from the pirates who've captured them. But it's just one of the many different games you can play on this vast, freely explorable tropical island.
Hunting wild game to make bags out of their skin is another. Guns, money, syringes and all types of ammunition require their own special container, and every size of every container can only be made from the skin of one particular species of animal. And while guns, money, syringes and all types of ammunition are abundantly available on the island, its people have apparently never invented the bag.
So you, American tourist Jason Brody, must bring your container technology to the island by personally inventing and reinventing various types of harnesses, wallets and sacks, culminating in your magnum opus: the Undying Bear Skin Rucksack, a masterpiece of dermatological engineering capable of holding up to 96 leaves.

For the most part, I had a good time playing Far Cry 3. Combat was excellent. With many different weapons and weapon types, you'll be able to set up an arsenal that allows many different styles of play. Wanna run into gunfights like a tank and cause as much collateral damage possible? There are plenty of LMGs for you to do that in a way that suits you. Wanna stealthily pick off enemies one by one without ever being seen? There is a ♥♥♥♥ing compound bow for that. As for A.I., with opposing factions having the ability to call in reinforcements and multiply in minutes, they often required a tactical approach. As someone who greatly enjoys tactical and stealth games, this was an enjoyable challenge. Another place that FC3 excelled in is it's world. Fighting pirates isn't the only thing the island had to offer. From hunting to hang gliding, there were many side activities that provided entertainment, but also added bonuses to your character(i.e. crafting a larger loot rucksack out of animal skins to increase your inventory space). Being both beautiful, and deadly to the unprepared player, the island was a great place to immerse yourself in. Beyond combat and setting, FC3 begins to go downhill. The story was... confusing to say the least. The first part of the story was great. It was simple, sensible, and interesting. As you progress through the game, it gets overly complicated and your objective sways from wanting to save your friends, to wanting to kill every enemy of the Rakyat, the native islanders. A was not a fan of this change in the story. It made you lose contact with most of the NPCs you actually cared liked, and made the story slightly boring because of this. Glitches were.. not uncommon. Most of them were aesthetic(textures not flowing with models correctly), but this did not inhibit my ability to enjoy the game. What did however were animations. They were so bad that I would like to think they were bugs, but they may have been so incredibly awful that they could be mistaken for bugs.
Overall, this is a nice game with a few flaws.
7/10
