I enjoyed this game for a little while- I really did. For a free game, it's got decent mechanics and the graphics are fine in my opinion. It reminds me of old Battlefield games updated to be a little more relevant today and that I like especially about the title. The terrain you fight over is pretty well done with decent amounts of sparse cover usually forcing you to fight from longer ranges, meaning there's a much heavier preference on rifles than submachine guns unless you're playing in one of the village maps. Topping it off, firing from the hip is usually very ineffective, so the game does have lots and lots of room for thoughtful gameplay. There are just a few moments where the mechanics tend to get wonky but I pit that one in with general inexperience and something that gets better with time. Some people complain about lag, but I personally didn't witness all that much- maybe one moment where I was killed even though I had full health and the enemy only shot one round from his submachine gun and it wasn't a headshot. The matchmaking-system does take a bit of time to put you on the ground, which is a turn off but it's not so distracting since the majority of matches I played lasted long enough to make waiting for up to a minute a non-issue. You can usually get into a match quick if you manually find a match.
In the tier one battles (basically the tutorial roster full of first rank players), my friend and I had quite a few of "those moments" in a shooter where you spot an enemy crossing far out who's obviously trying to flank, we'd take a position in some rocks near their path and wait for them in the trees, easily defending the base before they even got close. However, once you get placed ahead in the ranks, you immediately get thrown into a little bit more chaos and tactics can pretty often get left aside for a free for all brawl. Once you're facing enemies with tanks, these moments pretty much evaporate.
Despite how much I enjoyed my experience, I can't recommend this game in its current state. The game isn't well balanced at all. You go from rank one to fighting whole teams that clearly paid real money for tanks, bombers and powerful machine guns and sniper rifles. The amount of the free currency you get for winning missions is abysmally low, and the first anti-tank weapon you get costs nearly 90,000 of it, and then all you get is a Bazooka with four shots that you have to buy ammo for using more of the same currency. I didn't keep perfect track of how much I was getting per match, but I'd say it was usually around 5000 or less.
It was around my third hour playing that I started to notice how useless it felt to play in most battles and how much the developers seemed to be leaning on the idea that I should be tossing them my credit card if I wanted to really make a difference. The overwhelming majority of battles I took part in devolved into the US team getting ploughed like a two dollar hooker by a team full of higher ranked Germans or people that had paid a decent amount of cash to field armored vehicles. The only way I could do any damage to tanks was if there was a panzershrek spawn nearby, which are extremely rare, take forever to respawn and usually took more than two to destroy even the first level enemy tank. On top of all that, they were incredibly hard to aim, even when sighted in for range. On a different match our attacking team couldn't push forward because the enemy had three to five dive bombers that were constantly destroying any vehicle we got onto the field and could destroy the AA cannons that only spawned in one base deep in enemy territory before we could even aim the damn things. Small arms fire does hurt them, but barely, and usually only if they're flying low to the ground and straight at you... and if you know how the planes in WW2 usually worked, if they're flying right at you you're pretty much a dead man.
For these reasons, I can't see this game as anything but pay2win. It would take me hours and hours of time invested into the game to be even close to the same level as these people. Whole days spent finding matches that aren't being completely obliterated by an enemy team that paid up to a hundred or more dollars before playing, just so I could play and not feel that useless. The infantry fights and holdouts I've gotten into were great fun- amazing fun. The only thing I found odd about those fights was that players using an MG42 fired from the hip could instakill people at close ranges but they're heavy and not great for attacking with (I picked one up off the ground and went on quite a killing spree with his last mag). But as I've seen, once you get a vehicle, even if you purchased it with the free currency, you'd have to spend even more of the free currency just in maintaining it. So you wouldn't really be able to use it to advance to the next tier of tanks, especially since every fight I had with Germans was all bombers, tanks and AT. Nevermind all that, buying membership gives you an extra weapon and buff space (which could be an extra 15% stamina to sprint with, a 5/10/15% damage reduction, extra explosive damage, etc.) whereas free players get just one buff slot and only three weapon slots (which includes your melee weapon that you also have to purchase). Membership also gives you boosts to get these things faster even on top of having paid for them.
I know a lot of people will dispute this, but all they have to say is that it's merely possible to unlock it without paying for it. Time is money. If it'd take me 24+ hours in-game to not be worthless, it's pay2win. There's really no excuse a player could give me to prove the contrary.
Until the game is balanced and some more work is done on it, if you really want a WW2 shooter, I'd recommend checking out a different title. But as I said, since this game is technically free to download and play, you aren't losing anything for the first four hours you invest.

This game does have potential to get better, but in its current form I don't recommend it.  It is your basic "pay to win" formula.  As a free player, you start out with your minimal 1 to 2 weapon combo, and must grind for hours to be able to upgrade to new equipment.   Meanwhile those who opt to pay real money are given access to better gear, faster experience/credit rewards, and an extra badge slot (which basically allows for an extra ability).  I did have fun for the first few hours playing map after map as an infantryman saving up my money to upgrade to a pilot.  Once I reached pilot rank the game took a completely different turn (for the worse) in "dogfighting" mode.  I've played several flight simulators in the last 25 years, and I'll just say that this game needs some work on the flight system.  The controls are simply awful, not to mention there is no tutorial mode for flying.  Being up against "paying" players with superior aircraft, my plane was gunned down numerous times usually in less than 30 seconds. Been looking forward to getting the chance to play this having been a fan of the Far Cry serious so far.

Unbelievable.
Edit:
After sorting out crashing issue by install a new power supply, I am mostly enjoing this game.   It is typical Far Cry - better than average FPS.   I think that the story telling is getting a little better as the series progresses although the premise of this one is a little ridiculous and seems to try and appeal to teen gamers whereas you would think that the main audience would be those playing since the original FC and therefore late 20s up.   Also I feel that the engine has taken a backward in some areas such as environment destructability.   The addition of animals is interesting but they are far too frequent and aggressive, and in some areas it feels like a MMO where you have to battle the mobs to be able to traverse it.   Games like Skyrim are better balanced in this respect.
I cant think of anything that stands out as a marked improvement over FC2 except perhaps that it is less chokepointed and that locations with respawning enemy are much fewer.   It has probably improved generally in terms of graphics but that is difficult to compare without playing them back to back.
Overall, if you enjoyed the FC and FC2 you will probably enjoy this game as well.

After being disappointed with Ubisoft for a long time now, Far Cry 3 felt like a step in the right direction. In the past, Splinter Cell was one of my favorite franchises and I followed it very closely. I am still familiar with the forever-old/young Sam Fisher but his current adventures don't interest me. Blacklist was such an awful mess that I couldn't be bothered to finish the first campaign level. And that was playing it on console. But a lot of the mess that is Splinter Cell Blacklist involves the core game mechanics including the "stealth" system, which is the same exact detection system used in Far Cry 3. All the way down to the HUD graphics and sounds. Despite the massive failure that is the detection system used in Blacklist, that same system works enormously better in Far Cry 3. The levels of detection and suspicion along with the difference in game play styles made for a very good fit between Far Cry 3 and the stealth system also used by Splinter Cell Blacklist. Without going extremely in-depth about the specific differences between how the same system works differently in both games, I raise one question. Why is there no prone position in either game???!??!

Since the game is still in beta and still has more then a few flaws it's tricky to judge. But if you were to leave out some bugs and glitches the game would be more than a fine and quite realistic WW2 simulator. Played alone or in a coordinated team it is still very enternaining, but company makes everything easier and more fun and ads more realism to what operations looked like back in the day.
Now be careful: this is not a run and gun and trust me, I'm telling from experience. Try to run alone through a forest next to the enemy camp and I can assure you, you will die in a matter of momoments. Just one shot is enough to get you killed, one single bullet can take the best soldier of the army out if he's not being careful enough.
This game is all about STRATEGY, TIMING, PRECISION and about OUTSMARTING the enemy.
This is a free to play game but it is NOT a pay to win game, you can be the best soldier of the match simply by using the most basic rifle of the game, as it is all about when and where you fire your bullet. The makers of the game surely have to make money, that's why many of the camos, vehicles and extras; like new and different (but not neceessarily better) weapons are really hard to get and that, my friends, is where cash comes in, but as I already said you can unlock them just by spending more than a few more hours on the game, which will surely happen if you are enjoying it.
Of course it still has a few major bugs, the most typical ones are: when the bullet clearly hit the enemy but the hit isn't somehow counted so it doesn't affect the opponent and when you engage in melee combat and the stabs or wacks don't count. These are followed by many other small bugs that slightly affect the gameplay or visuals.
This game requires a little of skill with mouse and keyboard which luckily is easy to master, trust me folks if I did it you can do it too. Precision is always tricky and unfriendly when it comes to aiming and shooting all in a matter of moments.
I am no pro but I felt like this game is fun, and I wanted to give my opinion, the one of a simple gamer who's just playing for fun.
Keep in mind I'm just a young boy enjoying a game with friends.

Since I’m a huge Battlefield fan and seeing the death of the all-out-warfare behemoth makes me incredibly sad, I’m inclined to find alternatives. In my search, I stumbled upon the beta of Heroes & Generals – WWII FPS-strategy hybrid. It’s developed by Reto-Moto, a team consisting of ex-IO-Interactive founders.
What they have done here with Heroes & Generals is fascinating: they’ve combined two very different games we love to play – an FPS: playing as a soldier on the field and a tabletop wargame: leading the whole war campaign strategy as a commander.
Which leads us to some very interesting territory – metagame in the form of wars, taking weeks until one of the sides (United States or Germany) wins. It’s like eRepublik, in the sense that the FPS battles that players fight directly influence the whole campaign map.
You can look at it as an MMO or just a regular FPS. But before I tell you if it is any good I have to mention few important things about it though.
Heroes & Generals is Free2Play, which means it’s full of unlockables and all sorts of bars that measure your progress. The second warning is that this game is still in development, in fact, it was recently released on Steam Early Access (which means one of the two things – either there are going to be tons of micro patches or no mega patches at all (just kidding)).
The way the whole game is constructed is actually pretty interesting. Let me TRY to explain everything I have managed to grasp so far.
Imagine that the metagame is on a map with control points (CP) and roads in between them. Some control points are factories, that produce machines (tanks, planes, etc.) and cities, that produce ammunition and men.
The goal is for any of the sides to capture as many CPs as possible with assault teams (AT), that are created with men. ATs and supplies can be moved and commanders assign resources to each AT. When two opposing ATs meet in a control point, the matchmaker creates a room and regular soldiers fight in the so called Action Game – the FPS portion of this title.
The layout of main bases and capture points in the FPS map also differ, depending on the meta map. When one of the sides wins the battle, the according side assumes control over the point of interest.
Sounds interesting and at the same time confusing? It absolutely does!
My biggest interest is in the Action Game which I’ve spent 3 hours in so far.
The general impression I got from spending my time is that Action Game is very much like Red Orchestra (RO) – light realism and not fast paced Team Fortress 2. Depending on the map size and the resources the commander has made available, there are more vehicles in a given mission.
For example there is a hilly forest map where the only vehicles you will encounter are civilian bicycles. It is an adorable scene to watch people ride on this thing, given the fact that two people can get on it, while ringing its cute bell. But you might also fight in a map with light tanks that will shred you into pieces and planes that will drop payloads onto your little head.
One interesting aspect I noticed is the player count in Heroes & Generals – 18vs18. That seems like an odd choice to me, given the fact that most shooters go for 16vs16 or 32vs32.
The gunplay is not the most satisfying I’ve seen, but it’s not bad by any means, for me it’s above average. The gun recoil is actually pretty low, but the bullet spread is not a joke. The equipment you carry in Heroes & Generals compared to your regular $60 shooter is rather limited, here you start only with a rifle and few grenades. Unlocking additional weapons, gadgets and vehicles requires a lot of playing, hence the Free To Play structure of this game.
Usually I don’t like when shooters have 30+ weapons, but the case here is different – there are too few – only handful of rifles and machine guns. I hope they add few more to the rotation as the development goes further.
One thing I noticed that people may dislike is that the player movement can be described as “sluggish” – there is momentum to it, like Miasmata. Another thing that surprised me about it was that in the crouch and lay down positions it’s way slower than other shooters like Red Orchestra and Battlefield – I don’t recommend crawling. There is also sprinting, but it acts like dashing, since you can’t sprint hundreds of meters. Also, jumping is floaty, like on a lower gravity Earth, which I hope gets refined.
As it is in our age, doing all sorts of things on the field in today's FPSs earns you combat badges. Heroes & Generals lets you equip those and have minor buffs, like +7.5% damage to armoured targets when you use the Chauffeur badge for example.
There is also an interesting game mechanic where you can’t get in enemy vehicles, unless you unlock them with holding “E” for some time, depending on the size of the machine you are trying to bust in.
One peculiar feature about the tanks I noticed is that you can get in third person view, but that exposes your characters model for easy shots from the hostile outside world. I think this is an interesting trade off for those who like to be always aware of their surroundings.
Because Heroes & Generals is still not baked properly, if you decide to play it now, among the fun you are going to have, you will also be greeted with some frustrating and clearly not finished features.
While most F2P MMOs in engine rendering, server browser and character screens are seemingly in one window, this is not the case with Heroes & Generals. The 3D rendered scenes are done separately from the other features mentioned above, like Battlelog in the newer Battlefield titles. Which results in a relatively smooth Action Game, while the Commander map is working very slow.
Then there is the options menu that can be accessed only in the Action Game, where aren’t that many graphical options to begin with, but good set of sound ones. You can bind your keys, but one thing that bothered me was that I had to hold right mouse button to stay in sights, which I’ve never liked to do in any game.
All of this also means that the server browser/character screens have their own options menu, which makes things a bit confusing.
One of the weakest points of this game is its lobby user interface. The server browser is lackluster, where you can’t see the actual ping values. When I jumped blind into this game I tried to use the queue system – don’t bother. There aren’t that many people playing Heroes & Generals right now, just look for Enter Combat->Find Mission and then try to find a game that has Join Mission on the session overview screen.
The whole unlocking and finding the different customization options can also be a bit confusing at first glance.
Another complaint I have is when a war starts, you have to choose which side you will fight on for the duration of it. Which means that your account will be tied to either US or Germany. After the war ends you can change your faction.
To be honest even when I mention all of the problems Heroes & Generals has, just talking about the game makes me want to play it more. The game might not be the next Battlefield, but it doesn’t necessarily need to be either.
What we have here are some solid foundations, where something really cool can be made and enjoyed by a lot of people. Here is hoping Reto-Moto makes Heroes & Generals even better!

8/10, one of the most immersive RPG games I have played, with a shocking and nice storyline which gets you right in the action and fulfills the dreams of every guy who is bored with civilization and wants to become a dropout!

Far Cry 3 is a very fun, but deeply flawed game. For example, whenever I want to access the inventory, I have to wait whilst the game checks in the the Far Cry servers. I don't know why as they never seem to be available and it hasn't really changed my ability to eventually go into my inventory - but it does mean i have to wait for three minutes if I want to check what I can craft. As one would expect of a far cry game, the vehicles handle like a brick mounted on ball bearings and whilst that can be fun at first, it becomes borderline unplayable when the game can't make up its mind whether the little bush on the tundra is going to get run under the tyre or suddenly have the weathered resistance of a Korean war veteran with new Asian neighbours.

I just finished this game and I liked it a lot, but there were problems. Some were just annoying, like how when I climb a ledge, I am grabbing the air 6 inches away from the ledge or how if I got a phone call before getting a main mission, I'd have to hear it every time I loaded the game or completed a side mission.
The best part was combat. The enemies in the first half of the game are easy to hide from until you start shooting. In the second half, they will see you better, but you are wearing their uniform so they won't be hostile until you are, or if you go into a restricted area. My only problem with combat was that if I miss with the bow, the enemies know where I was shooting from, but if you hit, they didn't seem to know. What made it great though is how the enemies rally and more will come once you start making noise. What seems like an easy fight against two enemies can quickly become a fight against 6, coming from different directions.
This game fixes a problem I had with FarCry 2. In FC2, I was annoyed that to get anywhere easily, I had to drive through several outposts which were constantly manned by enemies that respawned rather quickly. There were not multiple sensible ways to get somewhere. Here, there are enemies around and you have to be careful, but there are choices, such as driving on or off road, or walking over hilly terrain. You also don't keep fighting enemies in the same spot every time. However, there is one big problem. There are these enemy controlled outposts throughout the island. They are avoidable, so they don't have the problem FarCry 2 had. However, while clearing them is fun, especially trying to go undetected, clearing the outpost makes the area "safe" meaning the tribe you are helping takes over. Now you will have allies in the area instead of enemies. The problem is that this makes those areas boring as there is no longer a threat. It also breaks my immersion. Where were all these fighters before? If the pirates have complete control of the island, why do they never take these outposts back?
There is actually some story justification for why you go quickly from inexperienced and afraid to a killing machine. It may or may not be enough for you, but it's something.
This was the first open world game I was able to stick with my attempt to not use fast travel. The world is big, but unless you are going from one end to the other, you don't feel like it takes forever. The island is beautiful and they really did great work and put in many detailed areas. The relics are meaningless collectibles, but they are worth collecting to see the locations where they are hidden. The Letters of the Lost, letters written by Japanese soldiers from WWII, were interesting and worth finding.
Finally, most of the side missions were fun. The supply runs were a blast because they make you drive over crazy terrain, not just a road. The Wanted Dead missions were also cool and requiring a knife kill made several difficult. However, some of the hunting missions are stupid, such as when you are asked to "hunt" rapid dogs with an RPG or flamethrower. That's the Path of the Warrior?
The main antagonist, Vaas was one of the best I've seen. They do a great job of exploring if your character is actually becoming like his enemy. However, they deal with him in a really stupid way. Basically, he beats you in cutscenes several times throughout the game. After one of these times, you go into what seems like a dream state where you fight him. You have no reason to think anything about it is real, but you wake up and are told Vaas is dead. That's it. Lame.
Edit: The story justification is actually really good, but it is horribly unsatisfying from a gameplay perspective.
The last problem is that the ending gives you a choice despite there being no choices to make during the course of the game. One seems to fit, but the other makes no sense and you have absolutely no reason to choose it. It's as if they tried to give you a Star Wars dark side option, or a choice like the original Fable. However because there were no morality choices throughout the game, it didn't fit. Also, something happens that made me want revenge. I have never wanted to storm an enemy camp and kick♥♥♥♥♥more than I did at he end of this game, but it didn't let me.
Overall, I do recommend it. It was fun, but there are problems that keep it from being great. 7/10

Good, but somewhat overrated
After all the praise I’ve heard and read about Far Cry 3 I approached the game with some high expectations.
I had played – and enjoyed - the original Far Cry. About the second Far Cry I read a lot of rather lukewarm comments and only purchased it on a Steam Sale  a year  or two later. As expected it was a mixed bag of an interesting open world gameplay (with an entirely different feel than FC1), but somewhat underdeveloped and riddled with annoying elements and a completely uninteresting storyline. Still I have to admit that somehow the game managed to keep my attention and I played it through to the end.
When I read about FC3 it seemed like once again a different kind of game than FC1 or 2. But once I started playing I found that FC3 is very much a continuation of FC2, but thankfully much better developed and with a lot of smart improvements.
The storyline is more interesting, the world is richer and more diverse and there’s a nice mix of gameplay elements to offer diversified gameplay experience. For the most part you can set your own pace, alternating between storyline missions and the various side missions to stretch gameplay and broaden up the experience.  Some elements, like the radio towers, were obviously adopted from Assassins Creed, but it’s a nice change of pace. The basic concept works quite well and gameplay all in all is enjoyable.
But while I thoroughly enjoyed the game some flaws and strange design choices kept FC3 from being a great game. Let’s ignore some of the weak spots in the storyline (and  skip over the pretentiousness of the “Alice in Wonderland”-quotes suggesting a depth the storyline simply didn’t have, and ignore the unsatisfying conclusion) and just look at the gameplay:
Crafting was basically an interesting idea, but I found it not all that useful and basically pointless in the second half of the game (Perhaps more useful on more difficult settings, but I played medium and don’t think I collected a single plant on the southern island). Money also is an important point in the beginning, but loses importance in the second half (most of the time I had more stuff to sell than my wallet could handle). I have the strong suspicion that shops originally should be spread scarcely across the map (as it was in FC2), but the integration of autoshops in most spawnpoints made shops pointless and gave gameplay a strange rhythm. That goes along with the quicktravel option, something I liked on one hand (especially later, when I hunted for relics), but it robbed the game some of its immediacy, since you could hop around the map (at least between unlocked points) and resupply as much as your wallet allowed. That’s the other extreme to FC2’s four travelpoints, which forced the player to travel long distances to missions. I would have wished for something in between: Less travel points, less (or even no) autoshops, no free weapons after radio tower missions.
And to be honest I found many gameplay elements repetitive after a while. Freeing enemies camp was fun most of the time, but many of the additional missions overstayed their welcome during the second half. IMHO it would have been smarter to introduce entirely new gameplay elements on the south island (if done smartly motivated by the different environment and enemy group). As it was the second half felt like “more of the same” and I found myself rushing through the missions.
Another missed opportunity was to integrate real sidequests. While inhabitants all over the map offer the player little sidequests, those have to be worked through immediately. How much more interesting it would have been to have quests, which can be accepted but finished either later, or might even have to be dealt with on a different spot on the map.
All in all FC3 was a definite improvement over its predecessor, but I can’t help but feel that some compromises and design flaws kept it from being even better. We will see if FC4 will correct some of those mistakes, but frankly as much as I enjoyed FC3 I’m not compelled to purchase FC4 immediately.

En cuanto a la clasificación de la ESRB de este juego (Sangre y vísceras, violencia intensa, desnudos, lenguaje fuerte, fuerte contenido sexual, uso de drogas). Ya que lo jugué puedo decir que sangre tiene, pero poca. Tiene la violencia de un FPS normal. ¿Víceras? ("gore"), dudo que lo tenga, no hay escenas de desmembramientos, lo que hace que las muertes no parezcan muy reales (por más que uses explosivos nadie pierde un brazo o una pierna, etc). ¿Desnudez? Bueno, si los pintados pechos de Citra es desnudez, que cada cual juzgue por sí mismo. Lenguaje fuerte tiene y uso de drogas; fuerte contenido sexual tiene, enmarcado como temas adultos (agresión sexual, etc).
Finalmente, recomiendo éste juego y le doy 8 / 10.
A very good game. Open world with a variety of guns and missions of various kinds. The game, in my opinion, would be short if you focus only on the main missions. That said, you should do all the side missions in order to lengthen "artificially" the game time. The game also has complete compatibility with the Xbox 360 Controller for Windows.
I recommend purchasing the game with all downloadable content available, so you add game time to the main product.  I refer especially  to the addition of the "Monkey Business" dlc, which I found quite hilarious with the added character. At the other hand, I found the cooperative to be a very nice addition (personally more than multiplayer), so I recommend purchasing all the co-op maps.
As for the ESRB rating of this game (Blood and gore, intense violence, nudity, strong language, strong sexual content, drug use), since I played it I can say that has blood, but little. Also it has the violence of a normal FPS. Gore?, I doubt it have, since there are no scenes of dismemberment, deaths not seem very real (nobody  loses an arm or leg by the use of explosives, etc). ¿Nudity? Well, if Citra's painted breasts are nudity, judge for yourself. Has strong language and drug use; has strong sexual content, framed as adult themes (sexual assault, etc).
Finally, I recommend this game and I give it 8 / 10.

Far Cry 3 spits the naive, arrogant and entitled Jason Brody into a spiralling world of violence, anarchy and survival, beset in a jungle, where survival by whatever means necessary is the norm as he restores order to the islands by takling over pirate camps and towers to reveal a map of the islands.
This is what a first-shooter, open-world game ought to be. Sure, it lacks character development in some scenes, such as Jason's thrust into the island without seeing his emotions unfold as he loses his brother to Vaas. And the main villain: He was really top-notch. Vaas played his role perfectly, though the game mechanics downplayed his role as a vilain. Taking down bosses in choreographed button mashes and simplistic scenes is no way to end a boss. Same went for Hoyt Voyker and Buck Hughes.
All in all, its' many hours of exploration, take-downs, gliding, sky-diving, killing and blowing up things. A journey you'll be begging to return to over and over again.
Second part: Co-Op. That is some awesome stuff. Adds many, many hours of hilarious gameplay and challenge-based system that add up XP , a'la Trials of the Rakyat in Single Player.
Multi-player: Well, this is probably my favorite so far. You can't play it once. Custom maps can also be built and be featured here too.
Notes: Mature content. Everywhere.
Overall rating: 9.5 out of 10.

I played 23 hours so far. It's a fairly generous 8/10 for me.
Good looking game, and some sights are gorgeous. Having said that, this is like far Cry2 in Far Cry (1) settings. It's a go get, do this, mission quest. Unlike far Cry which was about mercs and a crazy scientific experiment.
That does make Far Cry 3 a bit of a grind, albeit a good grind. I don't see myself doing much after the main quest is over. I mean I can't see me collecting every loot chest, relic, lost-letter, etc. There is no point to it really, so that part's just a grind, because there's hundreds of them.
Liberating outposts is better than expected. Getting in and cutting off the alarm before the pirates signal help is rewarding. Plus you get extra exp for doing it without an alarm going off. Another place where it excels is missions in the main quest  take you to amazing places. The sets they send you to are a bit Tomb Raider style, without the puzzles. All the up-sides then.
It is addictive. I liberate one outpost and think I'll just do another, and another. Then I might finish with a main quest mission. Then another outpost, including hunter mini-quests gained at the outpost.
If it was just a hint more Far Cry (1), I would rate it higher. Also, why oh why didn't they put an inventory/progress quick-save key on. We can go to the main menu and save progress/inventory. It's diabolical they didn't give us a hotkey.

The Good.
This best thing about this game is the wide open island world that is very rich in detail.  Wild animals all over the place, so you litterally have to watch your back.   Fantastic graphics.  Hidden caves with buried relics or artifacts of the island culture.  Temple ruins in jungles, caves and under water.  The storyline is also pretty immersive.  The RPG element is cool, as you can buy or find various weapons to increase the characters effectiveness in the game.   Crafting supplies or syringes to increase the characters abilites and capacity is also a unique element and fits the jungle/survival storyline. The takedown feature is also really fun, and you can increase your takedown abilities in numerous ways as you progress through the game.  The hang-gliding, and base jumping are also really original and a cool way to get around the island.
The Bad.
1) Character Mechanics are substandard.
The character mechanics are kind of dumb in that you can't step over a tiny obstruction without looking straight down.   So I walk up to a building doorway that has the equivalent of a two inch height over the level of the ground.    In reality you would step over something like this without even thinking about it.  In Farcry 3, the character stops dead until you remember to jump.  Ooops, jumping causes you to hit the top of the door frame, so you bounce back down and still can't go in.  Finally if you remember to look straight down, you can step over the tiny 2" inch sill.   I found this to be really distracting and it pulled me right out of the immersion of the game.  In the same way, the platforming is really lame, given that controlling the character is so cumbersome and imprecise.  Compared to other shooters, it sometimes feels like being trapped inside the body of a crippled person.  This is especially true as you try to climb the radio towers which involves a lot of platform-style jumping.
2) The interactive cutscenes are clunky and arbitrary.
The interactive cutscenes "missions" involve totally arbitrary input.  Letters flash on the screen and you have a fraction of a second to type the proper sequence of letters, or you die.  This is pretty frustrating, not at all fun, and tends to pull you out of the immersion of being on the island.  Then to make the experience even worse, it takes way too long to load to try again. (if the scene is already in memory, why the really long reload?)
And The Ugly.
1) Finally, the game (or more specifically, Ubisoft Montreal) seems to be really "preachy", and paradoxically they seem to be on some kind of non-violence kick.  The underlying message seems to be that the violence of the jungle will make you into a different and much nastier person.  Therefore you shouldn't be violent-- even in self-defense.    This seems a little bit scantimonious and hypocritical-- and even insulting-- coming from a game studio that makes its money by pedaling gratuitous violence.
Conclusion.
If you can put up with the "bad" and the "ugly" the "good" is really good, and really fun.

A suggestion though... If you're a purest, lke myself, I highly recommend you do the following wee tweaks to extend the life of the game (Once clocked) and play through it as i feel truely immersive games should be played.
Step 1 : Go into the gameplay options and disable EVERY assist (Also set difficulty to 'Master' to add realism & reset all outposts (Upon completing the main story)
Step 2 : Google a Hex editor (ie, HxD) and make the following changes.
Step 3 : Navigate to 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Far Cry 3\bin' and open the file 'FC3_d3d11.DLL' in your Hex editor. (Run as admin)
Step 4 : Search for "showuielement"

Great game. Player can customize his soldier and take multiple career paths.
-As an infantry man, choose to be a rifleman, close quarters specialist with SMG, Machine gunner, or an AT soldier with a Bazooka and Anti Tank grenades, or even AT mines
-As a tanker, specialize in light, medium, or heavy tanks, or hunt your kin in nimble tank destroyers. Provide support for infantry to capture the victory points, but dont be afraid to jump out and get dirty when your tank gets knocked out, your Sub Machine Gun makes you a force to be feared in close quarters, although you cannot carry much ammo, or much of anything else.
- Become a pilot and rule the skies, fighting enemy pilots and providing air support against enemies that your ground troops cant kill.
-Become a paratrooper, dropping behind enemy lines and causing havoc, with an aggressive play-style, Paras excel at breaking a staunch defense of a zone from behind, allowing allies to advance. Drop in alone, and you will probably die. Drop in with your squad, and you can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for the enemy team, harassing enemies, coming from any direction you want.
--->You carry less gear than the average soldier, meaning you must prioritize if you want to go with a full load of ammo, or fo you want just 1 magazine, forcing you to rely on enemy weapons, so you can bring extra equipment
------>(Drop Canisters might be implemented, allowing you extra gear. Paras are also being examined, there has been outcry against their dramatically lowered equipment carrying ability)
-And at last, the Recon soldier. Ideal for just that, recon. Equipped with a bolt action rifle, he can harass enemies from afar. Binoculars allow you to warn teammates of approaching enemies. Finally, Anti-Personnel mines allow you to deny paths to your enemy, forcing them right into your and your team's sights. Mechanized Recon vehicles are also available, Armored Cars equipped with light anti tank weaponry. Good for scouting ahead of armored units, or supporting infantry when tanks cannot.
-Battles, and the forces fighting them, are decided by generals, players who have played enough to unlck their own Assault Teams(AT's), in game slang), the units that partake in the battles on the Campaign map. This can lead to unfair battles, where one side might send tanks to support their infantry in taking a town, while the defenders must make do with Panzerfausts and whatever portable anti tank they have. When faced with these "lost causes", look to see what you can do to hurt the enemy the most. That could be knocking out as many tanks as possible, as they are expensive to replace.
-In battle keep your head down, whether you're a trooper or a Tank Commander. When the bullets start flying, hit the dirt and scan for the shooters. It takes at most 3 rifle shots to kill someone, unless you go to extreme range, rhile bolt actions rarely need more than 2, and can even one hit kill. Sub Machine Guns like the famous Tommy Gun and Mp-40 are rapid fire beasts, fearsome at ranges up to 75m, past that, they need an experienced shooter.Light Machine Guns and Automatic rifles are heavier infantry weapons, which must be fired from stationary positions, or while walking(hold left ALT). When fired from prone, they can tear enemies to shreds, and in close quarters, one can walk and fire bursts to suppress and kill enemies.
-Tank crews must be more careful. You can poke your head out of the hatch, but you become much more vulnerable to scores of rifle armed infantry eager to relieve you of your tank. Don't leave the tank, and if you need to, make sure you can destroy it so it doesnt fall to the enemies. Try to bring some fellow infantry to cover you, and you can cover them.
-As a Paratrooper, prioritize your gear. I tend to bring an SMG with 3 extra mags, that is the current max a para can carry. Try to get in and clear capture zones(Paras unlock later, at rank 7,so you will be experienced with your weapons by then). The Scavenger badge is a great help, although the parachute badges which allow you to choose when to open your chute are great help, allowing you to open at low altitude for a stealthier but riskier(Fall and hit the ground) landing, or high altitude, covering greater distance, but being more exposed in the air
---> When a para AT runs out of transport aircraft, it can deploy on the ground as normal light infantry.
For anyone who enjoys games like skyrim, but also enjoy strategy games, then this is the game for you.

Warband's inexcusably bad graphics are offset by a wide variety of gameplay choices. You can play as a trader, gather an army, become a bandit, and so on. Whatever you choose, Warband offers a world with dozens of towns, villages and castles to explore and a large countryside in which armies of hundreds of soldiers can confront each other. In combat, intuitive direction-based melee fighting (with swords, shields, axes, spears and so on) joins forces with horse riding, archery (bows, javelins, throwing axes/daggers and crossbows) and fun - although clumsy - castle assaulting. There are too many systems to discuss but, rest assured, Warband is a game that is easy to play but difficult to master, with a huge amount of variables that will affect your character and his or her team in every way, from strength to prisoner management skills. Engaging multiplayer and the ability to install mods round off a flawed but ultimately enjoyable game which you'll enjoy playing several times.

Disclaimer: Play Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon instead.  It basically takes all the flaws of Far Cry 3 and makes a parody of them, with a strong dose of 80's action movie and video game nostalgia.  It still wears on you after a while but as a much shorter game, you should be able to complete it while it's still fun.
Far Cry 3 is one of those games that seems to get almost universal praise and when I finally get around to play it, it mostly makes me feel annoyed and disappointed.  It's supposed to be a fantastic open world action game but it's just a thin illusion of freedom.
The main problem with the game is just how contrived and gamey everything feels.  It's all rigidly structured and feels incredibly fake.  There's an absurd number of collectibles you collect to somehow magically unlock special weapons.  Taking back radio towers reveals sections of the map and somehow gives you access to more items in the game shops.  The shops are just cabinets that somehow dispense infinite amounts of weapons and ammo.  Taking outposts makes all the bad guys suddenly disappear from the area.
Past that, there's a number of other things that really bother me about the game.  It uses slow and very repetitive animations for looting bodies and skinning animals as well as using vehicles and is very finnicky about the location you stand where you can interact with these objects.  The game is touted as a graphical benchmark, yet it has more broken texture seams and random extremely low res textures than just about any game I've ever played while the overall graphical quality is little more than above average.  It doesn't run very smoothly either, with constant microstuttering and frequent hitching due to loading new data while traveling around the world.
I've heard some people compare this game to Elder Scrolls, but it bears basically no resemblance other than some occasional poor voice acting that sticks out like a sore thumb compared to the rest.  Elder Scrolls actually feels like an open world game without artificial constructs holding it up, however limited it is.
One bright spot is the game's co-op mode which is structured similarly to other games like The Darkness 2: A set of short missions with characters outside the single-player story.  There's a good amount of content there and it's reasonably fun but it really can't compare to a proper full co-op game.  It does seem to exacerbate the game's microstuttering problem however.
Despite these problems, I was having fun with the game.  The gunplay is great and running/driving around the island is pretty fun.  The missions are well-constructed and most of the voice acting is good, though there are a few lines that are just cringe-inducingly bad.  And then I reached a point in the game where it's supposed to give you a new piece of equipment that's required to use in the next mission.  It didn't give it to me and I can no longer continue.  I tried going back to my previous save and replaying the mission in question without any luck.  That's when I discovered that Uplay encrypts savegames so the only way for me to finish the game is to start over from the beginning, play 3/4 of the game again and hope it doesn't ♥♥♥♥ me again.  No thanks and ♥♥♥♥ you Ubisoft.

If you’re deciding whether to buy Far Cry 3 for Uplay or for Steam, I’d recommend you just get it for Uplay. Sure the Uplay client is inferior, but you’ll have fewer problems getting the game to work (took a long time to get the game to run). Also, when you start the game in Steam, it just launches Uplay anyway so it’s basically just a shortcut. I had kind of a unique situation so I can’t say for certain that you’ll encounter the same problems playing the Steam version
First off, the game is very hardware intensive. It probably stressed my system more than anything other than Watch Dogs, which I just gave up on running due to low frame rate. I had to turn down the graphics a bit to get a nice 40 fps for Far Cry 3. If you have better than a GTX 460 video card you should be fine.
For gameplay, the game is very similar to Far Cry 2 (big surprise). It’s a first person shooter with 4 gun slots (you unlock them through crafting). Similar to many other modern shooters, when you kill a gun wielding enemy, they usually drop that weapon for you to pick up, or just scavenge the ammo. There’s a stealth component to combat where you are rewarded (with extra exp) for sneaking up and using takedowns on enemies rather than just running in shooting. Various styles of takedown are unlocked through skill points as you progress through the game (such as dropping down on enemies or pulling the pin on an enemy’s grenade and kicking him toward his buddies. I mentioned crafting earlier and the crafting system is very simple, if somewhat time consuming. You hunt animals for their skins and use the skins to unlock equipment upgrades. For example 2 goat skins might increase the number of grenades you can carry or 2 flowers can be turned into a healing item. I spent about 3 hours just hunting all the animals to upgrade my gear before tackling the main story quests. Similar to Tomb Raider and Deus Ex: Human Revolution, “leveling up” doesn’t make you stronger with more HP or damage. It just gives you a skill point to spend.
The game story is very well written and executed (completely new protagonist and story from the previous Far Cry games). I won’t spoil it for you but you start as a non-combatant and end up as a badass. There’s a ton of collectible items strewn across the game map telling the history of the island (kind of like Tomb Raider) and you’re rewarded for finding them with more exp.
Overall the game is fantastic and a definite thumbs up. I only have the basic version so I can’t tell you if the “deluxe edition” is worth getting. I kind of doubt it though. By the way, I thought Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon was a DLC for Far Cry 3. Blood Dragon is actually a total conversion and you don’t need Far Cry 3 installed (or even owned) to play it.

NOT an MMOFPS like the superior WW2 Battleground Europe or Planetside, but more a lobby based MMOG in the vein of World of Tanks and War Thunder.
That means you sit in a lobby some of the time, like the comparable Blacklight: Retribution or Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Phantoms (albeit a different time period), while you wait for a queue to put you into one of the 4-5 maps in total.
The strategic aspect of the game can best be described as a dumbed down Stronghold: Kingdoms.
The game designers tried to fuse arcade style gameplay (CoD customization, BF style spotting, stat based weapon/balancing system) With realistic style Red Orchestra/ArmA approach (slow paced positioning, strategic advancement, punishing oneshots, terrain collision).
* Great Free-to-play model with no BS.
* The grind is forgiving compared to World of Tanks and War Thunder.
* The gunplay is superb; rifles excel at range and SMGs/Assault Rifles are to be feared in CQC.
* Horrible terrain collission while being prone.
* Bad menu system (will be reworked in a future patch; "Squad 2.0")
* No Arma style freelook.

Far Cry 3 is an open world, action-adventure first-person shooter video game set on a tropical island between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. After a vacation goes awry, protagonist Jason Brody must save his friends, who have been kidnapped by pirates and escape from the island and its unhinged inhabitants. Far Cry 3 is a first-person shooter, which also features role-playing game elements including experience points, skill trees, and a crafting system. Far Cry 3 gives you the ability to take cover behind objects to break enemies' lines of sight and to peek around and over cover and blindfire.
You are also able to perform silent takedowns by performing melee attacks from above, below, or close behind. Equipment is controlled by a simple system. As missions are completed, new items are unlocked to be purchased or crafted by Jason, using the pelts of various animals that are found around the island. As the outposts of Vaas' pirate group are attacked and retaken, the vicinity around the outpost becomes safer, it unlocks new side quests for that area, involving missions like hunting the many different wildlife species on the island to upgrade ones equipment.
Skills are collected by gaining experience from completing missions and killing enemies, and are unlocked in three skill trees, which correspond to the Spider, the Heron, and the Shark. Each skill tree upgrades different aspects of Jason's abilities, with the Spider upgrading his stealth takedowns and hunting skills, Shark for assault takedowns and health, with the Heron upgrading Jason's long-range takedowns and mobility.
As skills are collected, the tattoo on Jason's forearm grows which is made up of several different tribal designs resembling the three animal skill trees. With all the new features that Ubisoft has added to Far Cry 3 I really think that this is definitely a huge improvement to the previous Far Cry games.
The story is very interesting and fun, the island you explore is very big and beautifully detailed and there is so many things you can do when your bored, for example there are loads of side-missions and hunting contracts scattered around the island. Overall Far Cry 3 absolutely deserves a score of 10/10 it is just truly fantastic, I'm definitely 100% sure that Far Cry 3 will not disappoint you in anyway!.

Mount & Blade. Where do I start? Born out of the love for games of one Turkish couple, it grew into a massive, beautiful sandbox of possibilities.
Have you ever wanted to lead an army? Of course, you have done so countless times. Have you ever wanted to lead your own empire? Sure, that's easy, you say. But have you ever wanted to shift the tides of war as a mercenary, jumping from kingdom to kingdom whilst building up your own relations? And who said you had to jump right into the fights? Why not use your natural charisma in order to bring in bucketloads of money out of dangerous, bandit-ridden caravan trails? Sorry, did you say you wanted to do all of that? You CAN, in Mount & Blade!
On to the game. It's a third-person/first-person RPG where you take the role of a new arrival on the pseudo-medieval continent of Calradia. From the get go, you're set loose and you carve your own path through the six kingdoms across the land, ranging from the Slav-like Vaegirs to the refined Rhodoks. The game gives no objectives to speak of, making Warband a true sandbox. Usually however, you'll want to start climbing the social ladder by doing tasks for the lords and kings of Calradia. Eventually you may become renowned enough that you're asked to join one of the kingdoms. With your vassalage comes your very own fief, which opens up the somewhat rudimentary fief management system, as well as entry into the realm's politicking and skullduggery. But you might not like the way your kingdom is run, so you'll find a so-called claimant of your kingdom and swear fealty to them over your current king in order to rebel and deliver the rightful ruler to the throne. And that's just one chain of events out of hundreds that can happen!
The two most important parts are the map travel screen and the combat itself. Map travel is influenced by how big your party is, how many horses you have and how much you're carrying in those saddlebags, but also by your own skills in trailblazing, for instance. Moving between towns you may come across other parties. Manhunters, bandits, lords, peasants and so on, even fights between enemy parties that you may sway one way or the other. Should also mention the feeling when you, as the realm's marshal, lead an army of 15 allied lords and their armies into enemy territory.
Combat is the biggest thing that Mount & Blade does right. Mounted or on foot, using projectiles or a fairly sizable variety of melee weapons, sending your enemies to sleep is always satisfactory and engaging. Every blade has a weight to it, every arrow and bolt carries with it flying death, every cavalryman is a solid force to be reckoned with. And when you have fights that contain 200 soldiers on each side, chaos all around you, small skirmishes all over the (randomized) combat maps, that's when you're playing Mount & Blade.
Warband, as a stand-alone expansion, brought with it essential improvements, such as being able to marry a lord or a lady who would help you in your political schemes, or being able to found your own kingdom and take a huge bite out of Calradia for yourself. Additionally, if you're somehow tired of the medieval aesthetic, there are hundreds of mods online that will take you to any place, any time, from Star Wars to the Old West to Lord of the Rings.
All that can really be asked of Taleworlds now is to GIVE BANNERLORD.

Warband's inexcusably bad graphics are offset by a wide variety of gameplay choices. You can play as a trader, gather an army, become a bandit, and so on. Whatever you choose, Warband offers a world with dozens of towns, villages and castles to explore and a large countryside in which armies of hundreds of soldiers can confront each other. In combat, intuitive direction-based melee fighting (with swords, shields, axes, spears and so on) joins forces with horse riding, archery (bows, javelins, throwing axes/daggers and crossbows) and fun - although clumsy - castle assaulting. There are too many systems to discuss but, rest assured, Warband is a game that is easy to play but difficult to master, with a huge amount of variables that will affect your character and his or her team in every way, from strength to prisoner management skills. Mount & Blade: Warband is one of the best games I have played in a while. The combat is solid, the factions have their own strengths and weaknesses and the battles are hectic and massive. This is one of the only games I have seen that actually lets you be part of the battle instead of some sort of skygod. Did I say the battles were awesome yet? If I did let me say it again, the battles can range from small skirmishes to large scale battles. In addition to the field battles you also have the ability to seige castles and cities and if that isn't your style, why not raid a few peasent villages for loot and plunder!
There are countless things I could say that are good about Mount & Blade: Warband including the Mod support. Like Game of Thrones? The have a mod for that. Want the game to take place in Feudal Europe? They have a mod for that as well! There are a bunch of other mods for the game so the replay value is extremely high.
The game does have a couple of downsides though.
One of them being the graphics. If you are looking for a visually stunning game this may not be for you. Along with that there is very little voice acting. The only voice acting you will hear are the warcrys of the soliders on the battlefield and the bandits as well as some farmers, so don't be expecting Morgan Freeman or Jennifer Hale as voice actors and voice actresses.
The early game is quite difficult as well (or at least it was for me.) You will constantly be attacked by Bandits, Sea Raiders and the like until you amass a big enough force to take them and then still they will  sometimes attack you.
But if you can look past these flaws I think you will have a great time. I know I did!
Thank you for reading my review for the great game and I am sorry if this review isn't that great as it is my first review!
Thanks for your time.
Best regards
-A Crazed Engineer

Quite a memorable game with memorable characters. Despite being mostly a free-roam game, with plenty of distractions and activities, like hunting, killing, swimming, gliding etc. it has a decent story.
As I mentioned in the beginning, the characters are one of the strongest points in this game, every character with their own strong personalities, each one with their own insanity, great voice acting and motion track. The motivation and choice freedom of the protagonist feel a bit wooden and not quite dynamic, but the diversity in the activities, making it feel not quite so linearity dependent, compensates for the lack of story control.
The story can be easily completed with minimum of effort, since difficulty doesn't really represent an impediment (if you play shooters often, you can aim for the highest difficulties), but making the side activities do help in certain cases, especially for the traveling part.
The vehicle control is quite fluent, reminds me of the car from Half-Life 2. The weapons can be customized in a variety of ways, from adding attachments to adding a camo, quite easy to use, they have ironsight, so for any Call of Duty player they should be a no-brainer.
It has a sort of RPG-like skill tree, which allows you to get new abilities and features, supporting your gameplay as well as your herb/animal crafting system.
The co-op is average, not much of a story, really linear levels, it's basically a cooperative competition, since each level contains a sort of mini-game with ranking, so you will be able to beat your friends and brag about it. It's sometimes bugged, you may be spawning dead, fall through the ground.
The multiplayer is quite...empty...not many people play it, it has basic game modes like team deathmatch and domination like modes, feels a lot like a "Call of Duty" style. You also have a multiplayer leveling system (not the same with the one from single player), which will unlock new weapons/skills etc. I also happened to encounter some cheaters and some bugs.
Also wanted to add that this game's antagonist (the cool one), Vaas, was a source of inspiration for one of my cosplay projects, feel free to check it out.

Mount & Blade. Where do I start? Born out of the love for games of one Turkish couple, it grew into a massive, beautiful sandbox of possibilities.
Have you ever wanted to lead an army? Of course, you have done so countless times. Have you ever wanted to lead your own empire? Sure, that's easy, you say. But have you ever wanted to shift the tides of war as a mercenary, jumping from kingdom to kingdom whilst building up your own relations? And who said you had to jump right into the fights? Why not use your natural charisma in order to bring in bucketloads of money out of dangerous, bandit-ridden caravan trails? Sorry, did you say you wanted to do all of that? You CAN, in Mount & Blade!
On to the game. It's a third-person/first-person RPG where you take the role of a new arrival on the pseudo-medieval continent of Calradia. From the get go, you're set loose and you carve your own path through the six kingdoms across the land, ranging from the Slav-like Vaegirs to the refined Rhodoks. The game gives no objectives to speak of, making Warband a true sandbox. Usually however, you'll want to start climbing the social ladder by doing tasks for the lords and kings of Calradia. Eventually you may become renowned enough that you're asked to join one of the kingdoms. With your vassalage comes your very own fief, which opens up the somewhat rudimentary fief management system, as well as entry into the realm's politicking and skullduggery. But you might not like the way your kingdom is run, so you'll find a so-called claimant of your kingdom and swear fealty to them over your current king in order to rebel and deliver the rightful ruler to the throne. And that's just one chain of events out of hundreds that can happen!
The two most important parts are the map travel screen and the combat itself. Map travel is influenced by how big your party is, how many horses you have and how much you're carrying in those saddlebags, but also by your own skills in trailblazing, for instance. Moving between towns you may come across other parties. Manhunters, bandits, lords, peasants and so on, even fights between enemy parties that you may sway one way or the other. Should also mention the feeling when you, as the realm's marshal, lead an army of 15 allied lords and their armies into enemy territory.
Combat is the biggest thing that Mount & Blade does right. Mounted or on foot, using projectiles or a fairly sizable variety of melee weapons, sending your enemies to sleep is always satisfactory and engaging. Every blade has a weight to it, every arrow and bolt carries with it flying death, every cavalryman is a solid force to be reckoned with. And when you have fights that contain 200 soldiers on each side, chaos all around you, small skirmishes all over the (randomized) combat maps, that's when you're playing Mount & Blade.
Warband, as a stand-alone expansion, brought with it essential improvements, such as being able to marry a lord or a lady who would help you in your political schemes, or being able to found your own kingdom and take a huge bite out of Calradia for yourself. Additionally, if you're somehow tired of the medieval aesthetic, there are hundreds of mods online that will take you to any place, any time, from Star Wars to the Old West to Lord of the Rings.
All that can really be asked of Taleworlds now is to GIVE BANNERLORD.

While at first this game seemed interesting (I mean, an FPS and an RTS?), it quicky devolves to grinding for your next unlock. The game uses 3 (That's right, THREE) currencies  (Credits, Warfunds, and Gold) that can be used to unlock various features. First I'll talk about the FPS side.
You start out as an infantryman, and as you level up, you get more unlocks and the ability to switch to a different branch of the military, such as being a tank crewman, pilot, paratrooper, recon, etc. Unfortunately, you do not get anything else, including getting a different weapon suited for your class (i.e If you choose Recon, you do not get a sniper rifle, and buying a scope for your ordinary weapon costs a very large amount of credits). However, once you get past the first couple of levels, the grind becomes much easier, but this is balanced by having the weapons cost a very large amount of credits.
Now the RTS side.
What, were you expecting something written here? I haven't tried the RTS side, not because I don't like RTS games, but because getting a group to fight for you, even the cheapest one, costs 29,000 Warfunds, and you get about 150 Warfunds per game (Which take around 10-15 minutes).This is my biggest problem with the game, is that the amount you get awarded is quite small compared to what you can unlock. Unfortunately, this is why I can't recommend this game.

Fire, animal attacks in odd places and flipping your car like a stuntman on small rocks are the only things that can hurt you.
All the characters were unlikeable cliches and the writing was cringeworthy at best. I understand what the story is going for, Jason is slowly getting drawn into the dark world of the island and it's changing him, but it just feels so forced. The attempts to increase tension with the boss fights and other "weird" segments only alienate from the rest of the game. The game promoted and made a big deal out of Vaas, but he's to this what Darth Maul was to episode 1. Then there's the horrible sound mixing and phoned in voice acting, especially from any of the generic NPCs and enemies.
The setting is interesting, even if it's been done before. But at the same time it reeks of wasted potentional. Aside from the missions with Buck, which were some of the best in the game, the ruins on the island are all but ignored. Even then, all the ruins you do explore are apparently made out of fire and explosions, so you spend more time just sprinting and spamming the button prompts through them, rather than actually enjoying the locations. There's only so many dirty tin huts one can look at before you're completely bored of them.
To top it all off, I get the feeling the game was rushed. The first island is full of little nooks and crannies, there's lots to explore and tons of little side quests and treasures and characters. Then you get to the second island. You're in contact with a whooping 1 character and the big baddie the entire time. You only go between a couple locations for the main missions, yet the map is still huge. Even doing the boring copy pasted sidequests there, a lot of the island feels like filler space. You'll have all your skills unlocked, crafted items completed, and the best weapons purchased by the time you get there, so you'll only just blow through it to finish the story.
Even with all that said, Far Cry 3 isn't a bad game, it's just not good. Again, it's very much Ubisoft's tried and true formula, and if you enjoy that, you'll love this. Anyone looking for anything deeper in terms of gameplay or writing would be much better served with another game.

With every Free-To-Play game comes.... Pay-To-Win aspects....
This game is quite irritating in that manner.
You could spend quite literally months saving up credits and/or earning experience enough to be able to buy and use a good tank.
OR
You could spend a certain amount of real money and get the most powerful tank available and screw up everyone else's game experience.
Overall for the gameplay I reccommend this game highly.
But also I do not recommend it to those who dislike PTW with a deep internal passion as I do.
Also let me say
I would spend money for the game. Meaning if the devs decided to make this a paid game.... I would buy it. Only if however, the pay to win aspects are completely removed from the game entirely.
This game could easily go for 24.99 USD. Very easily. This game is worth 25 bucks....but only if like I said PTW is removed

Yes, Vaas looks like a badass sitting on that beach, giving you the evil eye.
I bought this game during the Steam Summer Sale event because it seemed to have a lot of potential and it does. For me, though, it doesn't deliver.
The game play is rough at best with a semi-annoying control system. The hints pop up 20 at a time and not during logical times like they should - like when you might need them. I do like that the survival skills (creating items from animal skin) are realistic though nasty at times. The variety of animals is appealing and the setup of the world itself is vast and interesting.
Another plus is that they have given you almost any vehicle you can imagine. The crappy part is they're controlled by basically an on/off switch; Meaning that you have to tap W in order to move without crashing each time. Even the freaking NPC's do the stop-go driving which is kinda funny if it wasn't so irritating after an hour of gameplay.
However, my biggest issue is with the characters themselves. The main group is a bunch of deuchebag kids who do stupid stuff and get in way over their heads as a result. This game offers me no reason to give a crap about what happens to them. They did a lot of stupid things, they messed with a lot of people they shouldn't have, why the hell should I care if they get murdered on this island of pirates? There's nothing redeeming about them.
The main character, Jason, is a rather whiny kid through most of the game. Awkwardly and rather suddenly when you follow the main plot line, he becomes a jumped up Tarzan after some hoodoo $h1t takes place. He also dies about 10 times in this game, which is stupid as hell. The creators need to get over the drug-induced-hallucination crap because it gets old after the first dream-like sequence. It's not original and doesn't add a damn thing to the story or gaming experience.
It's not good when the only good characters are 1) the main villain (Vaas is insane yet awesome) and 2) the supporting protagonist. For these reasons I cannot recommend it for its single player option.
Now, the multiplayer is decent enough. It gets pretty challenging if you don't have a full group, but experienced gamers can chew their way through it.
There's a few minor things that games like Left 4 Dead 2 did better with the multiplayer, but I can't think of them right now and they aren't game-shattering.
Bottom line: If this game is cheap, try it out. If not, don't bother, it's sure as ♥♥♥♥ not worth 50 or 60 dollars.

You play as Jason Brody, an average guy having a vacation on a mysterious island with his friends. You and your friends then get captured by pirates and thus begins the story of Far Cry 3.
The best thing about this game is the open world feature. I, myself am an open world lover and Far Cry 3 just nailed the spot. You can capture outpost, hunt animals, wrestle with crocodile and lots more. You also have various weapons at your disposal and you can customize them. You can almost feel as if you were shooting a real gun, the recoil and the impact as the bullets tear through your enemy is an amazing experience.
The car driving mechanics in this game is phenomenal, easily one of the best I have ever experienced, although you will have the strong urge of crashing your car after every trip. The story is pretty decent too and I enjoy it. The voice acting though, is amazing and you can feel the emotions of Jason as he is struggling through hell.
As like every game, there are downsides. The radio towers, which you are required to go through to get map vision, are extremely frustrating and repetitive. I would always sigh if I see one and grudgingly force myself through it.
Overall, Far Cry 3 is an extremely good game, defenitely worth it's price point. An open world experience you do not want to miss.

I bought the game because I'd heard it was "like Skyrim but with guns." This is true only to the extent that is an open world game where you aren't forced into the main storyline. The sidequests are uninteresting and minimal, and while searching the islands for treasures is interesting at first, the different items you find are all only worth as much as the money you sell them for. There is no crafting beyond leaves, so searching for trasures is ultimately useless unless you want to buy a new gun. The multitude of items is thus meaningless because you just end up clicking sell all in the shop anyway.
Furthermore, whereas Skyrim let you play how you want, as a mage, assassin, brawler, etc, Far Cry is very limiting. Some missions require you to kill the final enemy with a knife. Hunting missions specify a bow, shotgun, or some other gun, limiting your ability to choose. Even the main storyline missions lack real choice, forcing you into dissapointing boss fights in which the only skill you need is how to move forward, literally, because you just have to walk to the cutscene where you kill the boss. I felt incredibly unsatisfied having killed a major enemy without ever needing to have done anything more than left a small weight on my w key.
As for the storyline, without giving anything major away, you try to rescue your friends from pirates and use the island natives as a means to do so. I personally felt no attachment to my characters friends. Frankly, they seemed like a bunch of jerks. The problem arises when the other half, the Rakyat natives, is equally unappealing. The game didn't give me any reason to like them either, as they all just seem obsessed with a woman named Citra, a meant-to-be alluring, sexy "goddess" who just turned out strange and arrogant. With the two options presented to me, I honestly was left wishing I could join the pirates and make some cash on this island.
Overall, I'd say this game fits a specific niche. If you like shooting things (except civilians, that kills you), this is probably a good game for you. If you like execution cutscenes, this is probably a good game for you (although the death from above is easily exploitable; any incline is enough to get the cutscene). If you're like me, and prefer an engaging storyline, personal playstyle, and/or any real reason to explore your open world, then you're likely to be disappointed.

To be frank, I LOVED this game. I loved the graphics, I loved the gameplay, I loved the storyline, I loved the characters (mostly, but I'll get to that later), and I loved the graphics (definitely didn't say that before). Now obviously, people will be saying "this game was just hyped due to the graphics, the gameplay isn't that good BLAH BLAH BLAH." to that, I say "to each his own, but you sir, suck". It would seriously be easier to list the things I didn't like about that game, so that's what I'll do. To do so, I'll start with the major thing that I hated; the MC, Jason. Throughout the opening, Jason seems like someone who cares for everyone close to him, friends and family. This is also shown through the first few missions, and is the whole point of him joining the Rakyat. Yet, at the end, he has a choice to kill them? I know the developers were just giving the player a chance to see just how the island had changed him, but would it really have? In the game, Jason seems about 20-30, (if it did say in the game i didn't pay attention). That means, for that many years, he has known and loved his brothers and for a few less years than that his girlfriend and company. To want to kill them all and stay on the island is older brother died on? That would be a big gap in character devolopment to me, actually, no, scratch that, a giant mother-f*ck*ng chasm. The change shown there would make people want Ubisoft to be the new President, since they're making sh*t happen. Now please, remember that this was one thing out of an amazing game. You can actually go through basically the whole game without giving a sh*t about Jason, and that's what i did on my second "playthrough". I would just go around trying to find every relic and liberate every camp. Speaking of the liberating camps, I can honestly say that it was the most fun I had in the game. The feeling of having 1000 ways to go about something, and being able to really do each one was amazing. I could have gone in rambo with a heavy machine gun, stealth with a pistol and some grass stains, or even sniped everyone and their mother from a nearby cliff or hill. The liberation was basically what I lived for, and it gave this game tons of replayability.
