Positives
•Immersive & Realistic WWII Setting
•Fusion of action and strategic elements
•Small plugin download for browser based play
•Pretty funny riding a bicycle the first few times
•Unique blending of genres
•Full scale wars that can take weeks to complete
•Mobile app to command when away from your PC
•F2P not P2W
Negatives
•The Game Lobby system can be very confusing
•Not graphically impressive
•Lag can sometimes be an issue (in beta though)
•The “full war” aspect of the game really caters to the more time invested players
•May not be interesting for some FPS players who are looking for faster gameplay
Overview
Heroes & Generals is a browser-based game set around the militaristic world of World War II.  Developed by Reto-Moto, it is an online war game with a number of playable modes in which players assume the role of an officer. In this role, players are in charge of formulating strategies that will lead to victory and have general command of the grand strategy. Every player within the battlefield will have a consequence to each of their actions, whether good or bad.
The highlight of the game is its team-based First Person Shooter platform, which ties into a persistent game world. It blends in strategy with FPS by allowing players to move around resources on the game’s world map. At any point if two Assault teams meet, a battle between them will play out in the game’s FPS aspect. By this design, the developing strategy aspect of the games feeds into the FPS action, closely influencing the entire gameplay experience.
Gameplay
There are three modes of gameplay in which players are able to compete in. First there is Assault, which resembles a traditional Domination mode. In this mode, the objective is for a player’s team to own all of the control maps on the map. Next is Skirmish, which is a classic Team Deathmatch mode. And finally, Interdiction, which centers on a player’s team intercepting the opposite team’s supplies, which feeds into the strategic importance of Heroes & Generals.
Heroes & Generals features a ton of vehicles that players can use during action based portions of the Campaigns. From aircraft to bicycles and beyond, you’re bound to find something to get you around faster and maybe provide some additional firepower.
In addition to its blend of strategy and action, Heroes & Generals allows players to use tactics not often seen in Online FPS games. One such tactic made available due to the game’s vast terrain vegetation is the ability to hide in brush and tall grass without the fear of being targeted by an enemy sniper. With this ability, players will be able to avert many enemy tactics beyond just enemy snipers, and makes guerrilla warfare possible.
Characters
In Heroes & Generals, a character is a player’s personal and customized soldier that is to be used in the FPS portion of the game. The character section allows for the creation, deletion, renaming, and customization of a player’s soldiers. Soldiers are able to carry different weapons and be assigned combat badges that grant in-game perks. These perks can range from increased running speed to the ability to pick up ammo from dead soldiers. Soldiers can enter into a battle if a character slot is available with a participating Assault Team with the available resources. There are seven available types of soldiers to choose from: Infantry, Paratrooper, Machine-gunner, Anti Armor, Recon, Fighter pilot, and Tank Crew.
Assault Teams
Assault Team(s) represent the smallest group of players in each game. Creating and joining an assault team is recommended, as it’s considered the easiest way for players to play together with friends. Only Assault Teams are able to initiate attacks, in contrast to Strategic Commands which are used for logistic purposes. Reserve Units (troops, tanks, etc) are assigned directly to the assault team and used in combat. The assault teams have a limit to their size, dependent on their type.
These types, categorized into strict types that unlock access to different specializations, allow the use of special weapons and vehicles. When an Assault Team is attacked, all friendly players can join the battle. They will need to have a character that fits the Assault Team’s specialization however.
Strategy And War
The overall Heroes & Generals game experience is focused on winning an entire war, not just individual battles. Wars can wage for days and weeks in some cases. At the start of a war, both factions (Axis and Allies) start in “home” European cities and all cities between the two armies are neutral. Through strategy game play (kind of RTS, but not quite) cities are slowly taken over until both factions collide and attempt to take over each other’s cities. As established supply lines fall and cities are taken over, an army can win the overall war through enemy surrender or the annihilation of the opposing army.

Like Far Cry (and not so much like the somewhat disappointing Far Cry 2), Far Cry 3 is a stunningly beautiful game. It's also loads of fun to roam around, do crazy things, blow stuff up, kill people and endangered species. The side quests are fun, too, and generally satisfying.
The weak point of the game is really the story and the main quest line. I read an article where the story writer argued that those criticising the story hadn't understood it. Well, if you need to explain the story, it wasn't told very well to begin with. What's left is posturing, trying to defend poor storytelling abilities.
There are games that tell their stories very well; Valve are particularly good at that, starting with Half-Life. GTA4 is another example, where you know that Niko Belic did some pretty bad things back in former Yugoslavia, but it never becomes specfic, and it doesn't need to be.
Then, there are other issues that take away from the fun. The game occassonally crashes, and if you're in the middle of a long mission, well, though. You'll have to start all over again. It happened to me at least five times.
Cut scenes cannot be skipped. There are a couple of examples where it's quite easy to die, and every time you have to watch the same boring cut scene again. And again. And again.
Which brings me to dream sequences. For some obscure reason, some game publishers are under the illusion that dream sequences are cool. They're not. They suck very, very much.
Some parts of the game are very dark, even with brightness and gamma all the way up. I need a bit more light than the average gamer, but I just can't crank it up enough to see everything. Maybe if I had a super bright TN screen, but no, it's eIPS. And other games don't have the same issue.
Finally, a dishonourable mention goes to Uplay, the Ubisoft launcher that you get without asking for it. Whatever the idea behind this piece of annoyware is escapes me. Maybe they're trying to create some sort of brand loyalty; they achieve exactly the opposite. Steam serves me just fine. I don't need another layer.
So, would I recommend this game? In a word, yes, as long as you get it on special offer. It cannot be stressed enough how gorgeous it looks (as long as you're outside at least), and there are so many fun things to do. The weak story is something you have to accept as part of the package.

This is the first game in the Far Cry series that I have played, so I'm afraid I cannot provide a comparison to the previous two titles. What I CAN do is share my thoughts on this particular game and my personal feelings on it.
My initial reaction involved the voice acting and characters. As countless people have already stated, Vaas was a phenomenal villain. I would say I haven't encountered a villain with such an extraordinary personality in a video game since Andrew Ryan from the original Bioshock. His appearance, his voice, even the way he carries himself is unparallel to any other character in the game, which is actually a bit of an issue. I wanted MORE of him. When you view him on the cover of the game and in the trailers for the game, you would certainly assume that he's the primary villain, but unfortunately, he's not. The game suffers from a bit of a "villain identity crisis" originally leading us to believe that Vaas is public enemy number one when in fact, Hoyt is, and he proves to be slightly underwhelming in comparison. The story in general takes a bit of a downhill spiral once Vaas exits stage left, especially once magic starts to get involved and it takes on a cheesy "Indiana Jones" sort of feel.
However, there is more to video games than just narrative, and this game excels in the gameplay department for the most part. There are numerous vehicular chases during which you drive the getaway car or man a turret on the back, and you'll additionally find yourself performing similar tasks in boats and helicopters. There's also plenty of interactive combat sequences, during which you'll be prompted to press certain keys at certain times, or in other words, the kind of battles that keep you on your toes. And that's actually something that impressed me about this game, you see, in many open-world games, you'll find yourself withdrawn from the action after an intense mission, usually given the option to continue to the next mission location and pick up where you left off, or simply wander aimlessly about the world exploring (also known as "wasting time"). But in this game, even when you're not doing a story mission, you may still be attacked by bloodthirsty (and rather crude) pirates, or mauled by an alligator while swimming in a river, forcing you to frantically mash buttons so as to preserve your life. This game requires your undivided attention, so you won't be dozing off anytime soon.
With regards to the open-world aspect, this game will not disappoint. Perhaps the best way I can describe it is a mashup of Grand Theft Auto 5 mixed with Skyrim on a tropical island. Yeah, it's that cool. You'll find yourself murdering pirates and hijacking their vehicles, then being hunted by their friends not unlike those pesky cops in GTA. Exploring is made relatively simple with the radio towers, simply climb to the top of one, smack a power box a bit, and you will be rewarded with a large chunk of vision on your minimap, AND you'll have access to free weapons from the store at Amanaki Town. It just makes exploring less of a hassle, which is always nice. And once you've discovered a town, you'll be able to quick travel there, so there's no need to worry about any extra long roadtrips.
There are multiple missions that are relatively difficult, and that was simply on Survivor mode. I may not be the best at shooters, but I know my way around a digital gun, and I can assure you that you won't be breezing through this one, unless perhaps you play on the mode below Survivor, whatever that is. But hey, when seemingly everyone is complaining about games being "too easy" these days, a little bit of a challenge may be welcome. Although, there were some timed missions and protection missions that I disliked, not even necessarily because they were tough, but rather because they were annoying. I've never been a fan of those kinds of missions though, but regardless of how I feel about them, just know that there are plenty of them. Take that as you will.
The final aspect that I wanted to touch on was the crafting. Now some people may find this frustrating, but I rather enjoyed having to earn the larger wallet, rucksack, and weapons holsters by skinning animals and using their skins to craft larger versions of my equipment. It actually provided incentive to hunt, something I probably wouldn't have even thought of if I hadn't been forced to do so, and more specifically, you have to hunt for certain animals that can only be found in certain areas of the island, which is just another one of those fun little challenges the game has to offer.
I would give this game a total score of 8/10. Very close to a 9 if not for the story suffering following Vaas's death, and some rather aggravating missions that you may have to repeat many times before completing. Otherwise, fun game, you should get many hours out of it.

I'm about two years late to this party, so I do apologize, but I feel like I need to say it: I ♥♥♥♥ing adore this game.
From start to- woefully quickly reached- finish, I enjoyed damn near every second of Far Cry 3. The game does a fantastic job of setting the stage from the first cutscene. You're away on vacation with your friends. You like your friends. They're kind of douches, but you're a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥too. From California, so you don't mind it when they try and be edgy and flip off your camera while sky-diving, because hurtling from a plane to their potential death isn't quite edgy enough for them. They're good guys, for the most part.
Then Vaas Montenegro captures all of you, and murders your older brother when you have the nerve to try and escape. From there the race is on to rescue your friends and implant a knife in the man who's flip turned your would upside down. But our destination isn't Bel Air, I'm afraid. Carlton isn't here to dance for you and make you feel better about your troubles. No, here, your only company are angry pirates and various wildlife that do not care about your missing friends and family, and merely want to see how good you taste.
And that suits Jason Brody just fine. The Rook Islands have been amazingly planned out- almost nowhere is safe here. Any civilization is almost assuredly packed to the brim with Vaas and his boss, Hoyt Volker's men, none of which are happy to see you- unless they've got you in their sights. Try to hide amongst the foliage, and you're likely to find your balls being chewed off by komodo dragons blending almost seamlessly into the greenery- or some form of big cat managing to sneak up on you despite clashing with the scenery and ruining your♥♥♥♥♥♥
Fortunately, the local resistance to these Pirates are a firm believer of Quid Pro Quo. Make their lives easier, and they'll be all too happy to provide you with guns and flamethrowers- a wide array of lead-firing equalizers for purveyors of all fighting ranges. Get in close with a pistol or shotgun, and let your enemy look you in the eye as you kill them... or hide behind a wall and spray molten lead on anyone dumb enough to try and rush you with both light and heavy machine guns. For those who prefer to stay out of harm's way, a simple hunting bow is perfect for hunting the Ultimate Game- as is its' advanced cousin, the sniper rifle.
Alternatively, you could say "♥♥♥♥ all that noise" and try to get through as much of the game as possible with just the Flamethrower. Which, like every other weapon I've mentioned, comes with custom paintjobs. Make that gun truly your own.
I'm going to talk about the story now- including the ending-, so time for spoiler tags.

Despite the two paragraphs I just whipped up, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. Far Cry 3 is a great game and an example of how a sequel should be. While Far Cry 2 had good ideas and was even brilliant in places, I oftentimes found myself bored with it. Far Cry 3 takes what was good about Far Cry 2 and expands on it, while cutting out or seriously improving on the stuff that didn't work.
Gameplaywise, the initial setup looks a great deal like Far Cry 2, dropping you into a gorgeous open world and letting you go about story objectives and side missions in whatever way you want to. The missions are mostly very open and generally give you a great deal of freedom. If you want to go into something guns blazing, you can do that. If you want to sneak around and take out everyone unseen, you can do that as well. Oftentimes attempts at stealth will go awry, turning everything into a chaotic rush to either get out of the situation or find some way to defeat the enemies with what you have. The battles are dynamic and the emergent gameplay this game has is wonderful. This was great in Far Cry 2 and it's great in Far Cry 3. One issue with Far Cry 2 is that everytime you completed a mission, you literally had to drive back to the center of the map to get the next one. This was extremely boring and led you to traverse the same areas of the map over and over again. Far Cry 3 alleviates this by giving you the location of your next mission as soon as you finish the previous one, which gives a nice feeling of progress and keeps you moving through areas of the island you haven't seen yet. It also allows for a fast travel option, which allows you to go to any friendly outpost you've been to before, which greatly expedites things. Furthermore, if you clear an outpost, the enemies stay dead, as opposed to Far Cry 2 where enemies would respawn (meaning you would have to fight the same battle many times). Side missions in Far Cry 2 were repetitive and unrewarding, but the sidemissions in Far Cry 3 have much more variety and give you a real sense of progress. Also, the guns feel much better this time around. In Far Cry 2, the weapons felt weak and unsatisfying, but in 3 they pack a real punch. Far Cry 3 has an RPG style levelling system that lets you upgrade your skills (including getting new melee attacks), and it's very enjoyable to level up and discover new abilities.
In terms of storyline, this game is miles above its predecessor. Far Cry 2 wanted to tell a raw, gritty story of war in an impoverished land, but forgot to make you care, and more or less forgot to have a storyline five minutes after the intro. Both sides of whatever conflict was going on were basically identical and the game didn't give you any reason to care about one or the other, and none of the characters were given any kind of personality or storyline. Furthermore, the villain had no sense of presence and you had no reason to want to go after him, other than that it was your job. Far Cry 3 on the other hand, blows its predecessor's story out of the water. Right off the bat, you are introduced to Vaas, a human traficker who has kidnapped you and your friends. Vaas is one of the most memorable villains I've seen in a game, and is brought to life wonderfully through a combination of brilliant voice acting and incredibly natural animation. His presence permeates through the game and he imposes a real sense of menace on the world. The supporting cast is awesome as well, and you'll meet a wide variety of great characters. As you save your friends and become more accustomed to the world, the main character, Jason Brody, goes through an interesting progression, and it's fascinating to see how he develops through the game.
Graphically, this game is gorgeous, and it performs very well. I have a GTX 780 (6gb vram edition), and on ultra settings, I usually got at minimum 40 FPS, although it was generally higher than that (at least when I ran fraps). Character models are extremely detailed and well animated. Foliage also looks great, and the lighting is brilliant as well. At times, the game looks almost pre-rendered. It truly is a nice looking game.
Overall, Far Cry 3 is great. It improves on Far Cry 2 in every regard and gives you a ton of content for your money.

M&B games are like an action RPG with political strategy overtones. I find the gameplay to be highly addictive, or at least time-absorbing. The real fun is in the mods, and although Warband is highly improved upon the original M&B, the original has a better mod selection. There's a demo for each of the first two M&B games so you can even try them out for free.

It took a lot of convincing to get me to try Warband. I’m not a big fan of brawlers, or multiplayer games, or of melee warfare in general. The graphics aren’t that great, the game is buggy, and the UI is terrible.
However, I can easily say M&B Warband is one of the best games I have ever played. Sometimes I think it might be THE best game I've played. The thrill of charging an opposing force, arrows and bolts and spears whizzing by your head… I’ve not found anything else comparable (not even the other M&B expansions).
The basic premise of the single player (and 95% of my time has been in single player) is to build yourself up from a lone nobody into the commander of an army and a political force in the land. M&B melds some very basic RPG elements (upgradeable stats, inventory, and conversation trees) with pretty good medieval combat (melee, horseback, and archers) to form something that is much more than the sum of its awkward parts.
You spend your time on an overview map travelling between towns, castles, and encounters. Enter one of those and you drop in to first person. You can run around towns interacting with a (very few) people and things, or fight battles on assorted fields. There are various quests and missions you can undertake, which generally earn you money (trading is also a possible employment). Spend that money on buying yourself better equipment, hiring special powerful followers, or building up large numbers of regular troops. Everyone gains experience through battles that can be used to improve the abilities.
The combat is where Warband shines. Even though the AI isn’t great and the animation can be awkward, the buildup, clash, and flow of the battle is amazing. You start with encounters of just a dozen men or less, but can build up armies of hundreds. By default only a few dozen will be present at a time, reinforcements coming in waves. I modded up the troop size to 500, so battles rage with hundreds on a side. I liked the way this made my troop preparation more important than my individual skill in battle.
You can capture towns and be awarded their control by the king of that region. This adds another interesting twist to you play, as you build up the infrastructure of you holdings and feed your troops to its garrison, while simultaneously defending it from enemies. You also need to lend your sword to your liege when he demands it in order to stay on his good side and generally secure the lands around you.
The multiplayer side of Warband sports the expected modes (deathmatches, CTF, and KotH varients), and can be a lot of fun when you get a group together, even just teaming up against the AI. But for me the best part of Warband is the modding community
. Both the single player and multiplayer mods add exceptional value to the base game, with many total conversion available. (I recommend the Battle Sizer
for everyone, and Floris
for those seeking a bit more content while staying true to the original game.

I bought this game so I could run around in an open world blowing things up and killing bad guys. What I got was a open world where I run around collecting plants and crates and hunting animals.  The persistent feeling that "I am not killing bad guys right now" is the primary reason why I detest this game.  For a game that does a decent job at stealth and an excellent job challenging you to figure out ways to take out enemy encampments, the lack of time spent in these activities is the game's single greatest tragedy.
Things that wouldn't stop me from playing the game individually, but taken together they really detract from enjoyment:
- Unlike Far Cry 1 and 2, this is not a PC game...this is a console port. Some of the laser sights are a big fat dot that literally obscure what you are trying to shoot. This makes things harder to hit since you can't see exactly where you are aiming. You can customize some weapons to avoid this. On other weapons (such as the game's best sub-machine gun) you can't.
- Some of the "gameplay" is reduced to the kind of button mashing you would expect in an arcade game at Dave and Busters.
- Random crashes to desktop. Given the checkpoint system this game uses, they result in lost progress.
- To play the game, I have to open Steam, which opens Ubisoft's pointless Uplay portal, which gives me the button I need to launch the actual game.
- You use a clunky menu often for crafting, weapons customization, maps, etc. It really interrupts the gameplay. If you are a fan of Far Cry 2's minimal interface, you will find the frequent menu interruptions to be unbearable.
- Unable to skip cutscenes. There are quite a few of them, and a fair number of them are long.
Things I liked:
- Stealth and take downs are very well implemented. This alone would have gone a long way towards making Far Cry 3 one of my favorite games of all time.
- The ability to have multiple weapons of the same type is very nice. The game has both an RPG and a grenade launcher available. Being able to carry both of them at the same time is fantastic.
- Excellent cinematics and decent plot.
- While I personally don't like or use the bow, it is very cool that they added it as an option. I'm sure some people are loving it.
- Great graphics.
- Bad guys were mostly interesting.
If you loved Far Cry 1 and 2, I would highly recommend skipping this one.  Hopefully they don't screw up Far Cry 4, but the way Ubisoft is going, I fully expect them to launch a fantastic game and then screw it up by adding too much fluff to it.

This is a long overdue review that I should have published last year after playing the game:
I pre-purchased and pre-loaded this game at full price. I was so disappointed in the game that I felt like I wasted the $60 I paid. The game itself seemed to be quite buggy and it even prevented me from playing it at full quality. Due to the fact that I have ATI drivers and not Nvidia, the game itself would not go over 15-25 frames at a resolution of 1600x900 on low quality.
When this game came out I was playing BF3 and Max Payne 3 at ultra settings getting 45-60 frames. There was no reason that this game should have been performing as terribly as it was.
I even contacted Ubisoft customer support to resolve the issue I was having. All they told me was the typical stuff such as update drivers etc. I had already done the basics and they couldn't offer more help except to casually claim there would be an update soon. It was an update that never came. The game was s*** and you guys obviously didn't care. All you cared about was raking in the cash while you could. ATI users were screwed and it was plain to see that it was just an overall bad port to PC. Just like the recent Watch_Dogs, lots of PC users were left sitting with a game that didn't operate up to the specs they claimed originally.
Now let's talk about the multiplayer. What was that trash? Attempting to create a fun or at least competitive multiplayer seemed none existant. The multiplayer probably should have been left out of this shiny gem. The map editor was fun, thanks for allowing me to make maps for a terrible multiplayer. Far Cry 2 wasn't the greatest but at least it was broken like the multiplayer and coop was for 3. And coop was not necessary at all. Again it was attempted to make a competitive/fun coop by allowing up to 4 players to run amuk. The only problem was the coop was close to being a rail shooter due to how linear it was setup. Making an "open world" game closed for coop was probably one of the dumber decisions you could have made in this game.
[Spoilers ahead]
So the story you guys made, it was okay I guess. It had some merits but some of it seemed quite childish and silly mostly. You play a typical white guy who despite his stupid rich friends seems to be able to pick up any gun and just blow away the baddies like it's no big deal at all. Later some how you become the leader of a bunch of islanders and start a revolution, while also tripping major balls on drugs and fighting weird tiki monsters that look absolutely ridiculous. Oh and let's not forget all the while this story is happening you are killing hundreds of endangered species and taking their hides to make a bigger wallet to store the money you take off the bodies of the hundreds of mercs you laid waste to. If you weren't busy skinning a giant helpless tortoise or gliding around oddly placed japanese bunkers you were likely blowing up outpost after outpost slowly boring yourself to death. Overall the story seemed way far fetched and just ridiculous. Who will you choose at the end? Your stupid rich friends, or your new crazy islander wackos. The choice is up to you bucko! Oh boy it's over, thank you!
So to conclude my review of this game. Thank you for a bad port to PC, again. Thank you for not catering to all drivers in the PC gaming world, again. And lastly thank you for wasting $60 of my hard earned money, again.

3 out of 5.  Fun, beautiful / repetitive, derivative.  The first few hours of the game were a blast to play.  In the beginning there are serious limitations to how many weapons, and how much ammunition you carry.  As a result I spent several boring hours hunting animals to make larger bags and whatnot, fun the first time, boring the tenth time.  Even after I was fully upgraded I still felt like I couldn't carry enough ammo to play the way I wanted to.  The story is alright, and the island is relatively fun to explore.  Many of the side missions are unoriginal, and the way you unlock parts of the map by capturing towers is soooo unoriginal and a chore.  I feel like the creators had a good game, then added boring filler (hunting, side missions, towers) to increase the play time.  You can ignore these parts of the game, but then your character will be weak in the late-game.  None of the vehicles were as fun as they should have been, mainly due to poor controls and poor physics.  I really wish I liked this game more.  I recommend playing it, but get it I on sale like me.  The guns are pretty good, and I loved how you could customize most of them.  I wish there were more customizations.  I didn't hate this game, but I didn't love it, I wish there was a sliding scare or a 5 star rating system instead of a thumbs up or down.

"MMOFPS" isn't exactly the phrase I'd use to describe this game. When I think of this phrase I think of a FPS game with literally hundreds of players in the battlefield, like Planetside. This game has a maximum of 36 players (18 each team) per match, and compared to a game like Battlefield, that's pretty much nothing.
In a way though, you do sort of interact with everyone in the game,  in that if the faction you choose (US or Germany) wins or loses a battle, it reflects as such on the Campaign, or the World Map. The "Wars" between the two factions last for a couple of weeks and whichever side has the highest number of deaths, highest costs, most vehicles destroyed, etc. ends up losing.
You can play as a "General" after you've reached the highest rank with a soldier. This is probably the "MMOiest" aspect of the game, in that you can look at the map and purchase assault teams for each and every battle with Warfunds. This creates a set up such that almost every game is unbalanced. One team might have aircrafts and heavy tanks, while the other team might only have jeeps and recon vehicles. Some may hate this, some may find this "realistic" and enjoy it, I'm personally neutral on it, I see it as good and bad.
The game itself sort of feels like a mix of Battlefield and DayZ. It has big maps, classes to choose from, vehicles to utilize, but also a strong utilization of stealth and environmental awareness. You can literally kill an entire team of players by yourself if you're using the right strategy, weapon, position, etc. It's a pretty hardcore game, and I like the fact that Teamkilling is on 100% of the time.
Like a good amount of FPS games, this game can occasionally suffer from "spawnkilling" on Skirmish type games, griefers do exist, and annoying bugs can occur quite frequently.
Like a good amount of MMO games, this game can suffer from a "Pay to Win" aspect, as if I wanted to I could whip out my Debit Card and purchase every single weapon in the game and every single assault team. But the fact that there's a lot of skill involved in the game, and that almost every item can be acquired through in-game means, the "Pay to Win" aspect is dimmed down a good bit at least.
Overall would recommend this game, it's surprisingly great for an Early Access game, and I can see myself wasting a lot of hours on it.

Far cry 3 game review.
Far cry 3, also known as 'Skyrim with guns.'. There's truth to that, I'll show you in this review.
'Far Cry 3 is an open world action-adventure first-person shooter video game developed mainly by Ubisoft Montreal in conjunction with Ubisoft Massive, Ubisoft Red Storm, Ubisoft Shanghai, and Ubisoft Reflections, published by Ubisoft for Microsoft Windows, Xbox 360, and PlayStation 3. The game was released on November 29, 2012 in Australia, November 30 in Europe, and December 4 in North America. A stand-alone expansion titled Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon was released on April 30, 2013.' (-Wikipedia)
In this review, I'll write about a couple of things:
-Story
-Gameplay
-Enemy AI/Boss fights
-Crafting
-Minigames
-Overal Pros and Cons
-Story.
The story start out with you, Jason Brody, partying in a club in Bangkok.  You're with your brothers, Riley and Grant, and your other friends. Lisa, Daisy, Keith, and Grand. You're celebrating that your little brother Riley got his pilot's licence. The group decides to go skydive over an island. As you land on the ground, you're captured by local pirates, lead by Vaas. All this is shown to you on a phone camera, held by Vaas as you sit in a cel. You and your brother manage to break out of the cel once Vaas is gone. Halfway through you get caught, and have to run. Once you're safely away from the camp, you meet Dennis. And then your mission to resceu your brother and friends begins.
-Gameplay.
As previously stated, far cry 3 is an open world first person shooter. There's plently of weapons to pick from. You start out with a knife and a pistol, and as you enable radio towers and do missions, you unlock more weapons. You can also buy weapons from the store, although the prices are fairly high.
There's also skills to be unlocked. One of the first skills you learn is 'take down' , which allows you to take down an enemy with a knife. As you go along, more skills get unlocked. Once you've unlocked a skills, it will be represented by a tattoo on your left arm. The more skills you get, he more the tattoos form a sleeve.
-Enemy AI/Boss fights.
I'll admit the enemy AI isn't the best. They'll run for cover, and sometimes try to get away from you, but they'll hardly do anything to prevent getting shot in the open. For example, if you're at a wide open field, they'll run towards you in a straight line. Sometimes they'll seek cover behind an explodable barrel. Overal, it could be improved, but it's not terrible either.
Bos fights are often handled in quick time events, much like animals fights. Quicktime events are made of the following: Left and right mouse button, E, C, and spacebar. Nothing special or hard, but the animation make it look very cool and impressive.
-Crafting.
This game also features crafting (Bet you geussed that already!). To improve you have to craft. More storage, more ammo storage, more weapons, more money, and more syringes are some of the things gained by crafting. You can craft multiple sorts of syringes, for healing and combat. There's also syringes for your surrounding, better senses to find animals, holding your breath underwater for longer, and being fireproof.
Syringes are crafted by collecting leaves, the other things are crafted by animals skins.
-Mingames.
If you're getting tired from killing pirates and animals, there's also minigames. There are seven of them:
Poker (A game of Poker)
Racing (Getting from A to B hitting checkpoints)
Shooting birds (Shoot birds with a shotgun)
Throwing knifes. (Press the button at the right time to throw the knife at the right place on the board)
Supply drop. (Get from A to B hitting checkpoints, within the time limit)
Wanted Dead. (Kill a pirate with a knife)
Hunting qeusts. (Hunt an animal with a specific weapon)
All these are unlocked by taking down outposts and activating radiotowers. There's also side mission, all unique.
Overal Pros and Cons.
Pros:
Fun gameplay
Nice graphics, even on low.
Large varity of weapons.
Good crafting system.
Interesting villain (Vaas)
Multiplayer (although I've never tried it personally)
Lots of Collectables
First person driving
Cons:
Can get boring if you let it.
Second island and villain aren't as interesting as the first.
Main character is rather bland and uninteresting
Activating radiotowers starts to feel like a chore after a while
Overal I'd rate this game a 9/10. Lots of hours of fun went into this game.

When Far Cry 2 released not many great titles were out at the time, at least for consoles. (It was one of the first games having trophies on PS3.) I remember many of my friends buying it and not liking it, but for me Far Cry 2 quickly emerged as a special title that I will soon not forget. Probably one of the most balanced games I've played online.
Far Cry 3 is a more fluid version, with more sidequests. One of the first things that hits you is how it emerges you in a exotic and this time tropical world. Visually a fantastic looking game. The guns feel powerful and sound and feel different from one another. It's unforuntate that one needs to use Uplay to play it, an annoyance, but to me "oh well" (and I despise Origin and will never install it). The story is inconsistent, not making sense at times, definitely more towards the end. However, compared to recent blockbuster hits its decent yet not believable. Jason Brody develops into a lame hipster, who quickly learns Rambo-like skills - it was a little too fast and like I said not believable to me. I think that's beside the point though, as Far Cry 3 really shines in moments where the player can move from a silent, stealthy, and slow approach to a fast-gunning and fast-paced gameplay. For example, when you want to snipe everyone in an encampment, get spotted, then blast everyone away with a LMG. Setting up IEDs on enemy roads or throwing molotovs into the jungle and setting everything ablaze are definitely setting you up for gaming moments that are unmatched. I think many people are going to hit their screenshot button. Overall, Far Cry 3 is a great game and it doesn't surprise that many are excited for its next installment (albeit releasing quite early after its announcement).

SINGLE PLAYER REVIEW
NO SPOLIERS
After playing Far Cry 3 for 34 hours, I finally finished the game's campaign. All I can say is..WOW! This game surpassed my expectations and is probably one of the best game of 2012 (I'm really mad I didn't play it sooner)! This game has so much to offer thorugh collectables spread out through the map, side missions to part take in, hunting to craft ammo pouches/arrow quivers/etc., island races/sea races, main story missions, and more!
Story:
You are Jason Brody - a cocky rich young adult on vacation with some of his best friends. While skydiving you land on Rook Island (really two islands; one to the North, one to the South) and are held captive by pirates/ raiders/ slave traders. Here you meet Vaas and Hoyt, the two crazy men running the show. I will not go into any more detail, but all I can say is that the story is pretty well done. It is not the best story I have been played in a video game, but it did a good job making you care about the characters. The cutscenes are excellent, and the motion capture is almost up to LA Noire standards. The character that really steals the show is Vaas. I personally did not find Hoyt to be as interesting as Vaas.
8.0 out of 10
Gameplay:
There is so much to do in Far Cry 3, and almost all of it is engaging and fun! Clearing enemy outposts and hunting were amazingly done; the way it implements into the game is great. Using the animal skins, you are able to craft ammo pouches to hold more ammo as well as holsters to carry up to four weapons. The weapon vary is great, and you have many to choose from. They all feel different from one another and are fun to play around with. What I found really made this game stand out as compared to other open-world games was the attention to detail, the level of polish, and how smoothly the animations were. This let the game flow very nicely, and lead to combat that was fun and refreshing. Stealth is also a pretty big element in this game, and is nailed in the game. You are able to hide in vegetation, takedown enemies, and hide their bodies. Some of the best FPS stealth I have seen in a long time.
9.0 out of 10
Graphics:
Rook Island is gorgeous! With an AMD R9 290, I was able to max this game out with frame rates that hovered around 50 - 70 fps outdoors and over 100 in-doors. The day-night cycle is back and works well. What I found so great about this game is how colorful and vibrant the environment was. In Far Cry 2, the graphics were great, but everything was grey and brown which lead the game to look washed out. In Far Cry 3, everything pops and really makes you feel immersed in the game.
9.0 out of 10
Audio:
Everything sounds as it should. The guns sound beefy, the reloads sound and look great. The animals are nailed. The only sound that stands out to me to be low quality is racking the slide back on the AK 47 which was kind of a let down (this is only being knit picky though).
8.8 out of 10
Conclusion:
Overall, I enjoyed Far Cry 3 immensely and I would recommend it to anyone that enjoys open-world games. The game has pretty good replay value (I can see myself going back to play though the game again). I can't wait to see how Far Cry 4 turns out later this November!
Far Cry 3---8.7 out of 10

An MMOFPS, combined with RTS, how many games have something like that?
Not a lot I can tell you.
I am a 2 year old veteran, with well over 1000 hours of gameplay (probably closer to 2000). I have seen a lot of builds come and go, a lot of bugs come and go (and come, and come more and more).
Now, I could just say that this game is perfect and everyone should play because it is. But it's not.
So I want to talk about the good things and the bad things.
First things first: 1 word, 4 letters: BETA.
RTS:
The thing that really grabbed me was the RTS part. I play together with a group called 'AHQ' (Allied High Command). We've been playing together for a long time and truly became brothers in arms.
The first think we always do, is put our units (assault teams) on the front-line. The power to decide which battle has how many resources is very different from other games. The game lives by a standard: 'The war is balanced, but not every battle is'. Sometimes you have tanks, planes, APC's, snipers etc. Sometimes you don't have anything and losing the battle seems certain.
It is exactly those battles that make this game so interesting. The enemy bombards you with tanks and planes and all you have is an old rifle and your trusty bazooka. You cannot fight them in the open, if you are fighting an assault you've already lost. But in a defensive match, you can win with anything. It will be hard, but if you manage to win, or even lose but kill off a lot of tanks and planes, the enemy generals will cry their eyes out.
In the current stage, the RTS is lacking. It's very basic and the balancing-factors are not yet in place. This creates unbalanced wars (axis almost always win) which are not always fun. However, BETA. The RTS is not yet fully developed and a lot is to come. If you cannot stand losing all the wars, come back in a few months.
FPS:
The FPS is very fun, the amount of weapons is still small, and things like bipods on mg's are not yet developed. However the FPS feels pretty authentic (note: authentic does not equal realistic) with pretty big maps. There are a lot of vehicles to chose from, including tanks, planes, APC's, jeeps and even bikes.
Vehicles are not spawned every X time on the same spot. Players spawn them from a certain assault team. When a general sents in 18 light tanks, you can spawn 18 light tanks. If the general does not sent you tanks... no tanks for you. To be able to spawn a tank or something else, you need the right character. An infantry-man cannot spawn a tank, so you have to wait till a certain level before you can upgrade (make sure you always keep 1 character infantry, otherwise you are stuck in matchmaking forever). You can have as many characters as you want.
There are of course a lot of bugs and glitches in the FPS, every once in a while when you step off a bike, you fly 50 meters into the air and die when coming back to the ground.

Far Cry 3 succeeds like its predecessors in providing an open world action / thriller set in a tropical climate.  Like similar games such as GTA and Batman: AC, the current objective is shown on the map... there are side missions and mini-games that can be unlocked and played at will.  Portions of the map details are hidden until radio towers are "unlocked" by scaling them and sabotaging the fuse box.  Weapons and skills are steadily unlocked as progress is made in both the main story line, collecting hidden treasures, and completing various other tasks.  Thrown in for good measure are hunting and crafting, and a completely separate and very challenging co-op campaign.
On the plus side:
> The world is beautiful and nicely detailed.
> The story is quite good and features one of the best antagonists in any video game I have ever played.
> The weapons look, feel, and sound excellent.
> The stronghold raids and "kill nasty dude x" side missions are the meat of the game and very entertaining, with many ways to approach them
> The takedown skills are challenging to apply and fun when they work.
> An excellent PC port with all the graphical and control flourish we expect.
On the negative side:
> The game ramps up too quickly... I found myself proceeding at a reasonable pace, and by act 2 I was becoming overpowered... this along with another mechanic in act 2 makes the second act seem anti-climactic.
> On the same vein, the first act Boss feels more threatening than the second.  He also was such a good character I was disappointed that he was dead.  Can he have his own game, please?
> The native peoples character models are too similar.
> The world does not feel "lived in"... it feels more like an action game set piece.  There is also very little variation in the game world.
> There is very little incentive to continue exploring after the game ends.
The co-op campaign is very difficult... you will want at least 3 players for that.  I bought the game on sale on steam for $5... was it worth it? Yes absolutely.  I would say $20 is reasonable for this since I got nearly 40 hours of entertainment out of it.

The first half of this game is a masterpiece.  The second half is terrible.  But overall, I am very glad I got it, and I will always remember it.
The first half of the game has very enjoyable gameplay, and I like that you can choose whether you want to be stealthy or just go full-on Rambo with guns ablaze.  Taking over strongholds were definitely the best part of the game for this reason - it's you, a bunch of bad guys, and it's all up to you how you deal with it.
The missions throw this tactic out the window.  For the first half of the game, you are pretty much forced to use stealth tactics, and for the second half, it's basically Call of Duty type shooting.  Speaking of which...
The second half of the game throws all tactics out the window, and in my opinion, it was thoroughly unenjoyable.  Whereas with any other part of the game, you can approach the enemies however you want, in several of the missions in the second half, they don't even spawn until you are about ten feet away, meaning if you were relying on the bow or the sniper (like I was), tough luck ya ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  If you insist upon playing the second part of the game, my advice would be to carry: a large machine gun, a shotgun, a rocket launcher, and one type of long range weapon.  Stealth matters no more.
Obviously, Vaas is the best character in the game.  But after he's gone (don't think I'm spoiling anything there), the game just felt empty - you're only halfway done after that point, and Hoyt is not the same, not by a long shot.  I kept playing just to see the ending that everyone was talking about, and even that was pretty disappointing.
So to sum it up: if you get this game, my advice would be to play the first half of the game and enjoy it to its fullest, then either go full-on sandbox and forget the story or drop the game altogether and just watch the ending on Youtube.  You're missing nothing between the two.

FarCry 3. One of the BEST games I’ve ever played in my years of gaming.
There’s so much to talk about, I guess I’ll divide this game into multiple categories to talk about.
– The storyline 10/10
Words literally how amazingly amazing it felt to play this game. The story mode was well thought out and executed perfectly, an original story with everything else was amazing. I do not wish to spoil the story too much because you NEED to play this game. Basically you are a tourist visiting an island when suddenly something goes wrong…
– The graphics 10/10
Graphic-wise the game is beautiful and detailed, when you’re playing it, it feels like skyrim but with better graphics and more realistic weapons. Sure some computers may not be able to run the game, but the majority of the people who can run the game on the best graphics will admit it you can feel a simple breeze from the wind. The weather system can’t be talked bad about at all because the rain wasn’t too annoying, but was made just perfect.
– The A.I 8/10
The A.I is the only element in the game I could complain about, yet it was marvelous. In times during the game I noticed some A.I glitching in the wall or just auto-noticing me behind a wall. In other times the A.I were just surprisingly professional by avoiding all walls and hiding behind baricades while shooting me only when I stand up to shoot them! Also the A.I of animals was made so they act like they do in real life, from turtles crouching in their shell to sharks slowly getting closer and going in for the kill.
– The Controls 10/10
Everything was designed wisely, starting from the basic-in-every-game controls like WASD and Shift to sprint to smaller details like switching items in your inventory around the way you like.
– The gameplay 10/10
This is the main element of the game which is most essential. The possibilities are infinite, you can play the game as vanilla as you want by using weapons you pick up from the enemy but you can’t taste the game truly unless you’ve tried the RPG’s or the Flamethrower. The leveling up system in the game is not like any other but a very original concept. You unlock new weapons and get them free in shops by claiming land from the enemy or climbing radio towers which noticeably become harder to get on top of with every new one. You can also convert to be a better warrior for the sake of the island by leveling up and getting “Tatau” aka Tattoo’s on your arm which give you abilities like holding your breath underwater longer or decreasing the damage you take from animal bites.
– The Ending 10/10
I really can’t talk much about the ending to not spoil it, but the way you want the game to end is all up to you. There are 2 endings so it’s all up to you how you end the game.
– Final Verdict 10/10
The Game as a whole is a 10/10. A First person survival which has more then 30+ Realistic animals. I recommend everyone to play it.

Enjoy.

Considering this game was hyped to all hell, I figured that I would at least kind of enjoy the experience. And to an extent, I did, but some horribly glaring issues with the game just ruined it all for me.
Now the first thing I want to note before I go into any of this is that I played through Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon before this, and I loved the experience. That game was silly and marvelous, and I would recommend it in a heartbeat. This game, however, manages to be worse than the game that was done on a significantly lower budget running on the same engine. Here's why:
First, the mission design is repetitive as all hell. For the most part your missions boil down to "Go into restricted zone X to find/kill/blow up Y and then leave restricted zone X". Practically every story mission is like this. And practically every side mission is like this as well, even the hunting missions. It turned into kind of a chore to do everything, and that's bad. It worked better in Blood Dragon because even though it had the same problem, it was on a much, MUCH smaller scale. You were a badass supersoldier who could zoom over to your objective in less than 10 seconds and it'd be done even faster. In Far Cry 3 it takes more time to get where you're going, and then more time to do what you're doing, which makes what used to be a niggling complaint a gigantic complaint.
Second, too many turret sections. I should not have to explain this, but I will: game developers and designers, nobody wants to sit in the same spot holding down LMB for fifteen minutes while you scroll a background for us. It's not fun, it's not satisfying, it's boring, and it's tedious, and Far Cry 3 has turret sections out the♥♥♥♥♥ This is a crime against game design, and whoever's smart idea this was should be hanged upside down by their pinkie toes for even suggesting it.
Third, crafting and RPG elements are super underutilized and feel utterly tacked on. If you're going to put crafting or RPG mechanics into your game, make it INTERESTING. Make it so you have to actually BUILD A CHARACTER, so you actually have to DISCOVER IMPORTANT CRAFTING RECIPES, not this. Far Cry 3's leveling system comes down to this: kill everyone in sight until you ding, get the next linear upgrade, rinse, lather, repeat. The skills you perk into hardly ever have an effect on gameplay, and when they do, all they are is another canned animation for your takedown that is hardly ever useful. I never used the grenade takedown, I never used the hanging takedown, I hardly used the double takedown, when I did it wasn't useful, I didn't use the chained takedown, I didn't use the knife takedown, and I didn't use the gun takedown. All I used were the vanilla takedown, the heavy takedown (which is just the vanilla takedown on big enemies), and the death from above takedown. Everything else was stupid and pointless. And the other skills were dumb things like "Reload faster" or "Get more money from looting" or "Reload when aimed down sights".
Part deux of point three, the crafting is terrible. All you do is farm out animals to get bigger bags and then just get all the green plants for nonstop healing items. There is no reason to get anything except green plants after you acquire all the bag upgrades, and it could have been used for something interesting. Let me make special weapons, or traps, let me use all this stuff, let me fashion some jerryrigged armor SOMETHING, ANYTHING. Instead it's "Got all the bags? Okay now all the animals are walking money go nuts." Horrible crafting system, they should have just left it out altogether.
And finally, the story is just absolutely pathetic. Now, before you jump down my throat about it let me make this perfectly clear: I loved Vaas and Hoyt. They were excellently written characters. Unfortunately, this game does not star either one of those characters, it stars Jason Brody, a moron who claims to have never shot a gun, yet guns down armies of pirates and privateers like he's been doing it since he came out of the womb, and is "super serious" about saving his friends, but can't keep himself from making stupid pop culture references every thirty seconds. This character ruined literally the entire story. The game can't decide if it wants to be silly or serious, so it tries to do both and it fails utterly. The ludonarrative dissonance in this game is just insane levels of bad, and you just want to murder Jason by the end of it all. I'll go so far as to say that this is probably the worst story I've seen in a game, not because the concept of the story is bad, but because the execution is just awful.
All in all, I would say skip this game and just get Blood Dragon. Blood Dragon doesn't have any of these problems, even the turret sections are more toned down, and frankly they're actually well executed. Blood Dragon succeeds in everything Far Cry 3 fails in and more, and it's cheaper as well. So, yeah, just get Blood Dragon. Just get Blood Dragon. What I'm saying is buy Blood Dragon.

Considering this game was hyped to all hell, I figured that I would at least kind of enjoy the experience. And to an extent, I did, but some horribly glaring issues with the game just ruined it all for me.
Now the first thing I want to note before I go into any of this is that I played through Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon before this, and I loved the experience. That game was silly and marvelous, and I would recommend it in a heartbeat. This game, however, manages to be worse than the game that was done on a significantly lower budget running on the same engine. Here's why:
First, the mission design is repetitive as all hell. For the most part your missions boil down to "Go into restricted zone X to find/kill/blow up Y and then leave restricted zone X". Practically every story mission is like this. And practically every side mission is like this as well, even the hunting missions. It turned into kind of a chore to do everything, and that's bad. It worked better in Blood Dragon because even though it had the same problem, it was on a much, MUCH smaller scale. You were a badass supersoldier who could zoom over to your objective in less than 10 seconds and it'd be done even faster. In Far Cry 3 it takes more time to get where you're going, and then more time to do what you're doing, which makes what used to be a niggling complaint a gigantic complaint.
Second, too many turret sections. I should not have to explain this, but I will: game developers and designers, nobody wants to sit in the same spot holding down LMB for fifteen minutes while you scroll a background for us. It's not fun, it's not satisfying, it's boring, and it's tedious, and Far Cry 3 has turret sections out the♥♥♥♥♥ This is a crime against game design, and whoever's smart idea this was should be hanged upside down by their pinkie toes for even suggesting it.
Third, crafting and RPG elements are super underutilized and feel utterly tacked on. If you're going to put crafting or RPG mechanics into your game, make it INTERESTING. Make it so you have to actually BUILD A CHARACTER, so you actually have to DISCOVER IMPORTANT CRAFTING RECIPES, not this. Far Cry 3's leveling system comes down to this: kill everyone in sight until you ding, get the next linear upgrade, rinse, lather, repeat. The skills you perk into hardly ever have an effect on gameplay, and when they do, all they are is another canned animation for your takedown that is hardly ever useful. I never used the grenade takedown, I never used the hanging takedown, I hardly used the double takedown, when I did it wasn't useful, I didn't use the chained takedown, I didn't use the knife takedown, and I didn't use the gun takedown. All I used were the vanilla takedown, the heavy takedown (which is just the vanilla takedown on big enemies), and the death from above takedown. Everything else was stupid and pointless. And the other skills were dumb things like "Reload faster" or "Get more money from looting" or "Reload when aimed down sights".
Part deux of point three, the crafting is terrible. All you do is farm out animals to get bigger bags and then just get all the green plants for nonstop healing items. There is no reason to get anything except green plants after you acquire all the bag upgrades, and it could have been used for something interesting. Let me make special weapons, or traps, let me use all this stuff, let me fashion some jerryrigged armor SOMETHING, ANYTHING. Instead it's "Got all the bags? Okay now all the animals are walking money go nuts." Horrible crafting system, they should have just left it out altogether.
And finally, the story is just absolutely pathetic. Now, before you jump down my throat about it let me make this perfectly clear: I loved Vaas and Hoyt. They were excellently written characters. Unfortunately, this game does not star either one of those characters, it stars Jason Brody, a moron who claims to have never shot a gun, yet guns down armies of pirates and privateers like he's been doing it since he came out of the womb, and is "super serious" about saving his friends, but can't keep himself from making stupid pop culture references every thirty seconds. This character ruined literally the entire story. The game can't decide if it wants to be silly or serious, so it tries to do both and it fails utterly. The ludonarrative dissonance in this game is just insane levels of bad, and you just want to murder Jason by the end of it all. I'll go so far as to say that this is probably the worst story I've seen in a game, not because the concept of the story is bad, but because the execution is just awful.
All in all, I would say skip this game and just get Blood Dragon. Blood Dragon doesn't have any of these problems, even the turret sections are more toned down, and frankly they're actually well executed. Blood Dragon succeeds in everything Far Cry 3 fails in and more, and it's cheaper as well. So, yeah, just get Blood Dragon. Just get Blood Dragon. What I'm saying is buy Blood Dragon.

Wow, this is a big game. I've been playing it for close to 30 hours so far, and I can't find much about it that I don't like. First off, the good stuff.... lots to do, lots of bad guys to beat up on, a great story, a "fast travel system", and an environment like no other. The landscape doesn't repeat and you can tell that every inch of the island had a lot of thought put into it. As for the stuff I really didn't care for, well, I could do without the "tripping on drugs" stages (so far about three of them). Frankly, it's been done to death and they're pointless. Also, I don't like is that, some hills and mountains are impassable on foot and you can't determine that by merely looking at them. Maybe if there was some more opportunities for air travel, it wouldn't be such a big deal. But, on the other hand, the vehicles you use drive fast enough on the road so that it becomes a small matter after all. I'm also not crazy about the missions where you have to climb not one, but eighteen, creaking, dilapidated radio towers to reactivate them. They're way too difficult. One false step and you plummet all the way to the bottom to start again. I remember playing one of these mission for over fifty-five minutes. Those things aside, two thumbs up.

Also handy is the fill er up style ammo bulk buy, so you can run into a shop, sell all the crap, load up on guns, then get right back into it...Easy.

Regularly cheap on Steam sales, pick up the bundle with Blood Dragon and get ready for FC4 and BD2, out soon.

Far Cry 3 is a game that made quite a stir back in 2012, when it was launched. It won multiple Game of the Year awards, and was considered by many one of the best FPS ever, and some few selected ones even said it was the best FPS ever. I bought it at the last summer sale by 4,99€, and had my expectations high. After a full 13-hours playthrough, in which I've made the main missions and one of each activities to really know how everything is, I must admit that I was dissapointed. I will divide this review in some aspects and rate them, in order to do a fairly imparcial, honest review about this apparently revolucionary game.
Graphics: probably the biggest asset of the game. Beautiful graphics that take computers to their limit (I imagine how the consoles should run this game) and give a good immersion feeling. Gorgeous views, variety of fauna and flora, good character models and some very nice effects. While one may note some recycling of scenarios, and some lazyness in some areas (which makes exploration sometimes tedious, boring and repetitive), the islands are fairly well designed and concieved. 90/100.
Gameplay: one thing said about Far Cry 3 was the innovative gameplay. I must disagree. FC3's gameplay it's like an improved version of FC2's gameplay. With some dumbing down in the middle, and some rather useless features, the gameplay adds some nice features that make it a fairly singular game. The feeling of dejà-vú is present, but, since it's an huge improvement of FC2's already flawless gameplay, it's almost perfect. The only problem, as said, it's the little dumbing down of some features and the lack of some obvious ones (like firing weapons while driving). 95/100.
Sound: I must admit that I don't really pay much attention to a game's soundtrack. Without much information, but with some reconsideration, I found that the sound gives support to the game. There isn't nothing remarkable, but it's made with quality. The voice acting is perfect, the sound of the weapons are brutal and realistic and all those little details make the sound as good as the game. Still, it has nothing really special or memorable. 89/100.
Story/Plot: the plot may be defined in one word: horrible. You are Jason Brody, a spoiled guy that looks more like a wimpy child, that goes together with is brothers, friends and girlfriends to a trip to a archipelago fo tropical islands. The trip goes bad: after a skydiving experience, they are all captured by a local group of pirates/guerrilla, led by the maniac Vaas Montenegro. Jason manages to escape and allies himself with the Rakyat, a local tribe led by Citra, Vaas' sister, in order to rescue his friends. Vaas was one of the most hype-giving characters in the last few years and was the main reason that made people buy this game, but it was just a marketing putsch. Vaas rarely appears and it's not really that interesting. It's a wasted character used to sell the game. The main villain isn't really Vaas, it's another character that proves himself to be more interesting than Vaas. Jason goes form a big ♥♥♥♥♥, spoiled guy to a mighty warrior that has sex with Citra just because they had to put boobs in the game, just because it's what sells. The whole process of going from city boy to jungle warrior is unnatural, badly performed and with many flaws. He is captured and executed multiple times, and yet survives them all, like if multiple miracles had happened. I could really get into more absurds and bad plot decisions, but I won't. Only the second part          of the game really delivers a more solid story (it's a part where you actually fight the real villain instead of the pawn Vaas). At least it allowed more unique, variated missions, which is very positive and really complements the gameplay. It has some good moments, but globally, it's bad. 65/100.
Other aspects and final score: the game, a being open world, sandbox like experience, offers many activities in the 2 islands you can explore, such as hunting, takeovers, exploring, etc. The longevity is quite good for an FPS, but I doubt it reaches more than 30 hours. The Uplay thing is quite dull, and it would only profit from Steamworks. I have not tried the multiplayer because I don't actually care about it, but from what I hear, it's acceptable. I have not played many games from 2012 (probably I haven't played any), but I can assure that this is probably one of the best. Far Cry 3 is a game that made quite a stir back in 2012, when it was launched. It won multiple Game of the Year awards, and was considered by many one of the best FPS ever, and some few selected ones even said it was the best FPS ever. I bought it at the last summer sale by 4,99€, and had my expectations high. After a full 13-hours playthrough, in which I've made the main missions and one of each activities to really know how everything is, I must admit that I was dissapointed. I will divide this review in some aspects and rate them, in order to do a fairly imparcial, honest review about this apparently revolucionary game.
Graphics: probably the biggest asset of the game. Beautiful graphics that take computers to their limit (I imagine how the consoles should run this game) and give a good immersion feeling. Gorgeous views, variety of fauna and flora, good character models and some very nice effects. While one may note some recycling of scenarios, and some lazyness in some areas (which makes exploration sometimes tedious, boring and repetitive), the islands are fairly well designed and concieved. 90/100.
Gameplay: one thing said about Far Cry 3 was the innovative gameplay. I must disagree. FC3's gameplay it's like an improved version of FC2's gameplay. With some dumbing down in the middle, and some rather useless features, the gameplay adds some nice features that make it a fairly singular game. The feeling of dejà-vú is present, but, since it's an huge improvement of FC2's already flawless gameplay, it's almost perfect. The only problem, as said, it's the little dumbing down of some features and the lack of some obvious ones (like firing weapons while driving). 95/100.
Sound: I must admit that I don't really pay much attention to a game's soundtrack. Without much information, but with some reconsideration, I found that the sound gives support to the game. There isn't nothing remarkable, but it's made with quality. The voice acting is perfect, the sound of the weapons are brutal and realistic and all those little details make the sound as good as the game. Still, it has nothing really special or memorable. 89/100.
Story/Plot: the plot may be defined in one word: horrible. You are Jason Brody, a spoiled guy that looks more like a wimpy child, that goes together with is brothers, friends and girlfriends to a trip to a archipelago fo tropical islands. The trip goes bad: after a skydiving experience, they are all captured by a local group of pirates/guerrilla, led by the maniac Vaas Montenegro. Jason manages to escape and allies himself with the Rakyat, a local tribe led by Citra, Vaas' sister, in order to rescue his friends. Vaas was one of the most hype-giving characters in the last few years and was the main reason that made people buy this game, but it was just a marketing putsch. Vaas rarely appears and it's not really that interesting. It's a wasted character used to sell the game. The main villain isn't really Vaas, it's another character that proves himself to be more interesting than Vaas. Jason goes form a big ♥♥♥♥♥, spoiled guy to a mighty warrior that has sex with Citra just because they had to put boobs in the game, just because it's what sells. The whole process of going from city boy to jungle warrior is unnatural, badly performed and with many flaws. He is captured and executed multiple times, and yet survives them all, like if multiple miracles had happened. I could really get into more absurds and bad plot decisions, but I won't. Only the second part          of the game really delivers a more solid story (it's a part where you actually fight the real villain instead of the pawn Vaas). At least it allowed more unique, variated missions, which is very positive and really complements the gameplay. It has some good moments, but globally, it's bad. 65/100.
Other aspects and final score: the game, a being open world, sandbox like experience, offers many activities in the 2 islands you can explore, such as hunting, takeovers, exploring, etc. The longevity is quite good for an FPS, but I doubt it reaches more than 30 hours. The Uplay thing is quite dull, and it would only profit from Steamworks. I have not tried the multiplayer because I don't actually care about it, but from what I hear, it's acceptable. I have not played many games from 2012 (probably I haven't played any), but I can assure that this is probably one of the best. With other strong candidates, like Borderlands 2 and Dishonored, which I haven't played, I think the fight for the title of GOTY 2012 would be fierce and tough. The final score, based on the average between the 4 scores I gave above and a factor of correction based on the other aspects, is of 86 out of 100. While it was a desilusion, it's still strongly reccomended.

I’ll probably never finish playing FarCry3.  The game suffered from front-loading all the best content.  The first half of the game was superb.  The second half failed to live up to what preceded it.  On almost every level – villains, objectives, scenery, atmosphere – the second half of the game was like a bad sequel.  But what finally drove me away was utter disgust for the character I was required to play.
Unlike a lot of games that try to implement moral choices and some sort of moral system, FarCry3 seemed utterly uninterested in whether what the character was doing was good or right or heroic, instead choosing to focus on other themes.  This was ultimately to the game’s detriment, as progressing in the game often required acts that were morally unpleasant – just because the game designers don’t particularly care if something is moral or not does not mean that the players won’t.
For example, the opening of the game did a wonderful job setting up the pirates as a force that I could wipe out in good conscience – they were horrible, sadistic and murderous men who made me feel like I was saving lives when I removed them from the gene pool.  Even those who may not have been so downright evil were enemy combatants in a war they had chosen to declare on me.  And the game did a good job reinforcing this with many of the random encounters.  Absolutely none of that can be said for the mercenaries introduced midway through the game.  I expect this was intentional.  The game makes a point of claiming it is about insanity, and this is a fair way of showing the character’s increasingly murky morality and perverted mentality.  But in choosing to do that, the game chose to create a protagonist whom I found progressively less enjoyable to play.   Inevitably, the game’s demand that I mass-murder a huge swath of these guys was more than I was willing to give it.
I'll admit, my attitude towards wholesale slaughter of the mercenaries probably had a lot more to do with the game than an objective measure of their comparative evils.  Hoyt himself was certainly as bad or worse than any of the pirates; and the mercenaries were following his orders, right?
When the mercenaries first appeared, I had no idea who they were.  It was a mission to provide sniper cover for my allies while they attempted to recover their people whom the pirates had taken prisoner... or so I was told.  Except the people who showed up weren't pirates.  All I knew about them was that they looked military -- for all I knew, they were the armed forces of a sovereign nation, or possibly even people sent in by the United Nations -- and that they decidedly weren't the people I was there to shoot at.  I didn't know these people, I had no grudge against them, I couldn't even be sure that they weren't the good guys, and I had absolutely no reason to declare war on them.  Except that if I didn't the game would not allow me to progress, so it was either murder these people for no good reason or quit the game.
I continued playing, despite the really bad taste that left in my mouth, because the game had been amazing up until that point.  Next, I find out that instead of the allies I was told I'd be rescuing, the military men were transporting my enemy.  So either my allies had suffered a catastrophic intelligence failure, or I had been lied to.  Worse, I'd just declared war on an unknown group and murdered a bunch of their people in order to set a horrible, sadistic psychopath free... for all I knew, I'd just launched an attack on the good guys just as they were taking action against the pirates!  To say I was unhappy was an understatement.  I had lost every bit of faith in my "allies" and I really wanted to be given the option to tell them to go ♥♥♥♥ themselves.
Of course, it turns out the military men were Hoyt's mercenaries.  But at that point, as much as I hated Hoyt, I was primed to want to give these guys as much of a benefit of the doubt as possible.  The first town was under their control, but they weren't slaughtering the civilians like the pirates would.  The first scenario where I really dealt with them had me sneaking past the first two mercenaries and listening in on their conversation.  One mercenary was reveling in psychopathic bloodlust.  The one with him was reining him in, telling him this was a job not a murder free-for-all, and that he was only to shoot where and when he was told to.  My reaction?  The first guy very clearly was a danger to society and needed to be permanently put down.  But the second guy?  He was working for a very bad person, yes; but he was actively preventing a bad situation from getting much, much worse.  I didn't want to put this guy down, just as badly as I wanted to take out the other one.  The islanders needed people like that in the enemy's camp.  Of course, the game had stripped away my ability to choose what to do in that scene; I couldn't kill either or the scenerio would restart.
I ran into those two again in one of the next situations.  Only this time, instead of not being allowed to take out the homicidal psychopath, I wasn't allowed to spare the other guy.  In fact, I was required to abandon all common sense, not to mention my characters skills, stealthy play style, and impressive custom sniper rifle, and make an absurd, bombastic rocket-launcher attack on a bridge and then carve my way out through all the people I had just carefully slipped past.  I was supremely not impressed.
Finally, I was taken to see Hoyt.  I was lead into his office fully armed for a private sit-down with the guy.  At which point, I killed him with my silenced SMG, then tried to sneak out the window.  A bit of a mistake -- the place was so crawling with guards that I really didn't have much of a chance the moment the alarm went up... made all the worse by there being only a single exit that I could use: the front gate.  But my brother was in the place, and thanks to my undercover ally, I was able to rescue him.  We got to the gate, and of course that triggered the final cutscene where I had to make a fatal choice... and I chose to make sure my ally got my brother to safety, making a last stand that left me a bullet-riddled corpse.  I have to say, though, a damn good ending...
...except none of that happened.  Because you can't shoot Hoyt even though you are alone in a room with him and you are fully armed.  But I was allowed (read: required) to ignore that the bad guys had video footage that would have told them who I was, blown my disguise and made (or at least should have made) everything I was told to do afterwords a painfully obvious trap.  Because the second half of FarCry 3 is pretty much awful.
I gave FarCry 3 every possible chance.  I played the first island exhaustively, finding every treasure and relic, doing every side quest, exploring every inch of the island... hell, probably spent days worth of game time just having my character hang out and play poker with the guys.  But in the end, the strikes against the game piled up so high that I simply couldn't enjoy it anymore.
