You are Jason Brody,a young man in his mid twenties,on vacation with a group of friends in Bangkok.During their vacation the decide to take a skydiving trip.Little did the know that they would land on a pirate-infested island known as Rook Island.
The game begins with you and your older brother Grant tied up in a hostage situation by a man name Vaas,the pirate leader.While you manage to break from captivity your brother gets killed by Vaas in the escape.Later,Jason is rescued by Dennis Rogers and the the Rakyat tribe,the island's natives.By that time Jason's adventure to find his friends and to extract revenge begins.
Throughout the game Jason will have to complete quests in order to gain the confidence of the Rakyat,Citra(the Rakyat leader,Cia Agent Huntley,Sam Becker and other stakeholders.After gaining their trust and their respect each one of the will assist Jason into rescuing his friends and killing the pirates and the Pirate leader Vaas who later is revealed to be just an employ of slave trader baron Hoyt Volker.
After Vaas' death the game's true villain is revealed,the slave baron Hoyt who resides at the southern part of the island.Jason is determined to kill Hoyt and save his little brother from his hand.So,with the help of Cia Agent Huntley and the undercover operative Hoyt's privatee Sam Becker,you manage to infiltrate Hoyt's camp,gain his trust and kill him after a lengthy knife fight.Shortly after Hoyt's death you save your brother Riley and escape from Hoyt's troops back to the Rakyat island.
At that point of the game Jason has realised how much he has changed.From a good grade Los Angeles resident to a bloodthirsty,revenge seeking,pirate slayer.From an active athlete and a loving and caring boyfriend to an almost sadistic vigilante who hesitate in anything until justice is met,Hoyt and Vaas is dead,and his friends and family are saved.
In the end Jason and Riley arrive at the Rakyat Temple where Jason has to make a tough choice.Either kill his friends and be free from everything in order to lead the Rakyat people alongside with Citra or save his friends and turn his back on Citra and the Rakyat.If you kill your friends you will make love to Citra,impragnate her and die from her after stabbing your chest ,apparently dying like a warrior.If you do not kill your friends and choose to save them Dennis tries to murder Jason who's saved from Citra but dying from the hit.After takign the hit Citra dies in Jason's hands whispering that she loves him.In both cases the ending cinematic is the same showing the ancient knife artifact stuck in the sand at the beach with a boat leaving in the island.
Gameplay
Far cry is an open-world first person shooter with adventure and role-playing game elements.The world of Far Cry 3 is bigger than his predecessor offering more opportunities in terms of exploring.Also as far as for the rpg elements the game utilizes a wide variety of skill trees,a simple crafting system and experience points used to gain levels and points used in the skill trees specializations.In the end you have a wide variety of weapons to use with extended customization to choose from,many vehicles and water travel to use to get to places and lastly besides the main quests,you get to complet side quests,hunting quests,wanted dead,supply drops and gather collectibles like lost letters and artifacts.
Co-op
The game also features co-operative mode too for 2 to 4 players.The characters are Callum,Tisha,Leonard and Mikhail who are scammed out of their money by Pirates and later decide to work together in order to pursue them and their Captain for revenge.The plot takes place 6 months before the single player campaign.
Multiplayer
Multiplayer consists of 10 different maps,incredible weapon and abilities customization options and require skilled players in order to take advantage of the game's full potential.Balanced multiplayer forgiving to the new player but deadly to the lazy cocky veteran.
Recap
I've finished this game over and over again more times than i can remember.In my list it's my number one game to play and recommend.Consistent plot,wide variety of customization,a jungle to hunt animals,pirates,privatees.What more can you ask for?By the way if you want to experience the island's locations and everythign this game has to offer do not use fast travel.Personally i hate fast travel and i do not use it.

Mount and Blade is a game that I have very mixed feelings about.
The game takes place in a fictional medieval world called Calradia. The player character leads a party of soldiers, and must develop his or her wealth and power by fighting and taking advantage of the politics of Caradia.
Combat aims for realistic. Fighting on horse back has been quite well done, which is good since your character will probably spend most of the time mounted.
Unfortunately, the game has some major issues. The original M&B was released in 2008, and even then reviews commented on the poor graphics. Nothing has changed with this 2010 release.
The skill system is slow and clunky, forcing the player to grind for hours with little reward. Fortunately, the game allows you to export a character file, edit their skills with notepad, then import it without penalty - something that I have always done since discovering it.
Third party tools are also available to allow you to tweak various game options, and I've personally found it much more rewarding to tweak things like renown and standings gain to speed up the game. The in-game methods for advancing your standing in the realm are so poorly thought out, forcing you to click through mundane, repetitive text conversations with various lords before being sent off to carry out equally mundane and repetitive quests. Once you've finished the quest, you then have to find where the lord has gone in order to turn it in - no small challenge since the lords constantly move around and the only way to locate them is to find a lord of the same faction and ask them where the other lord is, then ride as fast as you can before your target moves on.
It's a sad state of affairs when a game is virtually unplayable without the use of "game breaking" mods and cheating. Mount and Blade was a great concept, and I've spent many hours playing it, trying to ignore its shortfalls. But unfortunately it is let down by poor development.
It's worth a go, even if you use the cheats, as it's very easy to see what the game could have been. The battles are surprisingly addictive, and despite how negative I've been in this review, I did get a lot of enjoyment out of the game. Just don't expect too much from it.

Disclaimer: As others have said, yes you do need a Uplay account from Ubisoft in order to play, but many other games are like this in this day and age, get over it. At least with Uplay you can unlock additional free content just by playing the game, such as a unique hand gun for single player, additional single player and co-op missions, wallpaper for your desktop and an additional single player mission. How much do you pay for this content? Nothing. At All. Remember when DLC used to be beating a game with every charcter to unlock extra costumes? Yeah, only with this you register, log in once and click remember me. Done.
Although my time played is very much, I have previously played this game well past completion on PS3, and recently reaquired it through the Steam summer sale, incuding the entire Far Cry franchise. You play as Jason Brody, a happy, party loving 20 something who was skydiving over the Rook Islands with his older brother, Grant, an Army grunt, and younger brother Riley, a late teens kid that really looks up to his brothers, and a group of friends also in their 20's. When you land, something goes terribly wrong and you are all captured by ruthless, bloodthirsty modern day pirates led by second-in-command, the "Definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results" Vaas Montengro. He is insane. Truly, unabashedly beautifully insane. I say beautifully because the actors portrayal (in combination with the script, of course) is one of the best performances in video game history. Every moment is memorable, and every conversation disturbing.
What can I say, this game is excellent. Everything about it is enjoyable and it has something for everyone. Once you get past your initial imprisonment, (no Spoilers, but you HAVE to play at least the first 10 minutes of the games to get a feeling for how vast and immerisive it really is) the island is completely open for you to explore. Locate and climb increasingly difficult Radio Towers to increase your field of view of the island, reveal new points of interest and collectibles, and unlock new weapons from various vendors. Gather various types of plants from around the island to do anything from heal you, to increase your resistance to fire, assist you in finding animals in the dense jungles of the island, to increasing your sprint and siwm speed for a time.
Sneak around with a bow or machete, silently clearing out garrisons of pirates on the island, of go in assault rifles/shotguns/grenades blazing and slaughter every pirate in sight with an impressive array of weapons, including handguns, submachine guns and the well-known .50 caliber sniper rifle. Increase your inventory space by hunting a wide variety of animals, from bears and deer to ocelots and crocodiles. After clearing garrisons out and taking them for your own, take on new missions to take down rare and powerful animals with specific weapons, sometimes a bow vs. a pack of tigers, or a pistol or machete vs. a bear. Other missions include supply missions, getting from one point to another on the island in, again, (are you seeing a pattern here?) a variety of different vehicles, from old cars to ATV's to jeeps, and Hostage missions, where you must go to a certain part of the island and take out all the pirates without being spotted, lest the hostage be executed.
As for abilites, the unique Tatau (spiritual tattoos on your body that grant abilites to you) sytem allows you to design your experience your way. Will you go the way of the Heron, weaving in and out of battle with abilites that grant increased  hip fire accuray with guns, faster movement/mobility and more specialized stealth kills, such as the ability to do dual takedowns (simultaneously and slently kill two enemies that are close together)? If in your face is more your style, the way of the Shark offers an ever-increasing health pool, the ability to craft syringes that restore more health, faster health regeneration, the ability to recover health without the use of syringes, additional natural resistances to various elements, and brutal takedowns that can take down the most heavily armored enemies, the dreaded Heavies, or Defenders. Perhaps you are like me, and have played too much Assassin's Creed, and stealth is your best friend. For you, the way of the Spider is your go-to for fluid and/or  stealth-based combat with abilites such as increased stability when lining up long range bow shots, faster movement while crouching, the specialized Takedown Drag (allows you to perform a take down from cover, such as a bush, and hide the body in the cover, all in one fluid move) quieter movement, faster reloading, the ability to reload while sprinting, faster ADS (Aim Down Sights)/weapon swapping, and even being able to reload whilst aiming down sights. The best part about this system is that you don't have to choose just one type! You can dabble in all the different ways (and it is recommended that you do) to find the perfect fit for your unique play style.
As for enemy types, again, Ubisoft is no slouch when it comes to variety, the aforementioned Heavies, or Defenders are huge brutes usually wearing at least riot gear (at higher levels full bomb squad gear) and generally wield assault rifles to start, then miniguns, flamethrowers, and RPG's. Other enemy types include Snipers, Chargers (you cannot out run them and must take them out from a distance or silently) Molotov Throwers, Assault (default enemies, usually have assault rifles) RPG Shooters, and Berserkers, which run at your face with a shotgun and make hamburger out of the what was once your face. Later in the game, you begin to encounter less of the pirates, (which will generally fight for themselves rather than work together) and more Privateers. These guys are generally para-military trained mercenaries who will use advanced tactics, work together, and try to corner and eliminate you using every tool at their disposal. These are much tougher to take down in groups and stealth is recommended.
Ah crap, I forgot to mention attachements with weapons. You know, by this point Ubisoft decided you STILL didn't have enough freedom and customization to your character in your game. I won't into a huge amount of detail, but every weapon has customizable paint, various attachments including (but not limited to) suppressors, extended mags, reflex/red dot/night vision optics, extended barrel, even the bow has a couple of different optics available (and of course fiery or exploding arrows).
So I mentioned collectibles earlier, right? There is many, many different kinds of collectibles availible on the island, including memory cards, usually evidence of the illicit dealings of the pirates, Letters of the Lost, letters from World War II era Japanese soldiers that give more backstory on the island, and Relics, items from the Rakyat's ancestors that are quite old, usually depicting animals that were considered powerful. Oh yeah, the Rakyat. Kinda went off on a tangent again. After you escape Vaas, you join the Rakyat (the native inhabitants of the island) rebellion that is trying to overthrow Vaas and his boss, the head honcho, Hoyt Volker, leader of the pirates, employer to the privateers, and running his own drug empire from the Rook Islands.
So if you have gotten to this point and don't want to play Far Cry 3/haven't bought it yet, then you may not like it. This is the game, in all of it's complete and utter open-world glory. If you don't want choice, don't want the ability to whatever whenever and play the game at your own pace, whether that be fast or slow, go play something else. BUT, if any one small part of this sounds the least bit interesting, take the plunge. Hell, wait until it goes on sale if you want, but do not deny, nay, deprive yourself of this experience. I, for one, will never forget it and am waiting on bated breath for Far Cry 3.

I've played about 30+ hours of
on PC and another 40+ hours back on Xbox 360, meaning I've had quite some experience with the game. That being said,
is probably Ubisoft's prime example of advertising and hyping without fully delivering, hence my negative review: it's far from as great as people claim it to be.
The Good:
· Michael Mando's performance as Vaas Montenegro is very well done, simply one of the best motion capture in any game.
· The huge island allows for hours of exploring, hunting, and doing sidemissions.
The Bad:
· First I'm going to list what bothers me the most, and it also happens to be the thing I liked the most... Vaas. Ubisoft promoted
with Vaas from the get-go; putting him in the early demo, placing him on the boxart, including a wahini-figure in the Collector's Edition... his insanity was basically the center of the game. Unfortunately, those promises weren't met. Slight spoiler warning ahead so please skip to the next point if you don't want any bits of the story given away, but Ubisoft's oh so glorious Vaas Montenegro had a combined total screentime of 15 minutes. Yep. Durning your 30+ hours, only 15 minutes will be spent looking at or listening to Vaas. It's like buying a movie ticket to go and see Fight Club just to end up watching A Good Day to Die Hard.
· The missions are repetetive beyond believe. Save this person, do this for that guy, kill these guys. The sidemissions exist largely of racing- and huntingmissions, both equally boring after the first time. The only enjoyable mission -- spoiler warning, again -- was the one where you had to burn marijuanafield with a flamethrower to a raggae-dubstep beat. If only there were more original missions like those.
· The character development is so unbelievable it feels parodic at times. You go from a party-going teenager to a hipster Rambo that is able to murder hundreds of experienced soldiers in a few hours.
· There's no real reason to craft anything. Health syringes are useless if you have upgraded your manual healing skill that'll automatically heal you when you're out of syringes (by bandaging your scratched arm when you fall or pulling out a bullet when a tiger attacks you. Yeah...) Your wallet can only hold a certain amount of money, so maybe crafting a larger wallet would be usefull. But why do so if climbing all the radio towers will basically get you all the weapons for free?
The Visuals:
· The overal graphics are very nice, from detailed textures to great lighting, but the shadows were so overdone it almost felt cartoonish.
Final verdict:
· High expectations, even higher promises, and ultimately you get an avarage repetetive shooter.
is the best example of how Ubisoft spends more time hyping and advertising than polishing what could have been a much better product. 6/10

Many people dream of finding themselves posted on a white sand beach on an island in the pacific, sipping a tropical drink and flicking tenacious hermit crabs from their belongings. If you are ambitious and a bit stupid, like Jason Brody and company, then you may try to spice up the proceedings with a bit of skydiving. So begins, Far Cry 3, a game about a bunch of American yuppies on a vacation that has seriously gone wrong. Back and 2004 Far Cry's open world gameplay was revolutionary, roaming tropical islands slaying mercs and trigens created quite a splash before being encumbered by the tsunami that was Doom 3 and Half Life 2 later the same year. With S.T.A.L.K.E.R being the only other franchise to successfully merge open world shooting with light RPG elements, and Crytek moving toward more traditional levels for their Crysis games, the market is wide open for Ubisoft's vacation from hell simulator.

While living it up in Bangkok in order to celebrate his younger brother obtaining his pilot's license, Jason Brody and crew make the ill fated decision to go skydiving. They happen to land on an island infested with pirates and they are taken hostage where they are being primed to be sold into slavery. Jason escapes and meets some locals who aid him in his quest to find his friends and escape since they see it as an opportunity to have Jason liberate their island. It's a tale that's part Deliverance, part Indiana Jones with a dash of the drug abusing hijinx in Alice in Wonderland. Far Cry 3's narrative benefits from a number of eccentric personalities like Spike Lee's Island dwelling clone Dennis, gaming's most possessive and insane ♥♥♥♥♥ Citra,  and doctor who indulgences in enough mind altering substances to make Hunter S. Thompson blush. Topping off the insane cast of character's is Vaas, the leader of the pirates. Unfortunately, Far Cry 3 blunders Final Fantasy VIII style by shifting the focus away from Vaas partway through the game and substituting a far less engaging and charismatic villain. The well worn theme of civilized man reverting to a more primitive state to survive in a primitive environment is a bit hamfisted as every few missions has Jason returning to his girlfriend so that she can keep pointing out how he has changed... Also, the plot is tainted by a white messiah complex. For some reason it seems that the legions of native warriors are not the equal of one white guy with a crappy tribal tattoo and a desire to save his friends.

While Jason is not a soldier or gun toter by trade, he quickly warms up to carrying a firearm and explosives in order to liberate his friends. Missions give Jason the opportunity to earn money and experience which he can use to augment his skills and buy new weapons and attachments. Slaughtering the wildlife also gives Jason the opportunity to craft new storage for ammo, explosives and money. The flora can be harvested in order to create medicines that allow Jason to heal and enhance his senses. While all of these crafting opportunities help make use of the large game world and the critters that inhabit it, it also means that the game can have an agonizing start. Initially, Jason can only carry one weapon and very little ammo meaning that exploration grinds to a halt after only a few minutes before needing to resupply. You will want to craft new holsters to hold more weapons and compartments for more ammo immediately. Torching bears with flame throwers, using grenades as depth charges to kill crocodiles and sharks and running kommodo dragons over with jeeps does provide a depraved and perverted form of entertainment.

Also populating the world are radio towers that have to be scaled in order to unlock a section of the map a la Assassin's Creed and Outposts that need to be cleared out in order to keep those pesky pirates from roaming certain regions of the map. Both the towers and the outposts have unique layouts and terrain that distinguishes one from another but never the less you will fall into a pattern of uncovering the map then liberating the outposts as you progress deeper into the game which becomes terribly repetitive. The wildlife in Far Cry 3 doesn't exist solely for the benefit of adding pouches to Jason's belt either. Animals are often found in cages in enemy outposts where they can be freed to create havok. It just so happens that pirates are much easier to kill when they are trying to save one of their buddies from getting murdered by an angry cassowary. While Far Cry 3 provides weaponry and attachments that encourage stealth, it's also possible to raid outposts full shock and awe style with guns on full auto chucking grenades like Eli Manning throws interceptions. Both methods have their thrills but almost invariably players will lean on their overpowered weaponry late in the game to steam roll the opposition. The extra 1,000 experience just isn't worth the time saved by storming an outpost Rambo style.

Fortunately, Far Cry 3's main missions provide a much needed reprieve from the repetition of radio tower climbing and outpost raiding. Missions often take Jason to instanced areas like abandoned Japanese bunkers from World War 2 and ancient temples with Indiana Jones style perils. Even a handful of late game filler missions offer some riotous thrills and enough fireworks to please even the most jaded action gamer. Forced stealth sections are staged in such a way they they are painfully easy however and some really irritating quick time events rear their ugly heads and detract from the experience. Like wise a mid game string of quests that have you raiding ancient temples to reassemble a magic compass throw the tone of the game off. If all of the aforementioned content isn't satisfactory to you there are also extra missions that have you killing animals and special targets with a specified weapon, score-based Rakyat challenges and some small errands given to you by NPCs. It's a rather robust singleplayer that will last most gamers 15 to 20 hours.

The Far Cry 3 experience doesn't stop with it's campaign however. There are six co-op missions that tell the story of a group of rough around the edges characters who have been duped out of their money by the Pirates and are pursuing them on Rook Island. The narrative is sparse and the gameplay does little to really take advantage of having three friends playing alongside you. You earn experience that unlocks upgrades that can also be used for the competitive multiplayer suit. Multiplayer is a collection of variations of classic multiplayer modes like Team Deathmatch, King of the Hill, capture the flag and domination. The multiplayer does little nothing to take advantage of some of Far Cry's more unique features. Don't expect your foes to be mauled to death by tigers or to be able to jump into a vehicle to make a hasty escape. Odds are, players will get more time out of the main campaign.

It's a rather robust singleplayer that will last most gamers 15 to 20 hours.

The Far Cry 3 experience doesn't stop with it's campaign however. There are six co-op missions that tell the story of a group of rough around the edges characters who have been duped out of their money by the Pirates and are pursuing them on Rook Island. The narrative is sparse and the gameplay does little to really take advantage of having three friends playing alongside you. You earn experience that unlocks upgrades that can also be used for the competitive multiplayer suit. Multiplayer is a collection of variations of classic multiplayer modes like Team Deathmatch, King of the Hill, capture the flag and domination. The multiplayer does little nothing to take advantage of some of Far Cry's more unique features. Don't expect your foes to be mauled to death by tigers or to be able to jump into a vehicle to make a hasty escape. Odds are, players will get more time out of the main campaign.

This game, much like the previous two takes place on an island full of danger with top graphics for it's time. In this two island, massive, open world video game, you are faced with the task of saving your family members and friends from the hands of dangerous modern day pirates.
The game has a fantastic and entertaining antagonist but it's protagonists are somewhat bland (the teenagers that is, the island's inhabitants are much better characters). The music, sound effects and voice acting are all fantastic in the game, they all keep you fully engaged and entertained throughout. It's gameplay on the Dunia Engine is great but not too fluid, but gives your character plenty of weight; in game you get around via walking as well as using many vehicles and cars are especially fun to get around in. The world in the game is nice but not perfect as some parts have glitched textures and broken areas, but these are not too common (I encountered about 3 in 22 hours). This game's graphics are beautiful and fantastically detailed with great lighting, making it look polished and should hold up graphically for years to come. The AI in this game is fairly decent but nothing too special. The story of this game is nothing too complex on the surface but quickly explodes into life and is extremely interesting to see your character change from a feeble teenager into a somewhat hardened survivalist looking to kill pirates and get through pretty much anything in his way. There isn't too much bad to be said about this game for it is extremely well rounded, the only complaint could be a lack of fun replayability due to long very gameplay and linear storyline.

Now that I've gotten that out of the way, I had other issues with the game that truely ruined the experience for me. The main issue I had was that the game runs horribly on my PC, because I use an AMD card. Just about every Ubisoft game runs horribly with AMD cards. I went from the highest graphics settings on most games, to the lowest settings for Far Cry 3. Even then, I was only able to get about 30 fps while playing.
Along with the framerate issues, the game just didn't work correctly in some places. While driving in vehicles, the game would eventually stop rendering the world on the minimap. If I went past the area on the map that was not loaded yet, the game would immediately crash. I also ran into some random crashes about ever 20 minutes or so. This completely ruined the game for me, making me never want to touch it ever again after 2 hours of playing.
If your computer is using an AMD graphics card, then I cannot possibly recommend this game to you. Go buy a different open world game like GTA IV or Skyrim. This game is not for you.

Warband is pretty much as the original Mount&Blade should have been at the beginning. It's also still the best version of the game to get as we are on the wait for M&B 2. The sequels/expansions that are currently released are to me mods that are worked into a commercial release.
This the game where you start up as a lowly peasant and can develop into a warlord that leads a group of troops capable of overthrowing kings and kingdoms. You lead your forces to battle in a proper action game in a field whether outside in the field or storming castles. You can own and garrison cities of your own.
The politics and roleplaying parts are highly underdeveloped so you will have to fill those parts with some imagination or search for a mod to do what you want. The combat however is refined and I would even dare to say the game offers some of the best horseback combat there is when it comes to large scale fights. There are some tactics you can use to command your troops, but in the vanilla game they are mostly not needed. Perhaps grouping up and charging at the right time are most you will get out of it. Unless you really want to stand on a hill with 100+ ranged troops while waiting for enemy approach, would recommend a mod that actually makes use of that stuff instead.
Underdeveloped in parts, but still great enough to bring many enjoyable stories. And now we wait for the true sequel to deliver. I would say as of 2015, it's more worth to wait the sequel instead of taking the plunge with Warband.

Short review:
Mount & Blade warband is a great game but also a very unique at the same time. If you want to play medieval RPG and/or want to play relatively realistic medieval battles from 1st person view  without magic involved this game is basically your only choice.
Long review (why are you still reading this. Try the free demo!!!):
In Mount & Blade warband you are put into free open world of medieval continent named Calradia. The player moves his party on campaign map while the battles and interactions in towns are done in 1st or 3rd person view based on player's preference.
Although the world is open and there is no main story the the most common path of the player is to become a leader of a small party. The player just grabs a mount, blade, couple of party members and ever increasin host of unnamed soldiers and starts making his/her living by being the self proclaimed Robin Hood or bandit or both at the same time.
The main gameplay includes moving the player's party around Calradia searching for opportunities to get rich and famous. This usually means questing, raiding villages, trading and most importantly attacking any party of traders, peasants or nobles that you just consider a good target of opportunity (while avoiding getting beaten by those think you are a good target). As the game progresses the player usually joins a faction first as a mercenary leader and later as a noble. The game allows player also to become a king or queen. At that point the game almost becomes an RTS but unfortunately kingdom management of the game is not as fun as other elements of the game.
The battles are the best part of the game. In no other medieval game game you personally fight as a part of an army with up to 150 (use mods to increase this to as many as your PC can handle) soldiers on the battlefield at the same time. The awesome weapon controls make this even more immersive. The controls for fighting with the weapon are based on direction you move your mouse. This is so much better than the horribly bad design seen in many games where attacks are just scripted actions used by pressing certain buttons of mouse. Unlike most other medieval games you can also fight from horseback.
On top of fighting in these battles, the player can command his troops and in huge battles hiding behind your men shouting your commands might actually be better idea than riding to battle in front of your men. Being a fighting leader is however more fun and especially in smaller battles it is probably more viable tactic of the two even  if player has set full damage on player to be true. This is because in the heavy armor (especially on horseback) the player can be a real killing machine. Only boring side in the figting are the sieges because of being so identical to each other making sieges feeling repetitive.
The singleplayer has some minor flaws but thanks so many great things and just the uniqueness of the game there is no way I could give this game anything else than 10/10. In additon the rich modding community has remedies for most of the small flaws that the game has such as outdated graphics or battle being immediately ended if player is knocked out.
The multiplayer part is basically taking the battle side of the warband and throwing in some traditional game modes such as team deatchmatch and battlefield series like conquest. The execution of this is flawless and thanks to the fun and immersive combat mechanics the multiplayer is fun to play. The combat mechanic based on direction is not too difficult to learn but it is difficult to truly master. This is usually a good thing but be warned. I highly recommend you to first learn in single player how to fight (with manual blocking on) to avoid getting badly beaten by good playrs during your first multiplayer matches.
The most played mode in multiplayer is siege. This may sound strange as sieges were not that good in single player. I guess one reason is that that open land battles with human players become easily just skirmishes where each individual thinks just himself instead of moving as a group. This is in sharp contrast to single player's massive armies fighting against each other.
Meanwhile in sieges the players are much more dynamic than the repetitive AI but thanks to being somewhat funneled down by the shape of the castle the players cannot become too scattered. The multiplayer community (as of writing this) is not huge but it is definetly living. The servers have different sizes but curently the biggest one at the moment  has maximum capacity if 200 and each time I play it has had at least 130 players.
The reason for just 9/10 for multiplayer is that at least I feel that the multiplayer feels somewhat generic and I think it is not just because of the generic game modes. The multiplayer could be so much better for example with two simple fixes
1. Add dynamic destruction for castles.
2. Add some incentive for players to stay in groups especially in open land battles to make the battles feel more real instead of individuals being scattered everywhere.

Mount and Blade: Warband is the game that the original Mount and Blade wanted to be when it was released.  More polished, more complete, and in all ways improved, this is the best swording-mans simulator on the market.  The modding community is fantastic, offering new maps, troop trees, fief management options, etc.  The only remaining glaring weakness is companion management - in the game, your companions will not automatically equip themselves with improved gear (though many mods add this as a feature) and it is next to impossible to know, without switching through multiple screens, whether a particular weapon or piece of armor in a shop is an improvment over what your companions are currently using.
I have sunk more hours into the Mount and Blade series in the past couple of years than into every other non-MMO game combined.  If you haven't bough and played it, yet, you are truly missing out on one of the singular gaming experiences of today.

Far Cry 3 is an amaing game. Though many mechanichs don't really make sense and parts of the story seem to have hit the shark with a jetski and flown into space, this game is an absolute joy to play. The controls, weapons, and world give this game a smoothness and spontaneity that few games come close at replicating. Most of the mechanics strongly support the badassery that the game is incredible for. For example, one can ride a zipline towards some pirates before jumping off to stab one from above, then proceed to set the others on fire with a flamethrower. Even the cover mechanics are smooth: crouching and being behind cover will allow you to peek fire or blind fire by simply going nearest the edge you wish to fire around. The missions were much more restrictive than the vast open world, however most were still enjoyable. The story was for the most part enthralling and had one of the most interesting villains I have ever had to face in a game (Vaas). The game generally tends to be more interesting on the first island, as the story becomes less interesting and the gameplay tends to be more of a generic bullethosey/slow shooter (especially because of the amount of heavies one will encounter).This is a small qualm, however, as the freedom and badassery of the game is one of the most enjoyable gamimng experiences I have encountered.

The worst game I have personally ever played, and no, it's not the only game I have ever played. A lot of the game is amazing, a lot of the game isn't. I found that just about every aspect of the game has an inconsistent dark side. But I'll also point out things about the game i liked.
The difficulty of the game is ludicrously inconsistent. I played it on hard and I could easily take on a hoard of enemies, but if I found myself in some unusual terrain or up against an armored enemy or boss the gameplay becomes annoying at best. Armored enemies do more damage than normal ones, as they should, but are otherwise simple bullet sponges even when it comes to headshots and will be a pain to deal with unless you happen to have an explosive handy. The boss I am referring to is a big dude who breathes fire at you that has a chance to stun you, leaving you unable to even run from the flames, which would make sense if the game had a dodge mechanic. Most of the time damage can not be avoided in a logical manner during the battle, additionally crafting healing items is also disabled during the sequence.
Don't get me wrong, the combat in FC3 is incredible, so is the gunplay, certainly some of the best ever! However, the AI works in such a way that it occasionally creates some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments. Enemies react superhumanly fast if they catch you out of cover. The stealth system is bit odd as enemies can detect you when they definitevly shouldn't and then shoot you from uncounterable directions. Most of these are trivial and can be avoided by a competent player but the scripted story sections can get really annoying. At one one point you are put at the top of a water tower without any cover and a sniper rifle, right above a heap of enemies with perfect aim. In another situation you are put in a confined space with an armored enemy without any ammo or explosives nearby making you screwed unless you brought some or haven't used it all up, which I had. If you die you will either have to rewatch a cutscene, kill all enemies all over again or walk half of the way to a waypoint back to where you died, or the game will skip a large portion killing all the enemies you were fighting and spawning you right next to the objective you were trying to reach!
The soundtrack is amazing, the sound effects, not so much. The guns are great, so is the voice acting on major characters, but the effects? The crafting, inventory and skills menus feature a weird rumbling bass that has been distorted so as to make it sound like you're headphones are breaking apart. As someone who knows what that actually sounds like it makes me uncomfortable every time and pulls me right out of the immersion. Every action in the game has a sound effect next to it, sneak up to a guy and game the throws a big whoosh sound at you as the takedown prompt pops up and a big accomplishment metallic effect as the enemy falls dead to the ground.
The environments are beautiful, at night at least, but in the sunlight the shading gets really ugly, grass is WAY too green and the ambient oclusion looks absolutely horrendous, and there is no setting for disabling it! ALL the trees in the distance use the SAME EXACT LOD. Textures are great, however, water is opaque and distorts its reflection too much. But even then, the game looks amazing!
I’m not sure why the skill system is there. The takedown ability is unlocked by default and very few other skills are interesting gameplay wise. Half are either plain boosts like more life, faster sneaking movement, longer breath under water or more stable sniping. And the rest is useless stuff you will never use like being able to drag a body after a takedown, it slows your movement so much you might as well not bother. You will NEVER run out of money but will do ammo and items, a lot, and they can never be found when most needed.
It’s clear to me there were some idiots on the dev team, just like with any game, but it seems almost like the smart members just focused on their own parts making them incredible but letting the idiots run wild. The only way I can describe Far Cry 3 is with the word: inconsistent. It has these amazing things, the guns, the crafting/hunting system and the characters but it is let down by simple design flaws. Many love this game and you probably do/will too, but I didn’t :(

So far FC3 feels like a balanced mix of exploring, crafting, and story.  The exploring aspect is similar to most Ubisoft games (assasins creed) also you climb towers to reveal the section of the map that you are on.  From reading this you may feel that has been done, but while wearing decent headphones, the experience felt like climbing a broken down old tower.  The game really shines when it comes to the audio/video while exploring the island.  Crafting is a simple process of collecting materials and clicking some buttons, as you craft you level the crafts so it feels like your making progress and not just grinding.  You can chose to follow the storyline missions or do your own thing, something i appreciate in any "game" i dont want to just interact in a movie.  I don't want to give up too much info on the leveling system for spoiler reasons.  There is replayability for sure.  Now to sum up FC3 by comparing with other games.
Movement and shooting - Feels like crysis and any other FC game.

'Far Cry 3' came out a few years ago. It's an open world FPS, with some roleplaying elements, like weapon upgrades and skills, and a rather strong emphasis on story and characters, although at the cost of some interesting side mission. The game is all right : the main problem I had with it was that it uses 'Uplay', that it's a console port and thus badly optimized. I apologize in advance for ranting way too long about those part, and not talking more about the game. To me, these two parts are tied together, and I cannot just ignore the flaws of 'Uplay', especially if it has repercussions in the game itself.
'Uplay' is similar to Steam, except worse in every regard. That it is necessary to launch it, and Steam, at the same time, for copy protection reasons, shows just how much Ubisoft actually cares for a user friendly product. That it is slow and unhandy would be the core of my gripes with it. That it actually taints the game is unforgivable. Since the inventory menu in 'Far Cry 3' is in the main menu of the game, and said menu needs to check online with the servers for whatever reasons, it can take ages to do want you actually want to do in-game. That is not a correct way to proceed. Why can't I check my inventory if Uplay can't connect to the servers, although it could when I launched the game? Is it because I played during the release of 'Watch Dog'? Is it really possible that, because of the launch of another game overloading the servers of Ubisoft, I couldn't check on my inventory in Far Cry?! That's insane! Yeah, how can you even try to get some immersion going...
Oh, as a side note : I already had an Ubisoft account, before using Uplay, but I couldn't login with it using Uplay. I had to login through their website first, and then login through Uplay. Obviously Uplay never bothered to tell me that, only that my internet connexion was down and that the fault thus laid with me. Thanks. Very helpful, and user friendly once more.
It connects when Uplay launches, it connects when the game launches and it connects to the servers when you open the main menu of the game. Because of the poor optimisation, and my wish to tweak the game as best as possible, these logins delays were a serious pain.
There are troubles with SLI, and even crossfire apparently, even though it's an AMD game. The stuttering with SLI was finally resolve for me by using a third party program. Still, sometimes the game just bugged out and only one card out of the two actually worked (first time that ever happen to me), requiring yet another time wasting restart of the game. The graphic options menu leaves a lot to be desired. It's impossible to remove motion blur or ambient occlusion (which makes the game look worse in my opinion, and even cost more resources). You need to tweak that in the game files, and even then bugs appear, like sound bugs (how does a graphic option affect sound?!)
But the worst offence? The game doesn't even look that good for the resources demanded. 'Crysis', -the first one!-, which came five years before, looked way better in every aspect. It's even better if you take into account the fact that in 'Crysis', the game world was more interactive, and destructible: you could mow down trees and blow up sheds. Not so in far cry.
The game itself can be shortly describe as an amalgamation of 'Skyrim' mixed with 'Just Cause 2', except it leaves the best part of those games at home. 'Skyrim' had lots of different looking environment, and different cities with their respective style. 'Just Cause 2' had a very insane gameplay, which was quite fun, but repetitive. In 'Far Cry 3', the game world is quite small, which is probably for the best since repetition already sets in as it is. Secondary quests aren't that good, though the main plot is quite interesting. It reminded my of Hotline Miami : a descent into madness and mayhem. The gameplay is that of an average FPS : aim and shoot, although it can be pretty “organic” in Far Cry, with multiple approaches on how to overtake a stronghold. It sadly doesn't work that way during quests, either secondary or principal. You will often fail an objective because of unclear restrictions or arbitrary limitations, which is stark contrast with the free-roaming experience.
The characters are interesting enough even though I don't know if there are one step short of being campy or so insane that they transcend such definition. The tone of the stand alone, 'Blood Dragon', shouldn't be a surprise as the path visible here already alludes to such extravagance. The endings could use a lot more polish thought: they are just too easy and don't amount to anything. It's just a quick wrap up. There are worse endings out there, but you could have taken more than ten seconds to come up with one, surely.
As it stands, I'm glad to have played, but had I known before hand how horrible Uplay is and how poorly the game runs, I wouldn't have bothered. If you lack the patience and tolerance for such nonsense, I wont blame you and you wouldn't be missing out much regardless.

Mount and Blade is a gem. It may seem pretty outdated without all the flash of modern day games, but it makes up for it in substance. The systems put in place for this game are all superb, Combat, trade, war, lordship, questing. It's just such a well designed game that I can easily see myself coming back to again and again until another game like it comes out. Not to mention the community support for this game is insane, tons of mods that add tons of features (more options as rulers, units, diplomacy, maps, even Lord of the rings, star wars mods that has space combat). Surely their is something for everyone to enjoy in this game. In a way the game reminds me of the old days of gaming where things were simple but extremely effective. And that is what MnB is. Considering it was programmed by three poeple, I am amazed at the amount of fun the game  continually presents, whether through the native game or mods.

Possibly the best story-driven FPS ever made, in my opinion.
Everything in this game is pretty much flawless. The graphics are beautiful, the gameplay is fun and addictive, the story is compelling and shocking, the characters are all amazing (especially, Vaas, Hoyt, Dennis, Willas, Sam and the doctor), and the soundtrack is one of the best I've ever heard in a game. Despite having a pretty dark and intense story, there's moments of pure crazy fun and hilarity, such as setting fire to fields of weed with a flamethrower while Skrillex plays in the background, and shooting down and blowing up cars and helicopters in a helicopter as Wagner's 'Ride of the Valkyries' plays. These two moments were massive standouts in a game full of memorable and awesome scenes.
It's a fairly long game for an FPS. I put in 19 hours of doing all the story quests, as well as capturing outposts (insanely fun, by the way), activating radio towers, performing assassinations, and doing random side quests. The map (which is impressively large) is absolutely filled with stuff to do, so I guarantee you'll never get bored in your entire playthrough.

I feel as if I have to review the game systems separately from the story.  As far as the mechanics and the open world works, it's a 9/10.  The only thing hindering it there is the frustratingly stupid AI.  Increasing the difficulty makes you die faster, but you won't die often because your adversaries will blindly follow each other into the simplest of traps.  Aside from AI, gameplay is stellar.  Whether you utilize stealth or run in guns blazing, you're going to have fun.  That said, the story and protagonist are a 3/10.  The developers really thought they were being deep by putting "Alice in Wonderland" quotes in between cutscenes and giving you an ending that is meant to make you think about all of the horrible things you did during the course of the game.  Unfortunately, any depth falls flat when you remember the "50xp Headshot!!" and "200xp Triple Kill!!" that you saw for last 20 hours of playing.  Even without the pretentious message, Brody, your avatar is unbearable to listen to.
Overall, the game is very fun and I do recommend it.  This review may seem like I'm bashing it too much, but I had a lot of fun with Far Cry 3 and it is, by far the best in the series.

After completing Far Cry 3, I have to say I'm excited for 4 even more.
I do however have some issues with the game, that didn't break it, but annoyed me throughout the playthough.
One, Stairs/Tiny Ledges: I swear every radio tower I climbed I got stuck at the base of the stairs unless I jumped... even for some of the buildings when getting simple treasures.
Two, The Location: It's pretty bland, and I just started far cry 2 and I was liking the area much more, color palate wise. Far Cry 3 is just too green... like really green you'll only see greys and blacks of cliffs and buildings.
Three, Weapons: They weren't broken, not at all, they worked great, it's just the amount of them and variety of customization I had issues with. The ones given were very fun otherwise, so not too much to complain, I just wanted more.
Now for Pros, and I might spoil so, warned you... also it's like 2-3 years old, figure out the story already.
One, Characters: They are fun, freaky, and memorable all around. Vaas especially, although I wish he had more of an impact/appearance in story... Hoyt was even shorter, and kind of typical in most ways of a bad guy. The rest also get a good amount of screen time and you begin to care for them after a while... or hate them even more later.
Two, The Gameplay: It kind of evolves a bit over time, making you figure out some new tactics or strategies. You can never always stealth, at least how I played. The Tatau/progression system in the game makes it even more fun to combine everything you unlock to make yourself the ultimate badass.
Three, Jason Brody: He may seem like a typical hero/young adult, but his progression as he becomes stronger is very well written. He starts as a cry baby, fearing to kill, and then becomes a blood thirsty savage by the end. The progression, though may seem quick depending how you play, was pretty well written.
Four, The Forts: Although small, and pretty open, they are so vast in design that your strategy for them always changes and adapts. I'm sure lots of people talk about them, and I can see why.
Overall, I think everyone should play this so they know what they're getting into for 4. I'm also sure 4 will be much more polished and hilariously fun to kill however you want. I mean come on... riding elephants... that already sounds like fun.

This is a great open world shooter but a big problem I have with this is the story, the story from the beginning until mid game is awsome but when it get's into the lategame the story gets really weak und boring.

The AI's are not too infrequently buggy when handling stealth-related actions. For example, several times, an enemy saw a body through a wall. When it's not buggy, it's a bit unintuitive. The AI wouldn't be able to see me peeking around a corner near point blank, but it could see a dead body's foot hidden in tall grass from 15-20 yards away.
The story is awful--or at the very least underdeveloped--and wastes quite a bit of potential. Quite a few features of this game (namely finding relics and letters) are a waste of time. Sure, they add some sort of technical aspect to the game, but the findings themselves are 100% unrelated to the story. The relics add literally nothing (you find them, they reward negligible amounts of exp), and the letters talk about some alternate storyline of Japanese military research on the island during World War 2.
The fun aspects of the game are solely killing people, leveling up, and upgrading your weapons. (Actually, that could be false. I haven't tried doing the game's quests other than hunting wild animals.) I had some fun liberating enemy outposts, since I bought the game expecting a ton of stealth, and this was the only real challenging opportunity to do it (and it was definitely very challenging), but the only reward for this was to see the words "Success" and "Undetected +1500 exp" for a brief 3 seconds. Failing to get Undetected and finishing it just by killing everyone didn't mean that I could go back and try it again, either, unless I explicitly wrote a new save file before an attempt.
I also had a lot of trouble running the game smoothly. My graphics card is not great, but it's dumb that I can run the game very smoothly at medium to high settings and then frequently drop to 10-15 fps when the game decides that it should load more things. It's even dumber that hitting escape twice would bump my fps back to 50+ at least until the next time the game decided to load things. It happened less frequently after I moved the game to my SSD, but the problem still occurred often.

Uplay first, then game review.
As many other reviews pointed out, this game uses UPlay. I don't like that it uses uplay because I bought the game through Steam and would like to play it only through Steam. But as long as it's fast going through their servers and isn't a complete nuisance to sign on, whatever.
However, the first time I tried to play this it took me a ♥♥♥♥ing HALF HOUR to get in the damn game. At first it said uplay's servers were busy or offline, which took a while. I thought "Ok, fine, I'll play offline. No big deal." Guess what?! You CAN'T play offline the first time you run the game. So I HAD to go through their servers. When they were finally accessible, I got the Uplay captcha puzzle, which involved putting a single set of numbers from a single picture into two boxes. The rules: One box cannot be blank. The number cannot be copied into both boxes. The numbers cannot be split up. Think the audio captcha will help you out? It specifically says not to put spaces in, then says one set of numbers. Refreshing the captcha didn't help, I kept getting the same damn problem until I found one that had a letter tacked onto the end of the numbers which I put into the other box, and it finally worked. At this point I was pretty mad, I just wanted to play my ♥♥♥♥ing game and instead I'm wasting time trying to figure out the impossible captcha.
From this point on it was easy to log in, the only other problem I had was that at one point my game stopped syncing, so when my SSD got scrambled (uplay decided to install itself on my windows drive instead of my programs drive), I lost half my progress. I also didn't know it at the time, but I wasn't getting achievements for storyline events. When I played through them again, I got them. So back up your saves, guys!
FINALLY, THE GAME
The game feels very much like the new Tomb Raider except more open. I also got a few fleeting feelings of Assassin's Creed. Like how it feels to play those games? You'll probably like this one. There's a wide variety of weapons and I like that you can get a lot for free by unlocking towers. Going hunting is actually good for something, as you use it to craft holsters, rucksacks, etc.
The story didn't impress me at first, nor the character development, but I'm liking it much more now. I only wish there were more conversation opportunities with your friends! They all seem very one-dimentional, with the exception of Daisy, who just seems much more nuanced in her words and expressions. I will update this as I finish the game, 3 missions to go.
The graphics are great, albeit a bit repetative (but they are on an island, so... lots of palm trees are to be expected, I guess). A few problems where I see black/blue shapes but nothing terrible or constant. Sometimes characters vibrate, which makes it ridiculously hard to snipe.
Controls are great for the most part, the problem I have is when performing special actions. When I'm climbing a radio tower, stepping onto the very edge, and see ropes where "climb" should appear...it doesn't. I can wiggle one way or the other and sometimes it shows up, sometimes not. So I can jump and sometimes have the game catch me and climb up, or I can fall to my death and start over. Annoying. More annoying is when I'm sneaking around an enemy camp like a boss, killing people, when I sneak up behind someone and the "takedown" option doesn't appear. Again, I move around, sometimes it works. Most of the time though they either turn around and alert the whole camp, or I slice but don't kill them and they alert the whole camp.
Open world, lots of places to explore even if climbing towers and liberating camps gets boring. Can't wait to see how it ends.

Far Cry 3 is an open-world FPS with some RPG elements. It has a decent selection of weaponry. It has fairly extensive customization for most weapons. You have the option to either run and gun or use stealth. It has a FANTASTIC villain. It has an engaging story. It is gorgeous. Most importantly, it is fun.
However, there are some things I think people should know before they go spending their money:
This game doesn't exactly have great replay value. After completing the campaign, my most extensive gameplay sessions consisted of resetting outposts and retaking them. This gets old pretty fast unfortunately, and I've never had any real urge to play through the campaign again.
Co-op and Multiplayer, while not technically bad, aren't very fun. Honestly, they feel kinda tacked-on. This game probably would have done perfectly fine with just a single-player campaign.
The thing that really shot this game down for me was the Uplay implementation. While I can deal with technical issues, my primary concern here is a slimy business tactic Ubisoft uses for Uplay, unofficially referred to as "Steam Mode". If all of your Uplay games were purchased through Steam, access to the Uplay store through the Uplay application is disabled, and many of the free games and demos/trials in the "Free Games" section are removed. In order to have these features reenabled, you have to make a purchase through Uplay. Sounds pretty slimy to me.
I would give this game a thumbs-up rating regardless of its flaws. But the decision I have to make here is whether or not I would recommend that people spend their hard-earned cash on this game. Unfortunately, I don't think the people we are paying here deserve the money, and I cannot recommend that people give their money to people who don't deserve it.

After all the glowing praises I read about this game, I was severely dissapointed in this game.  This story is like some strange young white man-child dominance fantasy.  The young directionless white male finds himself in danger,  his strong reliable older brother is killed, and now has to save all his white friends from the savages and pirates, who all happen to be non-white.  He basically becomes some kind of invincible hero killing the pirates left and right saving everyone, becoming the savior of the native tribe, all the while running through all the action hero tropes.   Not to mention his companion's backgrounds seem to be specially crafted to pump up you ego as the directionless man-child.  You have the rich investment banker who becomes a broken useless person, the rich weed smoker, and dont forget the somehow super hot, super smart girlfriend who has been bankrolling your lifestyle.  The one who you yell out with terrible dialog during her rescue and throw her to the wayside when you "find yourself" and become independent (a serial killer).  If this doesn't make you face palm, what about the really weird sex scene with the native leader.  I read that the story is supposed to be some kind of satire, but I fail to see how writing a terrible racist story and saying that it is satire somehow makes it all ok.  Not to mention at what point does it become clear that the story is satirical?  Certainly not in the 12 hours I played of it.
The dialog in this game is just terrible.  How many times do I have to hear the same stuff from every native or pirate.  Didn't they play through the game and think, "Maybe we should record a few more lines".  The story line dialog is also generally pretty bad.  All the interactions with your old companions are just awkward and just really strange sometimes.
The gameplay is not bad, although it gets repetitve.  It's pretty much a blend of deus ex and tomb raider.  You run around with stealth and kill people with a bow, but also can do those cinematic take downs like in deus ex.  Beyond that its pretty much like any other shooter.  In terms of character progression, you can pretty much unlock all the equipment unlocks you need in the beginning of the game regardless of story progression, with only the skill unlocks being held back.  This means that if u start doing side quests and stuff you end up with everything unlocked with like 7 skill pts just waiting to be used.  By this time the game just starts becoming a hassle to play.
If you want to play a serious man child fantasy this game might be for you, but don't expect depth and cultural appreciation here.

I have really enjoyed this game. Although as a role-playing game it is rather weak, the medieval combat aspects and strategy are really fun.
Pros:
- Realistic medieval combat with many different weapons to choose from, both melee and ranged.
- Hero companions that you can train and equip individually, each with their own specialisations and background.
- Troop management and command on the battlefield with individual tactics for cavalry, melee, and ranged troops.
- Siege warfare and ability to capture strongholds and cities.
- Medieval politics and backstabbing with AI Lords and your spouse.
Cons:
- Bland role-play elements and quests.
- Bland interaction with AI Lords. Although a few archetypes of lords exist, the interaction with them is not very interesting.
- Interface is dialog driven and unwieldy to use.
Beyond the basic game, there is still the ability to run mods which change some of the above Pros and Cons.

Who was your father?  Who were you as a child?  As a young adult?
The land of Calradia opens to the player first in text, as you choose the history of your indivdual character. It doesn't bother you with the messy details of names of places you don't know or care about. Just simple descriptions. Once your character is made, you are thrown into a little scene where you can get a taste of combat, then get offered a quest, and can take it or leave it plainly and adventure in your own direction. Travel takes place on a 'world map', with entire armies represented by a single unit. The game uses its tools to convey only the information the player needs to know, and leaves the details to the imagination.  Due to the scale of this game, the mediocre visual and audio experience is a sacrifice that is made up by the depth of each aspect of gameplay.
The gameplay can be divided into three main categories: Action, Managing, and Role Play.
Combat in the game is resolved on a 1:1 scale. The controls are stiff, but once you get the hang of it, they are rather satisfying.  There is an interesting system for direction of attack. Hold mouse, move it up, down, left or right to ready your attack, and release the mouse to swing your weapon!  Weapon selection is nice, where there isn't a single Ultimate Weapon. Different types of weapons have different feels.  Blocking with a shield is easier than parrying with a weapon, but parrying is an option.  The smartest decision was to allow the player to change various elements of difficulty on a slider, without any sort of consequence to any achievements or game reward. If you think it's too hard--which it seems at first--feel free to change the combat difficulty. I found the game more enjoyable once I made it easier the first time I played. I encourage this.
When you're not fighting, the first thing you're going to be thinking about is your money.  Troops require weekly wages, which increase as they get more experience and you upgrade them to be stronger.  You also need to buy food to feed them, and if you have lots of varieties of food, you get increased morale and better field performance.  Eventually you can control villages and receive taxes, or have castles and need to keep and pay garrison.  There is a trading system built on supply and demand based on region and natural resources produced by nearby villages, and what nations are at war, preventing certain trade routes.  When you begin the game, you're not burdened with financial responsibilities. The financial management element of the game never gets more complicated than you allow it to.
What this is all leading up to is the third element of gameplay, Role Playing.  This game is one of the most sincere Role Playing Games I have ever played in my life.  Conversations are presented in a language that's very clean, in first person. Rather than giving every NPC a 'personality', the game sets up a system of motives for NPCs.  What a lord or lady does takes into consideration their family, their wealth, their faction's power standing, and possibly other factors.  Conversations with NPCs are thus generated. This means that specific lines will repeat, but NPCs only say the bare minimum needed to convey their meaning, leaving player imagination filling in the gaps, making the game flow smoothly.  You build rapport with other lords and ladies of the land, and gain reputation as you adventure.  There are friends to make, alliances to be made, people to betray, kings to serve, or overthrow, enemies to shame, bandits to hunt, prisoners to sell, quests to take on, and NPC allies with personalities, histories, opinions, preferences, and motives.
And there's where it shines best. Mount & Blade: Warband is a beautiful example of a role playing game, with immeasurable play time. You can make combat as challenging or as simple as you wish, making the game more about your success, or make it a gritty narrative experience by ramping up difficulty and enemy AI.  The game is about letting the player enjoy the fantasy of being an adventurer in Calradia.
There is a multiplayer element, which is easily described as a precursor to War of the Roses.  Multiplayer is 1:1 scale combat only, and there is no native multiplayer campaign support.
The modding community is impressive, and there are a few noteworthy mods. Some improve aesthetics, some enhance gameplay, and some even tweak the setting. One of my personal favorites turns it into a fantasy game, adding mages and magic as gameplay elements.
Mount & Blade Warband is an impressively large game for its price.  I cannot recommend this game enough.

Mount and Blade: Warband is the ultimate medieval combat simulator. Set in the violent world of Calradia, Warband provides players with a veritable sandbox in which they can fight from horseback or on foot. The game has an extremely active modding community. Lead customizable armies from six factions, each with their own strengths and weaknesses and recruit larger-than-life companions to join you in your struggle for dominance. Engage in diplomacy and intrigue with lords within your own faction, lead a rebellion to secure a claimant's right to the throne, raid and pillage villages throughout the land, or carve your own independent kingdom to rule with your spouse as king or queen. The choice is yours in this highly addictive acton RPG!

This game is a great story about morality in anarchy and how desensitization to violence occurs to those exposed forcefully to it. It has justifiable violence, which is a big this for me in games. As you save your friends you start to see their human nature, and the main character loses more and more of his humanity. The voice acting and character models are perfect to display this. The plot, while simple, plays out pretty well. Mechanically, this game is a beast. There's lots of hunting and plenty of side games to keep you entertained for long enough. I enjoy the tagging mechanic, and the stealth is pretty fun. Serums add a good element of ease to gameplay. Driving's a little shaky, but it's something you get used to. The weapons are fun, but I find myself sticking to a combination of silenced weapons, though I know others would probably enjoy going loud a lot. There are lots of ruins to explore as well. Pretty worth it.

Far Cry 3 takes leaps away from Far Cry 2 in many ways. I will compare and contrast them.
Far Cry 3 Pros over Far Cry 2:
Far Cry 3 is much less glitchy and random than Far Cry 2
Stealth has been much improved upon and encouraged
Open world exploration has been expanded upon greatly
Much better graphics and model movement
Far Cry 3 multiplayer is actually alive and entertaining
Similarities:
Many guns to choose from
Great stories can come from encounters with non scripted fighting
Difficulty levels (although I would say Far Cry 3 is still much easier)
Cons of Far Cry 3:
The biggest problems I had with this game as opposed to Far cry 2 was the atmosphere and the realism
In Far Cry 2 it was believable that you were an expendable mercanary in Africa who was weak with disease. This game tries to make you believe you are a white college student who magically gains super human fighting ability through tattoos. The game frequently takes you through drug trips where you hallucinate, which I found infuriating at one point. In one of these drug trips, you kill an enemy you have been looking to kill for a good chunk of the game. Thinking it was just a dream, I assumed I hadn't actually killed him and moved on, only to find out 20 minutes later that that was the games way of letting you kill him and one of the biggest cimaxes passed over my head.
Something about the world of Far Cry 3 does not compare with the atmposphere created in Far Cry 2. Yes the world looks beautiful, but it does nothing for the atmosphere of the game, where as in Far Cry 2 you actually fealt like the places you were attacking could exist today.
Summary: Far Cry 3 is a great game for those who like FPS, RPG, and open world elements, and who can get around the slightly linear story and completely unbelievable and ridiculous advancement of the character. 8/10

As you save your friends you start to see their human nature, and the main character loses more and more of his humanity. The voice acting and character models are perfect to display this. The plot, while simple, plays out pretty well. Mechanically, this game is a beast. There's lots of hunting and plenty of side games to keep you entertained for long enough. I enjoy the tagging mechanic, and the stealth is pretty fun. Serums add a good element of ease to gameplay. Driving's a little shaky, but it's something you get used to. The weapons are fun, but I find myself sticking to a combination of silenced weapons, though I know others would probably enjoy going loud a lot. There are lots of ruins to explore as well. Pretty worth it.

Far Cry 3 takes leaps away from Far Cry 2 in many ways. I will compare and contrast them.
Far Cry 3 Pros over Far Cry 2:
Far Cry 3 is much less glitchy and random than Far Cry 2
Stealth has been much improved upon and encouraged
Open world exploration has been expanded upon greatly
Much better graphics and model movement
Far Cry 3 multiplayer is actually alive and entertaining
Similarities:
Many guns to choose from
Great stories can come from encounters with non scripted fighting
Difficulty levels (although I would say Far Cry 3 is still much easier)
Cons of Far Cry 3:
The biggest problems I had with this game as opposed to Far cry 2 was the atmosphere and the realism
In Far Cry 2 it was believable that you were an expendable mercanary in Africa who was weak with disease. This game tries to make you believe you are a white college student who magically gains super human fighting ability through tattoos. The game frequently takes you through drug trips where you hallucinate, which I found infuriating at one point. In one of these drug trips, you kill an enemy you have been looking to kill for a good chunk of the game. Thinking it was just a dream, I assumed I hadn't actually killed him and moved on, only to find out 20 minutes later that that was the games way of letting you kill him and one of the biggest cimaxes passed over my head.
Something about the world of Far Cry 3 does not compare with the atmposphere created in Far Cry 2. Yes the world looks beautiful, but it does nothing for the atmosphere of the game, where as in Far Cry 2 you actually fealt like the places you were attacking could exist today.
Summary: Far Cry 3 is a great game for those who like FPS, RPG, and open world elements, and who can get around the slightly linear story and completely unbelievable and ridiculous advancement of the character. 8/10

If anyone has played Sid Meier's Pirates! game, they will probably quicky understand what this game is largely about.
There are, of course, no pirates in this game (unless you count vikings) and you do not go sailing.  However, you do ride around, building up your army, collecting trade goods to sell to cities, and increase both your social status with various factions, as well as invade and conquer cities... or indeed whole nations.
It is by and large an Action RPG, and one that I've sunk many hours into.  It does have a few problems, but many of these problems can be or even already are, addressed by mods, for which there is a decently sized community for.
Probably the biggest problem is the slow pace of the game.  Without any mods, it can take quite a long time to build up the renown, army, and influence to start taking over villages, let alone cities or castles.  When you do though, it is quite rewarding, and the game and combat are very fun overall.
