You play Jason Brody, some rich kid from California, who goes on a trip with some friends and ends up as a hostage of the local pirates. After he barely manages to escape he is recruited by Tribals who call themselves the Rakyat, and goes on a long and erotic journey to self-discovery.
While the initial Idea is pretty good, it is not executed very well. Jason never killed anybody nor skinned an animal, but after the cut scenes end and you can finally go out and explore, you can happily murder half of the Island´s population without hearing a whimper ever again. Well, except when skinning animals; Jason never gets used to that, even though you have to kill the whole fauna twice over to craft a wallet and a rucksack. This is something Tomb Raider pulled off better.
Another problem is that the faction you are working for (and you have no choice here) is not really likeable. Even though YOU are supposed to help THEM, you rarely see them fighting the pirates. There are several occasions where, after "liberating" one of the pirate outposts, I´d hear some Rakyat proudly proclaiming: "WHO`S THE MAN?! ME!" Yeah buddy, you sure are. This goes on and on, and after a while you ask yourself why you would even help them in the first place; your goal is to rescue your friends. But because some black guy who fished you out of the river, put some tattoos on your arm and sent you to the local drug king told you to, you´ll happily oblige. BECAUSE YOU ARE A WARRIOR, JASON. AND YOU NEED DA TATAU TO BECOME STRONGER. This part of the story is just unnecessary.
The game also has an obsession with drugs; on several occasions Jason ends up getting drugged, whether willingly, by accident, or per force. These dream-like sequences may be fancy for the first time, but are outright annoying the second time around. This is the part where you can guess what Ubisoft´s Target Demographic must have been.
The Far Cry series has always been known for graphical fidelity; this one is a slight exception in my opinion. While the game DOES look good overall, there are some things that are worse than in the previous games, if not♥♥♥♥♥♥in general. I can´t understand how a game that runs essentially on the same engine as the previous game looks worse, even though they even upgraded it to the second version. When you compare the two games side by side, several things just stand out negatively: the LOD and view distance are handled way better in Far Cry 2. I have never experienced such severe pop ins like I did in Far Cry 3, especially since it uses a rather obvious effect to do so. Secondly, Far Cry 3 uses way too much SSAO, to the point where objects have black halos surrounding them. Unfortunately you can´t disable this effect in game without switching to DX9; you have to edit the config file if you want to get rid of it. Another thing I really can´t understand is a weird graphical glitch that happens when you are inside caves. Sometimes the walls appear all shiny, like somebody spent two weeks smearing oil on random cave walls.
The sound is generally pretty good, the weapons all sound quite alright. Only problem here is that all suppressed weapons use the same sound, no matter if you are using an assault rifle or a shotgun. This can be kind of annoying when you tend to use more than one suppressed weapon. But this is nothing compared to the sound quality of EVERYBODY except the main characters. Every single civilian, pirate and rebel sounds like his voice was recorded with a microphone wrapped in a plastic bag; the sound quality is just awful at times. Couple this with repetitive voice lines á la "FOCK. DIS. HEAT" or "BURNS LIKE A MOTHER WHEN I♥♥♥♥♥♥ SHOULDA USED A RUBBER." and the problem will become really obvious.
The gameplay itself is what really saves this title. The gameplay is mostly fluid, rewarding and well, fun, that you can forget most of these annoyances when you get the chance to play undisturbed for more than half an hour. It is way more fun to ambush pirates with mines, surprise them with C4 or just stab everybody with your knife than playing the main missions, which sometimes severely limit how you can approach the situation. Maybe this is why I liked the southern Island more; the whole tribal hero ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is cast aside, and there is only the mission and how you want to approach it, just like the previous games. Unfortunately the game is almost over when you reach the second island, leaving you with such a low amount of missions that I wonder why they even bothered making another island.
The weapons are fairly standard, ranging from pistols to rocket launchers. But for some reason some weapons have their attachments disabled, something which really sucks in the beginning. This is strange because all weapons HAVE attachments, which you can use in coop and multiplayer. A simple mod can unlock all attachments for the weapons, which makes me wonder why they chose to disable them in the first place.
There is also a problem with the game´s difficulty. First of all, the AI is not that great. Even though your enemies can take cover and try to flank you sometimes, they just charge towards you most of the time. Couple this with aimbot like accuracy on the higher difficulties and bugged fire that you can´t put out because the QTE prompt does not show up and you know what to expect. Because of that, a stealthy approach is easier most of the time. If you do get spotted, you can abuse the takedown system by shooting even the armored guys until they stagger, walk around them and stab them in the back to kill them instantly. Things like that make some encounters ridiculously easy.
After all I have criticized, you´d think that I don´t like this game. But here comes the funny part: I can´t deny that Far Cry 3 is a fun game. It has some major flaws and annoyances, but at least this time the gameplay is decent. Stabbing people, blowing up convoys and hunting the local fauna just has a certain charm. While it is not a bad game per se, it is not a good Far Cry. Despite this, pick it up when it is on sale, it will keep you occupied for a while.

Far Cry 3 is probably one of the best FPS's I've played in a long time. The gameplay is simply amazing, featuring some of the most fun and satisfying stealth mechanics I've seen coupled with a very solid selection of weapons and a great variety of missions. The game looks great, the tropical equivalent of Skyrim : walking in the jungle grass slowly, swimming silently towards a group of unsuspecting bandits or climbing atop a huge, rocky cliff never looked so good. You'll feel like Indiana Jones or Robinson Crusoe, fighting against the elements, hunting dangerous animals or exploring ancient tombs. The gunfights are fast-paced and rightfully chaotic, the enemies' reactions are realistic (although it's hard not to miss some things the AI did in Far Cry 2, like soldiers trying to save their wounded allies) and the game world is tons of fun to explore and conquer.
The story is the only element, in my opinion, that truly lacks polishing. Through the whole single player mode, you feel like the writers at Ubisoft tried to set up something about insanity, about the villain, Vaas, about a lot of interesting elements that they end up litterally ignoring or throwing away about halfway through. It is extremely frustrating : it's a poorly told story, yet you constantly feel like it could've actually been good if only a few elements had been changed or added. It feels like it could've been good, which is even more annoying that something that's irredeemable. The story barely makes any sense, you can't help but hate its protagonist and the game's ending feels rushed. As usual, Ubisoft is great at introducing great ideas before depriving them of all their potential, just like they made Assassin's Creed uninteresting by adding the whole storyline about the Animus and Desmond instead of focusing on the actual assassins that everyone wanted more of.
Even as a gamer that wants a good story, though, I can still recommend Far Cry 3 to just about anyone because the gameplay simply feels amazing. Any fan of FPS will love this game, especially if you're a fan of stealth mechanics. I've played through this game twice, which is something I don't do often, because Far Cry 3 offers a fantastic game world in which you can truly feel like a lone predator of the wild, an action movie hero.

I've been a big fun of this game series starting from the Far Cry 1st edition. With each new version, the game always brings much better performance, interesting plot, great adventures, new items and challenges. Far Cry 3 is the so-called "merged " version that consolidates all previous in-game experience presented in the new light. From a common shooter it keeps turning into an adventurous and exciting story which includes aspects other than fighting, such as crafting, skill set developing, trading, hunting etc.
One of the new and most notable features of Far Cry 3 is also educational component. Player keeps learning and gaining valuable information on the different types of items - weapons, transportation, wildlife, plants, etc. When you come across with a new item you get an instant message that gives you a short but yet comprehensive information on that particular item.
And still being a game of an "open world" you have many alternate options to reach your targets and complete your objectives.
The freedom to act, the freedom to enjoy, the freedom to differ and re-attempt... that is the beauty of Far Cry 3, one of the leading shooter-games in the industry. Definitely, real players will rate it high for 100% satisfaction!!!!

Beautiful graphics are just not enough to turn this game around. These are the positives: responsive controls with customizable keyboard configuration that actually works (funny that I have to call that out, but many games execute this poorly), good graphics, and a large, often interesting area to explore. If that's enough for your gaming experience, then this is the game for you. If you like multiplayer, also, this is a great setting. However...
If you want a good single-player game, unfortunately, Far Cry 3 also has these things that I have to put in the negative column: really, really annoying major and minor characters (including the main character Jason, who must be the all-time worst ever created for a shooter - bad, whiny voice acting combined with no redeeming values), an awkward game interface for controlling inventory and crafting (obviously designed entirely for clunky consoles), endless messages popping up on the screen to tell you things that you already know or don't care about, poorly executed "big game hunting" that is both cartoonish and annoying, and worst of all: every major villain must be dealt with in some kind of "alternate-reality" setting that seems to be happening in the unlit hallways at Ubisoft. Note to game designers: every time you move someone abruptly out of the game world you have been carefully creating for them for the last dozen hours, you ruin the immersive experience. Boss fight with Vaas? Lame. Boss fight with the weird Australian guy? Lame. Boss fight with Hoyt? Lame. Boss fight with the giant island demon thingy? WTF? Lame.

In Far Cry 3, players step into the shoes of Jason Brody, stranded on this mysterious tropical island. You dictate how the story unfolds, from the battles you choose to fight down to the allies or enemies you make along the way. Slash, sneak, detonate and shoot your way across the island in a world that has lost all sense of right and wrong. Beware the beauty and mystery of this unexplored paradise and live to outwit its roster of ruthless, desperate characters. You'll need more than luck to survive.

It takes away the from the nice savanna atmosphere of FarCry 2 but the deep jungles are where FarCry was meant to be played in. Despite it being constrained by modern "leaving the battlefield" restrictions, the freedom in FarCry 3 is immense. I'd recommend this to any fans of rpg shooters or sandbox shooters. Crafting gear from animals, learning a variety of melee moves, and figuring out if you like playing stealthy or shoot-out guns blazing is all upto you. This game is quite lengthy so beware of that, and you'll need a pretty good PC to run it.

Ah, what to say about this game. You play as Jason Brody and the game takes place on Rook Island. Beyond that there is an adventure of killing, hunting, and occasional drug use.
The basic premise of the game is that you, your friends, your girlfriend and your brothers are all on vacation going around and living it up. Well surprise, surprise when you get kidnapped and taken by local psycho Vaas. The game spans across a large island and smaller sub island in the later part of the game that has you trying to relocate everyone who was taken before they are killed or sold off, and enacting revenge against both Vaas and Hoyt for what they've taken from you. What stands in your way is the feral wildlife and once sane residents of the island. Vaas commands an army of crazies that terrorize the people and you join the Rakyat. The Rakyat are citizens who have had their share of Vaas and fight to have him put down and reclaim their island. A sort of red vs. blue take on it, with animals being the purple team.
The psychedelic drug trips are always interesting. Walking across a walkway of old CRT TV's while seeing things to your sides, hearing voices from the past- it all comes together to throw things into disarray. Interesting imagery and vibrant colours that pop out or draw attention make the sections very enjoyable to look at, and you will be when they limit your walking speed to a crawl, which is something I personally hate in any game, this being no different. Past this brief description I won't say much in regards to this. I feel the little drug trips were something better experienced first hand than anything else.
The game features a FPS and RPG-esque like gameplay style that blends together quite well I feel. You earn the standard EXP that you would expect to see in RPG games, and more so if you dispatch of the enemies with more finesse. Headshots give more, and special kills with the machete earn the most. This EXP is then used to give you skill points which make Jason excel in his island life. With three skills trees to choose from, varying in combat, stealth, and survival aspects, you have some choice in how you want to see your character grow; however, it is possible to get all of the skills in the game before you finish it. I got them all about 65%-70% of the way through, but I personally tried to get as much EXP as possible because it I feel it added to the challenge and fun of the game. Remaining undetected while capturing enemy outposts and chain kills with the machete and the like,so your experience may be completely different.
Rook Island is nothing if not the biggest culmination of hateful animals in gaming history. I've been attacked by more tigers, bears, sharks, alligators, leopards, and stray dogs with rabies than I fired bullets throughout my journey. I've been attacked by more tigers than I have anything else put together. I get the feeling any fear I would have of a tiger in real life is lessened because I have just gotten used to seeing them and then defending myself before they try and maul me. One word of advice I can give is to keep a shotgun handy. The best way to deal with any animal you have to hunt is a shotgun, or a bow but it is not as powerful on animals as it is humans.
The visuals of the game are fantastic. Sprawling landscapes and deep waters, claustrophobic and haunting caverns, and the great outdoors. The graphics for the game are great, it looks fantastic most of the time, odd graphical issues rear themselves every now and then, but the entirety of the visuals is grand. Deep blues for the water, lush green for the vegetation, thick blacks and bright lights to assist the atmosphere, these all combine to give a memorable experience worth taking in when they present themselves, which is common. I often found myself over looking the lands from a radio tower or cliff face  and seeing a near awe inspiring world- the sheer number of screenshots that I took of the game offer no less to the game than what I am describing. I would recommend, while playing, to just take a few moments to breathe the game in. It really is something worth looking at when the over-saturation of games with painfully crippled colour palettes have flooded and overflowed our vidya market.
To keep this incoherent and already too long review of going on any further I will wrap it up here. This game is one I highly recommend, especially considering I put in near 40 hours and beat it in less than a week, which is something I don't do at all. The visuals of the game in both the worlds presentation and the mind bending visuals of the drag addled trips through your psyche set my heart fluttering because of my deep love of anything psychological or similar. The gameplay was entertaining, offering a high integrity towards playing how you want, even going as far as covering some outposts with grass that you can then blanket in flames. The sound design, quality, and soundtrack sealed the deal together offering excellent fidelity and mood/theme fitting tracks and ambiance.
Overall, this is a game I highly recommend. Even more so when you take into consideration the game goes under $10 during large sales. What excuse is there to not pick this up and live it?

The story is terribly written in my opinion and doesnt fit at all in the far cry series. the gameplay is very repetetive, with each outpost having the same structure. it comes too predicable that even at the hardest difficulty you can easily do well at the game just using a pistol.
In the story (Both co-op and single player) it's just cliche after cliche after cliche. It happens so often that it just gets annoying and it just feels awful. You get no connection to the protagonist at all, you won't llike him, you don't even want to be him and wish he'd just jump off a cliff, break his ankles and left there for no one to be found ever. Neither do you feel connected to the world. In most games you get a sense of where you are, roads feel familiar, certain parts feel like home. In this game it is just jungle after beach after dirt road and they all just seem the same.
The story is full of spiritual nonsense that could fit in a setting centuries ago or in a different kind of world (where magic and unicorns exist), but not in the 21-st century on a tropical island where everybody has 17 guns. If you have a gun, you don't need some pretentious spiritual power to kill just another thug with a group of his guards. Honestly, the only way the game is fun is to just avoid all storyline missions, not using the map and running around blindly shooting people. Basically what Far
Cry 2 consisted of.
The co-op is kind of alright in the game. The campaign doesnt really have that much story (this doesn't really matter though, it's about shooting things with your friends). It consists of multiple chapters which can be played chronologically. It's fun to do a few times, but the problem is that all these chapters are so repetetive and contain the same things, you never get a nice surprise. The worst part is the extreme glitchiness in Co-op. Anybody has a ping over 60? Fat chance that when you respawn after everyone dies, somebody on your team will just randomly drop dead and has to wait for the next checkpoint. Or he seems to appear on top of a building, while you're standing inside it. Good luck saving him when he gets incapacitated. Furthermore it is impossible to play with 2 players, as random kicks without a visible reason happen very often. if you play it with 2, and one gets kicked, you automatically get booted because 'there aren't enough players.' Say goodbye to your progress.
All in all, get off the store page, and spend your money on a better game. But not this, don't do this to yourself.

Not for the faint hearted or those who prefer to just run into situations guns blazing.
This game is a thinking persons game. You need to plan your tactics before entering most situations. Enemies are, mostly, smart and will not stand there for you to shoot them when you are in combat. Add to this an array of weapons big and small that would have John Rambo as excited as a kid in a candy store, an RPG like element which teaches you certain skills for various situations, a stealth system that actually works, and combat that never fails to get your heart pumping, you have a mix of elements that will have you getting really involved in the world.
Tactics: You really need to plan your actions in this game. The health system is kind enough to give you a certain amount of survivability, but get caught in the middle of 10 enemies all packing big guns, and you are gonna hit the dirt faster than you can get more than a clip of shots off (and that is on easy mode). This game makes you think, and gives you options for how you take on enemies.
Enemies: These guys have their flaws. But mostly they are smart enough to run for cover, aim properly, and use tactics of their own such as attempting to flank you. They tend to hunt you relentlesly if you run away, and will only give up after you have run a certain distance.
Weapons: This game gives you an array of weapons that are quite extensive and suited to any tactics you want to use. Most of them come with modifications that will enhance their usefulness. Some weapons become free as you advance in the game.
RPG Elements: This is kept somewhat thematic by the fact you are not a trained merc or anything like that. You are a civilian. So you need to learn combat abilities as you go. It uses the idea of you being initiated into the islands tribal warrior class using tattoos that mark your advancement in various areas of combat techniques. This element strongly has you thinking of the way you want to take on your enemies from the first time you get to choose an ability.
Stealth: This relies on, mainly, cover. Cover includes the obvious, such as walls, structures, and vehicles. But it also expands to things such as trees, bushes and the like. There are a few stealth based weapons available, meaning that you can really use stealth to your advantage. And There are abilities which allow you to perform stealth takedowns.
Combat: Fast paced, explosive and violent. Combat is very well implemented. Even when in combat with small groups of enemies. You will find your adrenaline pumping and your brain working overtime.
All these elements need to be experienced to get an understanding of how good they make this game. If you want a game that makes you feel Rambo or Mclain style. This is for you.

Many people praise this game, I will be one of those who do the opposite.
Good stuff:
• It looks nice
• The fauna is quite alive
• You can stealth around, shoot at everything like crazy or mix that up as you wish
Bad stuff:
• A pretty bad skill system
• A rather dumb unlock system
• Repetitive side missions
• Nearly unresponsive flora
• Unfitting music in some situations
• Too many collectibles that are scattered around in a big world
Let's go into detail on the bad stuff (because the good stuff doesn't need any further explanation):
The skill system:
Aside from the whole "get enough XP and level up to get a skillpoint each time" thing (killing enemies in a certain way, finding collectibles, doing missions, clearing camps etc.), the skill system itself is quite unrewarding and pretty bad in general.
Things you should know from the get-go (cooking grenades and sliding into crouch mode being the best examples) have to be learned. They may be part of the tutorial, but that's two skillpoints wasted on something I can do without military training.
And then there are skills that only get available when you've reached a certain point in the story, Ninja Step (the number one stealth skill) being the best example.
I want to be a silent killer at the start, just like in Splinter Cell!
Okay, bad example, because you aren't a trained agent who has more experience in his pinky than anyone else would have in their whole life, but seriously, if this whole skill system has to be so unrealistic (I never touched an assault rifle, a skill magically makes me better at aiming and shooting with it), then let people unlock the skills they want, whenever they want.
__________________________________________________
The unlock system and repetitive side missions:
This relates to nearly everything useful in the game.
It already starts with the map. Just like in the Assassin's Creed games, you have to climb and fix radio towers to unveil the part of the map they stand in. Additionally, every time you fix one, one of several weapons gets available for free in the store. Of course you can't choose which one, so if that revolver or sniper rifle you want so badly isn't on the list, you'll have to spend your hard-earned cash on it anyway.
Why "anyway"? Because you can buy almost every weapon you want right at the start. If you have enough cash that is.
Want a sniper rifle with a cool camouflage painting, a silencer and a better scope? You better have about 2600 dollars for that, otherwise you'll have to scavenge bodies and find loot chests. Or you do some of those other repetitive missions: Drive from A to B and deliver a package with unknown contents in time, kill a bunch of enemies with predefined weapons, assassinate group leaders (WHY IS IT ALWAYS MACHETE-ONLY!?) or help out a fellow islander. Over and over again.
Of course you can skip all that if you're lazy. The magical word is "trainer".
Oh and if you want to get special weapons, for example a silenced 1911 with a laser dot scope and extended magazine (no need to buy all those, it's a prefab), then you'll HAVE to do a certain number of side missions, so yeah, there's no way around that.
The same goes for some skills. Wanna improve your bullet-proof vest? Buy 3 and invest a skillpoint. Make sure you purchased the skills that make that one available, too.
So, we have skills, weapons, the map, what else could annoy the crap out of you?
Correct: HUNTING!
For example, you can carry only 1 (in a word: ONE) weapon at the start. Wanna carry more? Hunt a specific animal, skin it and THEN you can enhance your weapon belt. Of course this requires a different animal's skin every time. Not to froget that you need more than just one, because that would be too easy and destroy the purpose of hunting pretty fast (hunting isn't that rewarding money-wise). The final upgrade always requires a unique animal's skin which you get for doing a certain hunting mission.
The bad thing here: There's a skill that doubles the outcome of skinning an animal, so instead of one tiger hide you'll get two. Why it's bad? Because you probably already got all upgrades before you can get that damn skill!
Let's end this point here before I get a heart attack.
__________________________________________________
Unresponsive flora:
If you played Far Cry 2, then you must've been amazed by the flora and its reaction to physical contact and especially fire. The grass and every bush moved away as you passed through it, tree branches broke off when bullets passed through them and when you set things on fire, you could witness "the best fire physics ever" in a video game.
They left all that out in this one.
Okay, some bushes move around when you drive through them, but that's it.
Grass, bushes and trees catch fire, but the fire dies out after about 15 seconds and leaves black grass and still green bushes and trees. Either one of the game's designers was new, totally forgot about adding that or they just didn't want to bother with it and wanted to ship the game asap instead. No matter what the reason was, the atmosphere suffers from it.
Especially when you're that Flamethrower-wielding and Molotov-throwing kind of person.
__________________________________________________
Unfitting music in some situations:
I'll make this one short.
The music isn't that great overall, but I tend to lower the music's volume in most game settings anyway, because it makes it hard to listen to dialogue sometimes.
Still, I'd rather vomit into my enemy's face instead of stabbing him when I suddenly hear some dubstep-ish music that is supposed to add some thrill or whatever.
__________________________________________________
Too many collectibles scattered around in a big world:
I'm a perfectionist. I tend to get 100% completion in the games I play. All achievements included (as long as they're doable). And I highly doubt I'm the only one who is like that.
You can't compare Far Cry 3's world to Just Cause 2's, but the lack of fast travel points (camps and towns/villages only) make this world even worse in comparison to Just Cause 2's, because that has a village, a town, a city or whatever else around every corner and behind every third tree. Not to forget that Just Cause 2 has more and faster vehicles than all Far Cry games in general.
Still, you can buy "treasure maps" which show the locations of collectibles on your main map, but that still doesn't make things easier.
"See that little island there? There's a relic (a little stone statue that grants 250 XP, there's 120 of them, aside from 20 letters and memory cards which are also scattered around).
You know you want it, so go there and get it, you freak!"
"But the nearest fast travel point is almost a kilometer away from it! Even if I drive there, I still have to find a way to get to it if it's in a hidden cave or on a hill!"
"Suck it up!"
I could ignore that stuff. I could just play the game like most people do and only collect what's on my way through the story, un-install the game as soon as the credits roll and play something else. But that doesn't change the fact that I know I haven't bothered getting 100% which wouldn't let me rest whenever I think of this game or whenever UPlay tells me that I haven't unlocked that one achievement thousands if not ten thousands of people already got. If they can do that, then why shouldn't I?
__________________________________________________
So yeah, that's it. My (supposed-to-be) little review for this oh-so-epic game of the year.
In case you're wondering, I haven't mentioned the story, because I haven't really touched that yet. It's neat so far, but maybe that'll change to the better or worse.
I'm not telling you to not buy this game, but I'm not telling you to buy it, either.
You should get the idea.

I have only played the first two Far Cry's for a few minutes, collectively, but Far Cry 3 looked like a damn fun time. I waited for the sale, picked it up, and I must say - the sale price of $7.50 is an amazing bargain for this game. The DRM is U-play, which requires you to sign up for their service and then it runs in the background while you play. Sometimes it doesn't close out, either, and inflates your hours played for Far Cry. It's not too obtrusive though, all things considered. I also have to give the game major points for having the uncanny ability to alt-tab perfectly. No artifacts, no bugs, no crashes... you can just Alt-Tab in peace.
Far Cry 3 has two very distinct dimensions to it. The gameplay, and the story; separate on purpose, because while the gameplay is incredible fun, the story is absolutely embarrassingly bad and the writers should be ashamed of the end product.
You'll have a ridiculous amount of fun with pretty much everything about the game. The guns all feel great, the driving is gritty and realistic in a great way, you can decide how to approach any situation. If you want to sneak around and silently kill enemies with takedowns and the bow, you can do it. Light the entire compound on fire and bombard them with grenades, leaving behind a burned husk? Sure! Plain old shooting? Fantastic idea! It's satisfying on all fronts. The missions are varied enough to be interesting, and there are a lot of them. The sidequests can feel lame, some of them being simple fetch quests, but the quests that force you to silently take down a commander or use a certain weapon to hunt down a wild animal are refreshing and entertaining.
The AI can also produce a lot of radiant gameplay that can lead to comedic conclusions. A few examples of things I've seen – three guys creeping through the bushes looking for me after I caused an alarm, only to get mauled by two leapords; A jeep full of speeding islanders suddenly careen off a cliff; A horde of pigs killing a lion, only to get fried by a guy with a flamethrower; A couple of enemies trying to fix their jeep only to have it explode on them (and one time another jeep crashed into a group trying to fix one); and many more.
But the story? I cannot believe that there are people being paid to produce this garbage. You'll experience pretty much every single awkward trope you can think of, from an awkward rapey creeper character to the mystical minority. It's incoherent and kind of makes no sense. The attempts at twists are hilariously bad, and the whole damn thing just drags on and on and on. You also go on a few psychedelic trips for whatever reason, and there are a couple of pot fields to burn. And dubstep. It tries to start off with something and definitely makes multiple attempts at tugging at the heart strings, but falls awkwardly short.
I vote that you just ignore the story, for all it is worth, and just enjoy the core experience of blowing things up, lighting things on fire, using vicious jungle beasts as weapons, and all that jazz.

An engrossing open-world FPS, but not without its faults.  Beautiful graphics, intense gunfights, legitimately fun (if simple) stealth gameplay, and tons of content are the good parts. The not-so-good stuff: a) the storyline tends to pound on the "You are just like the bad guys, GET IT?!" theme in the dumbest ways possible; b) the people you are supposed to care about are aggressively stupid or bland, c) your character has the worst voice actor in the game, and d) the only memorable character (Vaas, who is plastered all over the marketing) is given relatively short shrift, but perhaps that's for the best - he's the best actor in the game and more exposure might have ruined his impact. That said, my gripes pertain mainly to the story missions (the majority of which are legitimately fun and/or exciting) and aren't enough to overcome its strengths; the game is definitely worth checking out and it's the best of the Far Cry games overall (I'm lying, Blood Dragon is the best).

FarCry 3 is a great game. The scale of the map, as well as the great combat features and the graphics is in perfect balance.
Let's start with combat. FC3 has a fantastic takedown system. Some takedowns are automatic, like jumping off a ledge and killing an enemy below. Some need more skill, like doing chained takedowns. Of course, you need to unlock these takedowns.
Shooting is fluid and fun, and the satisfaction of ridding an outpost of pirates is a constant fuel to play this game.
Hunting, on the other hand, is fun at first, but there are times when you go to the designated hunting spot only to find nothing is there. This has happened to me numerous times, and even using a Hunting Syringe didn't do squat. Hunting is fun at times, but does become a chore.
As for the story, it is rather generic. A bunch of kids get captured by pirates and one of these kids, a sore loser who was going no where with his life, manages to pick up a gun for the first time in his life, and liberate the islands from the pirates, while the Rakyat (People of the Island) stood around doing nothing.
The vehicles are great fun. The driving mechanics are fantastic! Driving cars through the lush forest, or driving jetskis around hunting for sharks is fun and responsive. The gliders however, are a bit useless and are always difficult to disembark as you always lose health from doing so. \
However, I will say this now. The game lacks guns. There are not enough guns!!! The only guns you get are four or five assault rifles, four sniper rifles and so on. By the end of the game, signature weapons were the only thing I was using (along with a silenced sniper rifle)
Also, the main menu feels very clunky and weird. And I wish they had not implemented the loot rucksack in the main menu. It drives me mad, especially when you want to drop unwanted loot, but have to keep clicking it, deleting and clicking yes to delete it.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. Everything from the lush vegetation to the water is really well made and detailed. Explosions look realistic and everything in this game is amazing.
Also, I felt as if they did not use some entities as much as they should. For starters, Vaas only appears a couple of times. At the start, and somewhere halfway into the game. To me, Vaas was a great and interesting character, and they should of used him more. Same thing goes with Hoyt. After reaching the South Island, I was expecting to have a long war dance with Hoyt, only to find that his time as the main enemy is short.
But multiplayer is where this game becomes bad. FC3 multiplayer is AWFUL! It's worse than Blacklight: Retribution, it's worse than COD: Ghosts. It's just a generic, non interesting pirates vs rakyat. Coop is a massive letdown. Instead of having the ability to free roam around Rook Island with your mate, you're pitted in a semi cliche set of linear missions that involve killing tons of pirates. It's ok, and can be quite fun at times, but the worst thing is the BLOODY BOMB CARRYING MISSIONS. Throughout the campaign, there are parts which involve you picking up bombs or rockets and carrying them to certain locations. When you pick one up, you can't sprint, you can't crouch, you can't do♥♥♥♥♥♥but carry this bomb to its location. It is boring, and a chore especially when your teammate doesn't do♥♥♥♥♥♥but get downed forcing you to drop the bomb and revive them. It is instantly noticable that Ubisoft just went lazy with the Co-op. After almost an hour of playing through one of the missions, my friend discovered a unique spot where, if you keep running against it, you glitch and fall out of the world, killing yourself in the process. you can also glitch yourself inside Seto's truck by running to its spawn point just as it spawns. The Co-op maps are just poorly made, and are incredibly tedious and repetitive. They also removed the fire spreading system. In Co-op, flamethrowers held by Flamers are OP as hell. But once you have the flamethrower, it does absolutely squat. What was wrong with a free roaming coop mode? Driving around together liberating outposts and ridding the island of pirates.
That sounds far better than the crappy boring coop mode they gave us.
I usually get bored of games very quickly, but I found myself playing this game for hours on end. If you don't want to do the sometimes boring missions, you can always go around liberating outposts, exploring Rook Island and looking for Letters, Relics and so on.
Great game, fun gameplay, great combat system. Don't get this game for its multiplayer.
This is the kind of game where you turn down the in-game music, put on your favourite power songs and play. This is what I did for my second and third playthroughs, and it was amazing! Some of the songs I listened to are forever associated with my killing of pirates! Great experience, one that I won't likely ever forget.

"Welcome to the island,".....well, thanks but when the hell can I get off?
Unfortunately Far Cry 3 is just as mediocre as Far Cry 2. The vast majority of your time will be spent running around the island hunting collectables, clearing the same generic outposts or doing the same hunting/killing missions over and over again. The main story (CAUTION SPOILERS AHEAD), which shoots itself in the foot immediately entertainment-wise, is quite short overall and leaves you feeling unfulfilled.
You play as Jason Brody, an average American who skydives onto an island full of slavers and is of course the chosen one for a group of native warrior tribesmen. Intially you are captured and your brother shot and killed immediately. This removes any form of future shock value as well as -any- reason to be attached to any of the friends who were captured on the island with you. After you escape you are thrust into the arms of the local villagers who hail you as the chosen one come to save them. Thankfully they have the power of giving you magical tattoos which give you superhuman warrior powers which try to explain how you are suddenly a master marksman, hunter, survivalist, demolitions expert and so-on.
Having seen this game hyped up from various sources and reddit I expected there to at least be one memorable character. Vaas. The downside is that he really isn't memorable at all. Like with all boss encounters in this game you actually defeat him in a short QTE (Quick Time Event) and that's that onto the next link in the command chain.
The story isn't the only thing wrong unfortunately. DRM in the form of U-Play has kept a huge amount of people from purchasing, graphical glitches are abundant, the audio is poor at best and vocals can't be heard at times during cutscenes.
Would I recommend this? No, not at all. Not even on sale.
If you want a good Far Cry title, stick to the first in the series.

A Study in Missed Opportunity, Plagued By Bizarre Design Choices
First, let me start out by saying that FarCry 3 is a fun game.  It's a very cool, original concept that's well-implemented, and right from the very first scene, it's filled with heart-pounding action that does a very good job of making you feel like a normal guy thrown into an extraordinary situation.  It's a sandbox-style game, with an absolutely enormous map that's gorgeously rendered, thoughtfully designed, and a lot of fun to explore.
But there are a few design choices that are just absolutely baffling, and really inexcusable in a PC game from a major, experienced developer that's been around for well over a decade.
For example, there is only one volume slider in the audio menu.  You can turn the music on or off, and subtitles on or off, that's it.  Why!?  In every game I ever play, I adjust dialog volumes up a little, and sound effects and music down a bit (actually this is default in most games), so I can clearly hear the dialog.  This isn't a 'cheat', it just makes it so I can hear what's being said no matter what else is going on.  In Far Cry 3 on the other hand, there have been times when an important phone conversation has been completely drowned out by a combination of music and a thunderstorm.  Just bizarre.
Also for some reason, you can't use both mouse and keyboard, and controller, at the same time.  Enabling one completely disables the other.  The controller setup is reasonably well-implemented, but there are times I really wish I could use the mouse to aim for more precision.
A smaller gripe is that if you alt-tab out of this game, it reverts to Windowed mode, so each time you do so, you have to go back into the menus and turn it back to full-screen.  This by itself wouldn't be a bizarre choice, except that if you're playing on controller (which you pretty much have to -- vehicles are completely uncontrollable by keyboard), your mouse is still disabled any time it goes over the game screen (which by default fills the entire window).
Now, let's talk about missed opportunities...
This is a sandbox shooter with as much land mass area as any Bethesda game, and with a story that's deep enough to make it compare favorably with RPGs, despite the fact that the player doesn't really have any choices other than when to advance the main plot.  Because of its depth, and the level of immersion it almost manages to achieve, I can't help but wonder why certain features weren't implemented, even optionally, that would complete the immersion.
For example, throughout the game, you hunt and kill an amazing variety of wildlife, all of which is very well implemented, with a living biome that feels very real.  Tigers hunt prey animals, prey animals run from predators, and the resulting chases soon blend the spawns into a very pleasingly realistic and diverse biosphere.  There are camps dotting the islands, with campfires in most of them and beds in all of them.  There is already a crafting system built into the game.  It's the -perfect- opportunity to introduce basic survival simulation, like hunger and thirst and the need for sleep.
It would make hunting an even more central part of the game, as you'd have to hunt to survive.  It would also be more pleasing to me, to actually utilize the animals I kill.  Instead, just like the rich prick the main character started out as, he kills them for their skins, to craft pouches and slings and holsters, nothing more.  Why would they not also have him take the meat?  They even have stores all over the islands with signs begging for meat, offering money for meat, even listing prices paid for various types of game animals.  Even if they couldn't afford the extra development costs to implement a basic needs system like in Fallout: New Vegas, it would have taken almost no extra effort to just add the animal's meat to your rucksack in addition to its skin, so you could at least sell it for other people to eat, instead of slaughtering every animal you see just for its fur in a morally troublesome manner.
Also, there was a great opportunity for character development, that I feel was almost entirely missed.  Jason Brody starts out as a whiny, entitled, self-important little brat, living off of daddy's money as he vacations in an exotic locale with his friends.  After weeks basically alone, fending for himself in a dangerous tropical archipelago, hunting down pirates, learning advanced combat and stealth techniques and guerilla tactics, and getting himself entangled in a complex struggle between pirates and the native Rakyat tribe, the Jason Brody I play most of the time is a badass.  He's self-sufficient, he shows no fear, he carefully crafts battle plans to take out entire outposts of well-armed enemies without even being detected.  If he is detected, he keeps his cool and uses hit and run tactics to whittle the enemy forces down one man at a time, until he's victorious.  He's like a Navy SEAL on crack.
And then he speaks....
And he's the sams god-forsaken whiny little self-entitled brat, making the same completely idiotic choices time after time after time... (how many times does he have to shout at the top of his lungs while sneaking into an enemy stronghold, so his friends, after week of captivity, won't have to go twenty more seconds without realizing they're being rescued, before he realizes that's NOT A GOOD IDEA!?)  In short, the silent killer I play 95% of the time has developed from a kid who barely knows which end of the gun to point at the enemy to a total badass.  They do a -great- job of communicating his inexperience and helplessness at the start of the game, and the progression from that to uber-badass feels smooth and intuitive.  But the character the developers wrote and voice-acted remains unchanged, completely static and basically unaffected and unenlightened by his experiences as a guerilla warrior.
There are other issues with this game, a huge number if missed opportunities, and a lot of points where it's clear there just is a lack of attention to detail (one skill for example, lets you move at full speed while crouched.  Your perspective and your held weapon jostle and move rapidly, as if you're doing just what the skill says: Jungle Run.  But they forgot to change the foley!  Your footsteps remain the same slow, measured pace they always were when sneaking.  I mean... was someone in the audio department asleep that day?)
All of that being said, if you're willing to put up with a lot of annoyances, it's still a fun game, and worth playing.  I wouldn't have taken the time to write this, and I wouldn't be so disappointed in its shortcomings, if there weren't a fantastic game lurking behind its issues.  In the end analysis, I do recommend this game, but cautiously.  If you're a member of its target audience, grab it if you already haven't.  If you're the kind of gamer who plays Hardcore New Vegas on the other hand, a roleplayer looking for true, total immersion?  It could do a lot better.
And seriously Ubisoft... the gaming industry in general figured out that more player choice in terms of volume controls and control configurations is better in like... 1993.  Get your act together, guys!

Far Cry 3 is a decent enough game. It has its flaws, such as an unlikeable and unrelateable protagonist. It's supposedly set on an island in the Pacific, but instead of having its own identity, it feels more like a mash-up of touring a pirate/mercenary-ridden Hawaii with New Zealanders, South Africans and Australians.
The combat is well done and the main characters are memorable. The level-up system works well too. The voice acting is good but some NPC's get annoying after a while. I played in 1920×1080 and the graphics looked fine; I only had one instance of a graphic bug in 35+ hours of play.
One game play issue with using a game pad (I used X360) was the "hold X to do something" such as loot body, swap weapon, enter vehicle or enter door; all mapped to the same button -  which became frustrating during moments when I couldn't stop to see which option "hold X" would do. 
To me, tap X to loot or enter door, hold X to swap weapon or enter vehicle and remap reload to something like tap Y, and then hold Y to heal would have been better.
Overall an enjoying experience.
Requires Ubisoft's Uplay too so be prepared to deal with that.

TL;DR- Far Cry 3 manages to improve on its predecessor without abandoning most of its basic mechanics. Does have a ridiculous plot that is terribly handled at the end.
I had a love/hate relationship with Far Cry 2. I loved the weapons, the world, and the combat. But I hated the way the place was populated only by people who wanted to kill you on sight (except for in the closed cities). I didn't like the way enemies respawned automatically and the beautiful world was somewhat marred when I couldn't enjoy a senic boat ride without getting sniper fire, even though I'd crushed that outpost five minutes earlier. Unlocking weapons tended to be a bit tedious as well, though it was worth it to get some of the best ones. The mortar in FC2 is one of my favorite weapons in ANY game. It took patience to figure out, but once mastered it could be used to desolate an enemy encampment in dramatic fashion.
FC3 keeps the nice variety of weapons, with the facepalming exception of the above-mentioned mortar. I guess it was unbalancing because of how useful it could be against outposts, but I still wish they had left it in somewhere. Vehicles are still fun, as are boats, plus handgliding is actually a bit more doable in this game- even useful when the game doesn't cheat and turn on the invisible walls for missions. Best of all, not everyone is out to kill you at all times. There are different factions in the game and only MOST want to kill you at any one time! You can actually see battles between the different factions where you can help one over the other. When you take out an enemy outpost, it stays down... unless you decide to revert them back to enemy control so you can have fun blowing them up again- a neat option by the devs to placate both sides of the 'respawning enemies' argument. Plus they've added carnivors. If you remember in FC2 they made some kind of hand-waving statement that they couldn't do that because it would wreck the simulation... or something. Well this time they said "screw it, add more tigers!" Bravo.
There are a lot of gimmicks in the game. You can blow open the cages of conveniently placed animals to screw with enemies, use hand-gliders or zip lines that just happen to be near enemy outposts, or... all sorts of other stuff that sometimes gets a little old. But there's enough variety that the fun makes up for the head-scratching about why the redshirts don't learn not to leave a man-eating tiger around the middle of their base. There are plenty of unscripted surprises (the first time a croc tries to eat you, for example... happens to everyone) and the whole thing is just a fun romp. The plot... well, I don't really care much about the plot. They botched it a bit by having the sub-enemy be more interesting than anyone else in the game, and there's a lot of trippy psycadelic fight scenes. The free-form part of the game is the draw. There are some RPG elements that really don't need to be there and don't serve much purpose, other than to seemingly check off a box on the list of things every game is supposed to have... but it's not a big deal.
Also a shame is the lack of a day-night cycle as in FC2. It worked so nicely and could have been used to great effect here with easier stealth at night and movement by day, or some other trade-off mechanic. Much of the plot is also nonsensical and a QTE torture scene is so hamfisted I had to roll my eyes when the protagonist looks at his hands afterwards. The whole plotlineis a contrived piece of garbage that could have been solved by your character or his combat-knife equipped buddy just killing the Big Bad who is sitting three feet away and jumping out a window... the same kind of thing you can do at every other part of the game that isn't a cutscene. But instead you have to wait until another QTE-ridden dream sequence... or something... to finish him off. Then have an awful on-rails sequence that, again, makes no sense and seems to be there just to annoy the player. Oh, and combine that with an escort mission. And the escorted person is a moron who seems to purposely get you shot down.
The plot is a necessary evil. The way its handled is... well, an unnecesary evil. Frankly the entire last mission arc is crap. But FC3's island is worth the price of admission... maybe be smarter than I was and just ignore everything after the second island gets unlocked, plot-wise.

This game is rather awesome. I was skeptical when it first came out becuase it appeared to be "just another shooter" with an adventure feel. I have already put nearly 30 hours (27 as I type this), and I have less than 10 of the story missions complete. I have less than a quarter of the map discovered. This game has EVERYTHING any gamer could want. Don't like shoot-em-up games with an annoying fast pace? Equip and customize the bow to your liking and use stealth to defeat your enemies! A fan of huge explosions and action-packed gun blasting? Equip one of the "big boy" guns like the flamethrower or RPG and roll up on your enemies' front door in a (relatively) military grade vehicle! You are playing as Jason Brody, after a vacation goes wrong, you try to save your kidnapped friends from pirates and escape from the island. While the island itself is huge, it does not offer you much variety if it comes to locations however it is graphically stunning and feels alive, populated by various animals, nothing is comparable if you hear a tiger roaring behind your back. Gameplay wise the game is very good if compared ot other shooters, you are given the choice how to approach the threats you encounter wheather doing it the sneaky way or the more direct one. The story itself is rather simple, yet it feels believable and the characters are amazingly executed, I'm refering to Vaas at this point. Also the soundtrack is beautiful, all in all the game is fantastic and is truly a worthy purchase if you ask me.
Also some people may advise you to stay away from this game since it has 2 layers of DRM, one being Uplay, speaking from my own experience I had no difficulties at all. Similar to Origin or GFWL you register the key and just keep it logging you in automatically.

I have mixed feelings about Far Cry 3:
The good:
1. Great world environment.  The jungle, water, caves, underground bunkers, ancient temples all look beatiful.
2. Hunting is fun and exciting.
3. Open world to explore.  I'm a fan of open world games :)
4. Good selection of skills and weapons.
5. A lot of side quests and collectibles.
The mediocre:
1. Building textures look pretty bad.
2. This game is very taxing on PC's.  It's the only game where my FPS drops to the 30's here and there.
3. Hunting becomes completely obsolete after you acquire certain upgrades, which can be very early depending on how you play.
4. Save system absolutely sucks.  You can lose a lot of progress if you forget to "save" by buying or selling an item in a store.
5. Most of the side quests are unneccesary.  I only did the supply runs, hunter quests, and the trials of the rakyat.  I still managed to get all the money and experience for all skills.
6. Animals and humans don't look that great.  Except the main characters during cut-scenes.
7. Taking over outposts is fun... for a while.  Once you see one, you've seen them all.
8. Some folks criticize the main story, and it's nothing we haven't seen before.  I don't expect much out of the story in a FPS anyways.  I mean, this isn't Mass Effect.  Both endings are kind of crappy I must say.
Overall it's a good, fun game.  But for all the hype it got, I expected a little more depth and less repetitiveness.  It's very similar to Just Cause 2, but with added hunting and stealth.  A good experience while it lasts, but I wouldn't play through it multiple times.
*EDIT: If you want to read up on the game or on whether to get the game or not, don't bother with the Steam forums.  All you'll read are posts about how bad Uplay is.  Uplay runs fine on my end, in games including FC 3, Blood Dragon, and Assassin's Creed 2/Brotherhood/Revelations*

TL;DR Edition: Great free roam game, lots of content, great graphics, decent story, great gameplay, decent realism, and decent AI.
When to buy: If you absolutely want this game and you're not willing to wait, then buy it. It's worth every penny. If you have time, wait for a steam sale and pick it up for 75% off.
The More In-Depth Review:
This is an absolutely amazing free roam experience.
Most people did not like Far Cry 2 because it was boring, and it was boring to those people because it was trying to be too realistic and it was repetitive. Despite that, I still loved Far Cry 2, and this game really just takes what Far Cry 2 had, and made it better in almost every aspect.
No more having to find a bus station in order to fast travel. No more running out of breath from running 15 meters. No more having to fight the mercenary island dwellers at any and every last turn, even when you just cleared the area out 5 minutes ago. Last but not least, your weapons will not wear out after having shot 3-4 mags worth of bullets.
I'm not trying to be for the whole "Needs less realism pls" thing though. I do think the game is rediculous in regards to skill upgrades and "super-power" herbs which I never use (except for the healing one ofcourse). Then there are missions where things just auto explode when you shoot at them, guess they had to cater to the CoD Kiddies.
The story is far better than what Far Cry 2 had aswell, and the main missions are far less repetitive. However, side missions such as those listed on the bulletin board are practically copy-pastas. Also, the ending(s) to Far Cry 3 are terrible In my honest  opinion, feels like they rushed it, which I suppose isn't a problem considering the amount of content in this game.
Speaking of that, after having 21 hours played on SinglePlayer alone. I have beaten the main story and have done various things around the island. Still, I am just a bit pasted 50% completion. Oh sure that doesn't mean too much, but the time you put into 100% completion, jumping on coop and completing all the missions for that, and playing multiplayer. You could easily clock around 50 hours out of this game, which would be 60 cents per hour played. Even moreso if the multiplayer is decent (I'm not sure since I have yet to try it).
Now I'd like to talk about the thing that shouldn't ever be a factor in deciding how good a game is.
Graphics and physics.
It's been awhile since I've played Far Cry 2, but 3 definitely has better graphics in every aspect. A couple of turn offs though would be running into extremely low res textures in various parts of the island(s), another thing is that Far Cry 2 had MUCH better physics. Grass, plants, and alot of trees would react to you shooting them, running into them, or driving over them. In Far Cry 3, most plants, grass, and trees are completely static. I even did some google searching and it turns out Far Cry 2 had better physics in even more aspects than that. Then I found the reasoning behind this, Far Cry 2 has Nvidia Physx on at all times, even with AMD cards. They probably didn't implement it because the game is already graphic intensive enough as it is. Running everything maxed without AA and I'm getting anywhere from 30-45 FPS, Which is actually very playable, unlike other games such as Battlefield or Counter Strike.
Lastly, the AI in singleplayer could have been better. They like to not be able to see you until you're practically in front of them. When you fire a gun without a silencer though (sometimes even with a silencer) they will be able to see you practically across the island if need be. Then you'll occassionally see them drive off a bridge or cliff. I consider these issues minimal though since in a way it increases the fun factor (seriously, why even bother playing sneaky-beaky like when they already spot you as you come over a hill?).
An enjoyable experiance but, lacks a story and direction near the end.

I would give this game a solid 8 out of 10.
Here's some pros & cons and then I'll talk about each of them.
+ Storyline
+ Environment
+ Graphics
+ Collectibles/Stuff to do
+ Animals
+ Characters
+ Soundtrack
+ Achievements
+/- Gameplay
+/- Missions
- Weapons
- Ubisoft
Short info
Storyline: The storyline is one of the best I've experienced. It flows great and is very interesting. The concept isn't very original but still I think it was an amazing storyline.
Environment: You are at 2 tropical islands that look gorgeous. Hidden caves with old chinese temples inside them can be found too and everything looks pretty.
Graphics: The graphics are really good and impressive since it's such a big world.
Collectibles: After the story there's still a lot to do which will prevent you from getting tired of the game.
Animals: I really like how there's so many different animals. You always have to be on your guard and the animals look fantastic. You can see how animals attack other animals or guards passing by making it realistic.
Characters: The characters are extremely well made, you will feel sorry for them and hope for their best. There's a lot of talk about Vaas but I expected a lot more. To be honest you don't see him too often and I don't understand the buzz around him. He was great the times you saw him but I think people overreacted.
Soundtrack: The soundtrack is amazing. Fitting songs in fitting moments and good choices for the game. Check out the main theme for Far Cry, it's the best IMO.
Achievements: If you're a achievement hunter like me you will love this game since it's really easy to collect them all.
Gameplay: The gameplay is quite repetetive and can be annoying at times.
Missions: The missions are like GTA, all the time you're on your own and have to fight masses of enemies. This is probably something most people like but I like a mixed campaign where you have to do stuff without killing all the time.
Weapons: Weapons are a minus to me. I think they're horrible to use in fact. I don't know why but the weapons feel annoying, slow and just dreadful to shoot with. They also seem very weak and I have a good shot.
Ubisoft: I hate the fact that you need to have the Ubisoft thing instead of that it's bound to Steam. Achievements go there and I have no passion for collecting achievements on there.

(NOTE:  This is a review ONLY of the single-player aspect of the game, though many aspects apply to the multi-player game.)
Far Cry 3 is like a beautiful painting--into which someone has slashed repeatedly with a jagged knife.
Like the previous installments in this series, in FC3, Ubisoft has created a truly majestic open world.  Epic in its breadth and scope, and breathtaking in its richly detailed scenery and landscapes.  It is a world that truly comes alive around you, with interactive wildlife, the cries and clamor of distant battles, and villagers actively going about their daily lives.  Simply wandering around the landscape is a wonder to behold.
Yet, as the aforementioned painting, this beautiful scenery is fatally marred by the heinous gashes in its canvas.  And, sadly, they are not merely defects in the painting, but deliberate wounds, inflicted by the develops for insane reasons only understood by them and the gods above.
The storyline?  It goes something like this.  You are a young, spoiled rich kid who falls prey to terrible circumstances, leaving you to fight for your life on a hostile deserted island.  Yet you quickly become a fearsome warrior, gunning and knifing your way through foes like a scythe through a field of grain.  But does anybody care?  No.  Even after you've slaughtered hundreds of seasoned warriors--often with nothing more than a big knife, faced off against wild tigers, and wrestled sharks to death, everyone you meet treats you like an impudent child.  And for some unfathomable reason, you just take it.  A man threatens one of your friends?  Rather than putting the guy's fingers through a meat grinder and forcing him to eat them, you decide to become his errand boy, sucking up to him while you run all over the island doing his dirty work.  The crazy bad guy who's about as dumb as a box of rocks?  He somehow keeps capturing you and torturing you, no matter what you try to do.  You have the opportunity to simply kill the head bad guy and end all of your problems with a simple knife thrust.  Instead, you engage in some ridiculously convoluted and dangerous plan, then let him capture and torture you.  And I won't even get started about the ending, which is, to put it simply and mildly, just plain dumb.  This isn't the story of a hero.  This is the story of some pathetic sap who keeps getting the crap beat out of him.  And for some reason, the developers at Ubisoft decided that would be fun to play.
Fortunately though the main storyline is an epic failure, the many sub-adventures offer some redemption.  You can conquer enemy bases, hunt wild game, delve into ancient ruins, dive for sunken treasure, participate in tournaments, or even sit down to a relaxing game of Texas Hold 'Em.  These side quests, rather than the main story, are what help to make the game somewhat fun and interesting.
The mechanics of the game have as much bad as good.  You can sneak around, using cover and ambush, or you can snipe at your foes from a distance, or you can simply charge in with guns and grenades.  The variety of tactics, weapons, and equipment is impressive and allows for very varied gameplay.  Yet, at the same time, things are absurdly awkward.  The inventiry screens and menus are unnecessarily difficult to navigate.  You can carry 15 tiger pelts, but you can't carry another 20 bullets.  You can unload an AK-47 into a tiger's head, without it even flinching, but it can kill you easily with a single swipe of a paw.  You can drive a wide variety of vehiles, but they all handle worse than a beat-up Model T with 2 flat tires.  And this is what I mean by slashes in the painting's canvas.  These aren't bugs in the programming--the developers deliberately chose to put these ridiculous things in the game.  And like the painting, for as much as you can enjoy the beauty in it, you are continually frustrated by the sight of those deliberate and unnecessary slashes in the beautiful artwork.
And you'll be frustrated by dying.  Many times.  Often for reasons completely unknown.  No matter what your skills, weapons, or preparation, you will die.  You'll fall off cliffs.  Animals will pounce on you from hiding and kill you in an instant.  You'll die because you didn't know you were supposed to press a particular key, until the game told you to, but then you had only a fraction of a second to do so.  You'll just be walking through the jungle and die, without knowing what killed you.  And though death does not end the game, it does often mean that you'll have to re-do the same things, over and over again.  And, apparently, the game developers thought that would be fun.
Another annoying slash in the canvas is that the game can quickly become pointless and boring, especially if you re-play it.  There are long, drawn-out cutscenes you cannot simply skip.  There are also some of those quasi-interactive cutscenes, where you're prompted to press a particular key, but you're not really making any choices--you either press the keys, when prompted, or you fail.  And unless you race straight through the main adventure and skip the side quests, you'll quickly learn all of the skills you can possibly learn, and you'll have more money than you can spend, so there really is very little motivation to keep doing anything.  It's like the developers created this massive world, for you to explore, but then made it pointless and boring to bother exploring it.
And so, like the damaged painting, Far Cry 3 can be beautiful and fun--but it can also be unnecessarily frustrating and aggravating.  I wouldn't have payed full price for it--but for the ten bucks I paid on sale, I'm sure I got more than my money's worth of fun out of it.
One final note.  The game includes multiple inferences to homosexual domination and sadism.  Since none of it was really integral to the story, I have to assume this is just the result of the type of people who work for Ubisoft.  I think that a game should be entertaining and enjoyable, and regardless of one's sexual orientation or tolerance or kinks, gay♥♥♥♥♥♥is not entertaining, and I feel it is inappropriate and will be offensive to some people.

I'm a little far behind on the times, but I made good use of 10 bucks this earlier this week to buy the discounted deluxe edition of Far Cry 3 while it was on the awesome Steam sale. I'll be upfront, I never played any of the Far Cry series before. Most of my FPS experience came from Halo, COD, Bioshock, Borderlands, pretty much most mainstream FPS titles.
I had read the reviews and saw about everyone saying the same thing: "this map is huge" ... and that's no lie. I've put 25 hours into this game already and I have less than half of the map exposed. Let alone grabbing the trinkets that lie along the way.
This game has a feel from some of the bigger games on the market. There are towers to open parts of the map, much like what was in Assassin's Creed. The map is massively open world, something that could be seen in the newest GTA. The side quests are never ending, and there's an element of Mass Effect for you. You're not limited to two weapons and 4 grenades like is seen in Halo, which is welcome.
But what may be the coolest part of it all is how much it operates like something you may expect in a jungle. Items are crafted by hunting in the jungles. Animals behave like wild animals. Bears hunt deer, wild dogs attack, buffalo rampage, and even birds can be shot down. Experience is gained and perks are awarded the more you gain experience. But while the map is massive (and I mean, it is MASSIVE), it doesn't feel like it oversteps itself. The world blends in very nicely, graphic detail is spot on. One of my favorite perks is seeing cars and people move around on the map, regardless of where I am. I could be on a mountain on one side of the island, look through my sniper scope, and see action happening on the other side. It gives it a more lifelike feel, something that's tremendously well done in my opinion. There's no more of that annoying, slgith blip that you would find when a car or a person loads on the map on the other side of the door. It's already there.
This is a game that you could easily launch 60, even 80+ hours in and still never finish it. But each item that you pick up (these could be relic, letters, etc) you gain additional experience, so while it's nice to have that 100% completion at the end of the game, you constantly are gaining experience and getting strong for each thing that you do. In fact, the only thing you won't gain experience from is walking or driving around. Shooting a simple deer gives you XP.
Beyond that, there are also outposts in the map that you can take over from the pirates and give back to the native people.
While I'm nowhere near beating this game, I haven't been so drawn into a game in I'm not sure how long. It certainly is a game worth getting, whether you've played the series before or not. It's a fantastic FPS game, with great storylines and great acting as well.

Far Cry 3 is an interesting return to form for Ubisoft.
What is it? Well it's adventure to put it bluntly, and it seems like they geared the whole game around it. Adventure, action, survival. It's plot bares very interesting similarities to 19th century adventure stories like Treasure Island, with the protagonist having to face pirates and psychologically grow stronger as a character.
In terms of gameplay the game is fundamentally very similar to Far Cry 2, but at the same time very different. The plot structure is more cinematic and focused on story. Adding to that, animals are much more heavily focused upon. The game introduces a crafting system and inorder to carry more guns and ammunition you must skin specific animals. This actually makes the game very interesting with how you hunt animals in the overworld and breaks up the monotony of killing pirates fairly effectively.
That's not to say the game is without flaws. While the protagonist is portrayed as an everyman, even on the hardest difficulty you are death incarnate outside of cutscenes. Adding to that the game's sidequests are more or less just "Kill this particular enemy with a specific weapon" or "find this particular animal".
Ubisoft designed the world very effectively. Overall it's kill pirates, get money, ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥es. Not necessarily in that order.

The best way I can sum up Far Cry 3 is Skyrim, but with guns. Well okay, it's not quite as deep, with only a basic crafting system and a single layer of plot, but what Far Cry lacks in depth it makes up more than enough with its fast action, dynamic missions, and luscious graphics.
Set on a chain of islands in somewhere in the south Pacific ocean, Far Cry places you in the shoes of a thrill-seeking vacationer who must rise to the challenge of rescuing his friends and overcoming the local drug smugglers embedded in the area. You've got an ever-growing arsenal of weapons, whatever vehicle you can jump inside of, and a variety of items to upgrade as you wage war across the islands. The views are beautiful and the locals (and wildlife) are deadly.
The sense of scale in Far Cry 3 is incredible. Virtually every part of the landscape you can see -and there's a lot of it - is somewhere you can go. Cars, boats, hangliders and more are scattered throughout, and there are pockets of enemies and roaming packs of animals waiting for you everywhere.
The real targets, aside from the game's primary mission, are the small bases where enemies conduct business, and each is different in its design and position in the landscape. You can run in guns blazing or sneak through, sabotaging traps and disabling enemies one at a time - it's up to you.
I enjoyed the story of Far Cry 3, which is slightly predictable, but still has its share of twists. My favorite part of the game was exploring the islands and taking out the enemy bases.
Normally with this type of game, I get tired of the tedium and eventually quit, but this wasn't the case with Far Cry 3 - I stuck it out and finished it, and was sad when it was over. With a ton of hidden locations and hard-to-find collectibles though, it's easy to find more to do.
My only complaint about Far Cry 3 is that it requires uPlay to be installed and started up when launched. I'd prefer that games I buy through Steam only have one launcher. But that's just me.

The sandbox world has just about everything you could ask for. The only thing I can think of that is missing is an actual volcano, otherwise the two islands that make up this game's playable area are everything you'd expect on a tropical island. The addition of wildlife in this game adds such an aspect of realism, I found myself stalking a tiger just to watch him take down a deer or goat. This addition also adds a new type of terror/suspense to the game. There is nothing like quickly trying to escape a firefight that you plundered into, running through the jungle and finally escaping your assailants, just to be mauled and pummeled by a tiger. While the resilience and toughness of some of the animals detracts from realism, it certainly adds to the anxiety.
The firefights, especially towards the beginning are very intense. Until you unlock enough of the "skills" to boost your health bars and make body armor more effective, only a couple of bullets will drop you on the intermediate setting. However this is followed by most of the enemies being easily eliminated by a small string of fire to center mass. What is different for this game is the implementation of cover. While the system is a little rough around the edges, it does allow you to hide behind cover and then peek out and fire rounds off at hostiles.
The challenge in this game comes mostly from the improved use of enemy AI. While they are still not brilliant, they do notice sounds and are spooked by finding their buddy lying dead on the ground. The enemy itself will work together to suppress and kill you, as well as take cover to hide from your fire. The confrontations with some of the islands predators is also challenging, as well as occasionally terrifying, though the idea of a shark attack bothers me anyways. The enemies are also specialized, making some of them quite difficult to kill and makes plotting strikes against enemy establishments require careful and thorough planning.
The game overall is worth every penny just for the single player. The addition to weapon customizations and the improved system controls, should also make this an interesting and likely worthy multiplayer. This game has a few small quirks, and no one should expect a Shakespeare story, but you should expect hours of thrills and plenty of enjoyment.

Now, the not so good things about this game: It can be very short if you just do the story. It's not very difficult, even at the highest difficutly. It's a very resource demanding game. You eventually get all the unlockable skills through leveling, as opposed to choosing one tree or specialist branch, you just get everything and become an over powered being at later parts in the game. The difficulty doesn't ramp up to match your powers, it doesn't throw anything new at you to make you think.
If you are looking for a game that is good looking, has a fun combat system, and aren't looking for multiplayer or anything super difficult, this game will be right up your alley. Multiplayer isn't horrible, but it's pretty dismal. I only played it when it first came out, so I cannot comment on the online population these days.
